Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Timor-Leste president says stalled gas project 'finally happening'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Timor-Leste president says country to sign Greater Sunrise gas agreements within months Jose Ramos-Horta says the Greater Sunrise gas project is "finally happening" after years of "deadlock". ( ABC News: Warwick Ford ) Timor-Leste President José Ramos-Horta has declared that his country will sign the first agreements for the long-stalled Greater Sunrise gas project early next year, as the South-East Asian country pushes on with the hugely ambitious and contentious development. But there is still widespread scepticism in the sector about the commercial viability of Timor-Leste's plan to pipe gas from the Greater Sunrise fields to the country's south coast, where the government hopes to develop a multi-billion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant and domestic gas facility. Timor-Leste says that will generate badly needed jobs and economic activity in the country, but the project has been beset with delays, disagreements and doubts. In November last year the Australian energy giant Woodside Energy, which holds a stake in the venture along with Timor-Leste's state-owned oil and gas company, struck an agreement to "mature and progress" the plan. The Greater Sunrise gas project was meant to transform Timor-Leste and bring billions in revenue, but locals are still waiting for the jobs and opportunities that were promised. And Mr Ramos-Horta told the ABC in Sydney that Greater Sunrise was now "finally happening" after "years and years of procrastination [and] deadlock". "I was told by Prime Minister Xanana [Gusmao] that he's confident that within the next few months they will sign the agreement, [that] we will finalise the three main documents," he said. Those three documents will help Australia, Timor-Leste and Woodside establish the regulatory and fiscal settings needed for the exploration and development of resources in Greater Sunrise. Mr Ramos-Horta's government previously said the parties reached technical agreement in Canberra on three documents: the Petroleum Mining Code, Production Sharing Contract and fiscal regime. But analysts, as well as government and industry sources, all caution that there is still no guarantee that Timor-Leste and Woodside will strike a commercial agreement on a development plan, and that any final investment decision is likely years away. Woodside and Timor-Leste's government said last year that the first LNG from Greater Sunrise may be produced "as early as 2032-2035, subject to concept selection and investment decisions". One-third of the Greater Sunrise project is owned by Australia's Woodside. ( ABC News: Margaret Burin ) Last month, Timor's petroleum minister pushed the production start date back to 2034-2035, saying the country hoped for a final investment decision by 2029. Mr Ramos-Horta said the regulatory agreements should be signed early next year after being checked and approved by both governments and Woodside. He struck a bullish tone, suggesting it was a significant moment for the project. "We cannot wait much longer. We have to do it now," he said. "Now is the time, is the opportunity." An airport built in anticipation of the gas project opened almost a decade ago, but it has hardly been used. ( ABC News: Nick Sas ) The issue is urgent for Timor-Leste because it remains heavily reliant on past oil and natural gas revenues invested in its Petroleum Fund. The lucrative Bayu-Undan gas field, which pumped billions of dollars into the fund over the last two decades, permanently ceased production last year. And while the fund now contains $26 billion, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned last year that it could be depleted by 2038 if Timor-Leste continues to rely on it to finance fiscal deficits without replenishing it. Mr Ramos-Horta warned back in 2022 that Timor-Leste would run off a "financial cliff" if it could not get Greater Sunrise up and running within a decade. Timor-Leste has also warned the Australian government that it would turn to Chinese investors to make the project a reality if it cannot secure agreement from Woodside, although analysts have previously questioned whether they would have the appetite. In the meantime, the airport built in anticipation of the project lies idle , while roads and other infrastructure constructed for the processing hub are beginning to crumble. But Mr Ramos-Horta said he was confident that Woodside was "determined to follow through" with the project to pipe gas to Timor-Leste. "It's beneficial to Woodside, beneficial to Australia, beneficial to Timor-Leste," he said.

events.title: There was 'no sex' at this reality-show-style incubator for founders — but the drama was juicy
events.summary: Founder teams anxiously wait for the leaderboard to update at 9 a.m. at a reality-style incubator in rural Pennsylvania. Truman Dickerson There was only one thing on the minds of the founders at this reality-show-style startup incubator. It wasn't sex. Founder teams had two weeks to become profitable, and potent social media was paramount. At 9 p.m. on a recent Friday night, Max Harding had just returned from a barefoot run in the woods. The eccentric 20-year-old Californian was back in a large barn in rural Pennsylvania — still barefoot — alternatively working on his startup and asking me about the point of life. Though not an especially adept programmer, Harding possesses a more adroit, perhaps unteachable skill that has never been more valuable in the current landscape of founder culture . "Max captures the attention of the camera, keeps us center stage," said his cofounder, Skyler Ji, who added that Harding's role includes "spreading our philosophy" while he runs the operation behind the scenes. "Max brings some of the grander things," Ji told me. The pair's startup, Hivemind Research, aims to build "digital brains" in the form of social media. Harding and Ji were among 66 mostly young, mostly imaginative startup founders taking part in a two-week "incubator" workshop called Launchpad. The novel event was hosted by Stan, the company behind a moderately successful platform for independent creators to advertise and sell their services. At the last meetup Stan organized, startup founders jet-skied the East River at golden hour. At the incubator event, the entirety of which was filmed for use in a reality show that Stan plans to release sometime soon (though it is uploading Instagram clips daily), magnetic personalities were among the most valuable commodities. Max Harding (left) with his startup team at the launchpad event. Max Harding Stan cofounder Vitalii Dodonov told me that the 30 participating teams were chosen from a pool of 700 applicants, primarily for their existing social media followings and their ability to grow them . "It's not the building that gets you to revenue, it's the distribution," he said of today's startup culture. Of the many metrics competing teams were required to meet daily (10 sales calls, for example), social media videos were among the most heavily weighted. Everywhere I looked, people were talking about their companies into phones attached to tripods. Their products ran the gamut of usefulness — ranging from an AI facial scanner that tracks acne to an AI app that connects parents with babysitters. Startup founders film social media content while having dinner. Truman Dickerson Dodonov and John Hu, Stan's other cofounder, were trailed at all times by multi-person film crews, who glared should you emit an ill-timed sound while the cameras rolled. (The Velcro rip of my messenger bag earned me some leers.) Even outfits were choreographed. On the advice of the camera crews, Hu wore a "cream" colored getup while Dodonov donned a "charcoal" number to emphasize what was described to me as the "yin and yang" paradigm between the two. I spent about 16 cumulative hours at the event over two days earlier this month, at Stan's invitation. I ate meals with the founders, did a 7:30 a.m. cold plunge in the on-site lake alongside a Danish guy selling an AI to-do list, and commiserated with the startup founders who routinely pulled all-nighters to hit their metrics. Yours truly, soon before jumping into a freezing lake at 7:30 a.m. The visible mist is fog, not steam, in case you're wondering. Truman Dickerson Here's what I learned from the experience. Reality TV meets hackathon The event was billed as a sort of reality-TV-style game show-slash-incubator in the vein of hits like "Love Island" and "Squid Game." As in those shows, founder teams at Launchpad were subject to firepit eliminations, discreet alliances, and competitive drama under the ever - watchful lenses of dozens of expensive cameras. Except instead of a bunch of promiscuous co-eds doing risque challenges on a tropical island somewhere, contestants at Launchpad were mostly tech geeks with an unhealthy number of hours notched building software on their MacBooks. "There's no sex," laughed Jacob Snarr, a 24-year-old from Philadelphia. "Nobody here is thinking about that." Snarr and his cofounder, RJ McLaughlin, built a web browser game that lets friends debate their tastes and preferences, from their favorite foods to other everyday questions. The pair enlisted me as a product tester one morning, and we debated the merits of empanadas in the chilly barn. McLaughlin and Snarr were in second place on the leaderboard when I talked to them on Saturday morning — saving them from elimination. Rey Mendoza, who at 41 was one of the oldest founders in the competition, had already been eliminated. When I spoke with him, he was fighting for a chance at redemption. He showed me his sleep tracker for the six days. He hadn't slept more than six hours a night. Stan cofounder John Hu explains marketing to Rey Mendoza during a closed-door meeting. Truman Dickerson "Here, you're just fucking building, like 24/7," Mendoza, fatigued, said reverently. Event organizers added a number of less-intense, more fun-oriented events to the schedule, which were largely ignored by teams scrambling to upload more videos to social media. A "Mario Kart" meetup in a room adjoining the cafeteria was attended by precisely nobody. Two TVs showed the game's start screen, while maybe a dozen people sat at tables squinting at laptops. It's hard to imagine binge-watching some 60 sweatshirt-clad nerds drearily prompting chatbots to refine source code for yet another quirky AI startup. After all, everyone and their cousin is vibe coding their way into progressively nicher business models these days. In 2025, a record number of business applications — about 5.7 million — were submitted by Americans, according to census data. However, the number of businesses the government estimates will be successful enough to require employees actually declined. Those kinds of numbers mean it takes more to stand out. In our interview, Hu pointed at my phone and said I could use AI tools to start three or four businesses today — but, of course, they likely wouldn't be profitable. That, Hu said, is where the founders' personalities are supposed to come in, together with a bit of manufactured drama and endless streams of social media content. In the first challenge of the event, held on the first day, for example, teams were required to submit one social media video for public review around the firepit. Then, in front of everyone, Hu tore into them. "I was very honest," he said of one particular "roast" that produced tears from the submitters. "I was like, 'Guys, would anyone ever watch this? events.title: Seventeen's hot new JxJ unit are showing off their chemistry — with a little help from Pinterest
events.summary: Seventeen's Jeonghan and Joshua are debuting as a duo on October 19 — and hyping up the album with a joint Pinterest diary. Pinterest Jeonghan and Joshua from the boy band Seventeen are debuting as a duo. To promote their much-hyped album, they've launched a visual diary on Pinterest. The duo told Business Insider about their chemistry, their music — and their joint mood board. Jeonghan and Joshua from the mega K-pop boy band Seventeen  are offering fans a dream to lose themselves in and a mood board for shopping. The two vocalists are debuting as a much-hyped unit, a spinoff of the 13-member band's activities. As of Monday, they'll be working under the name JxJ — releasing their album, "DREAMSCAPE," and hitting the road together for a concert tour in six Asian cities. In the meantime, they've been populating not only their Instagrams, but also a sprawling visual diary on their joint Pinterest account. It's an interesting choice, as far as K-pop goes — usually, teasers are limited to platforms like YouTube or the K-pop-centric social network, Weverse. In a written interview with Business Insider, the duo described their interest in Pinterest as a means of introducing the "visual world," concept, and vibe of "DREAMSCAPE." The mood boards and the buffet of photos they've posted for fans to feast on are also a "little gift" to their audience. "JxJ Diary is a space we created to share the concept and vibe of the album more directly with fans before its release. We spent a lot of time thinking about what kind of content they would enjoy, and decided to launch our first-ever Pinterest channel featuring different sides of ourselves," the duo said. The singers said they wanted to explore the concept of "dreams" with the posts on their joint account. They've curated a collection of photographs and behind-the-scenes moments, including everything from candid shots to sneak peeks of their album photoshoots. "We hope fans will take inspiration from the album's imagery and vibe, and express it in their own ways," they added. "It would be really fun to see them create their own version of 'DREAMSCAPE' on Pinterest by collecting photos, experimenting with styling, and curating images that reflect their personal tastes." The business around the boys That invitation for fans taps into a K-pop fan economy in which an album is not only heard or watched but also worn, collected, decorated, and remade. The two Seventeen members belong to a group whose fan base collects their photo cards , travels to their concerts , and goes all in on albums and merchandise. Seventeen's 2023 album, "FML," still holds the record for first-day sales for a K-pop album, with more than 6.4 million copies sold. The band's "NEW" tour from 2025 to 2026 saw them play 31 shows in stadiums across Asia and four US cities, drawing close to a million fans, in person and online. JxJ now gives Seventeen's fandom something else to get invested in: Jeonghan and Joshua together, and the similarities in their personal style . Ayumi Nakajima, Pinterest's APAC head of content partnerships, told Business Insider the platform had seen a surge in interest in K-pop, making it prime territory for JxJ to establish a foothold. Nakajima said that the collaboration with the duo's agency stemmed from the idea that K-pop fans connect with more than just the music. Pinterest gives fans a space to "explore the visual inspiration behind the artist's stories" and "save what resonates with them." Pinterest has seen a strong surge in interest for all things Korea on the platform. Searches for "K-pop style" rose 19% globally year over year, while "K-beauty" searches rose 114%. In Japan, searches for "K-pop fan art" climbed 368%, while "trading card decoration" rose 77%. "What visual experiences like the JxJ diary do is bring fans into an artist's creative world earlier, giving them more time to engage with the aesthetics, ideas and storytelling behind a release," Nakajima said. "That early engagement can really shape fandom-led commerce, because fans aren't just showing up at the point of purchase," Nakajima added. "A look, a mood or a visual reference can spark interest weeks before someone decides what to wear to a concert, what beauty look to try, or what pieces they want to buy." Chemistry JxJ's album, "DREAMSCAPE," drops on October 19. Pinterest As for the boys behind the Pinterest board, they're prepped to serve up seven tracks spanning genres they're "exploring for the first time" on the new album. The duet songs, from early teasers of the music, involve experiments with house, synthpop, and dance rock. There are also two solo tracks — Joshua's punk rock offering, "Not Personal," and Jeonghan's dreamy bop, "Coloring." "Seventeen has a certain energy when all 13 members are together, but we think the two of us have a different kind of chemistry when we are together," they told Business Insider. "Rather than trying to showcase something entirely new, we wanted to bring out our natural sides and individual charms as much as possible." The album is also the product of "a lot of conversations" about the kind of art they each wanted to create. "By sharing our ideas and the images we each had in mind, we were able to understand each other's tastes on a deeper level," the duo said. They took a couple of trips together, too, which helped them "get to know each other better and shape a direction that felt uniquely ours." "We also experimented with our vocals to show a new side of ourselves, so we hope fans will enjoy and support this album," they added. "DREAMSCAPE" launches on October 19 at 6 p.m. Korea time. events.title: AI trade reversal pierces Asia’s star picks-and-shovels stocks
events.summary: Investors have turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. Asia’s AI hardware stocks fell as US tech shares sold off and oil rose, raising fears that higher borrowing costs could slow AI infrastructure spending. Big winners such as Nan Ya Plastics, Unimicron Technology and Samsung Electro-Mechanics dropped sharply, while CoreWeave’s bond slump highlighted funding stress in the AI boom. Analysts warn that delayed investment could hit earnings for TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix, though some investors still expect AI demand to stay strong. A deepening sell-off in US technology stocks is exposing a new vulnerability in Asia’s artificial intelligence trade: mounting financing costs could choke off the spending needed to sustain the boom, threatening earnings across a supply chain that has powered the region’s stock-market rally. The pressure intensified last week as oil surged to US$110 a barrel for the first time since May, stoking inflation concerns, and investors turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. An eight-session rout in US semiconductor shares – the longest since 2008 – wiped roughly 16% off the sector’s benchmark, while the Nasdaq 100 suffered its worst week since April 2025. For Asia, where chipmakers and the hardware suppliers that make printed-circuit boards, precision components and manufacturing equipment have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI frenzy, the implications could be significant heading into the Oct 19 open. A Goldman Sachs Group basket of regional AI hardware stocks tumbled 11% last week, its steepest decline since mid-July. The sell-off showed little sign of abating despite an upbeat revenue outlook from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing , underscoring how concerns over AI spending are spreading across the hardware supply chain. Some of Asia’s standout performers were hit particularly hard in the maelstrom. Nan Ya Plastics , a maker of printed circuit board materials and the best-performing stock on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index in 2026 , tumbled 12% from a record high. Rival Unimicron Technology , the index’s second-best performer, fell 14% in a week, while Samsung Electro- Mechanics , which makes an array of electronic components, plunged 23%. “Financing costs are like gravity for the AI boom,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich. “Rising borrowing costs could make infrastructure projects harder to finance and delay spending. Even a delay could trigger a reset in Asian suppliers’ earnings expectations and valuations.” The concern is no longer just whether demand for AI chips will hold up. It is whether hyperscalers and neocloud operators can keep financing the infrastructure needed to deploy them – and whether the expected returns will justify the scale of investment. Bonds of neocloud provider CoreWeave sank to levels signalling distress last week as investors questioned whether AI demand and revenue could support the borrowing behind its expansion. Its shares slumped 12% on Oct 16 , resulting in the stock’s worst week since November with a 25% drop. The episode brought the financing risks of the boom into sharper focus, with surging oil prices adding to worries that inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated. While TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics supply the chips and memory needed for AI computing, their earnings ultimately depend on continued investment in the infrastructure that uses those products. Component makers and equipment suppliers face the same underlying risk, potentially with less visibility into the timing of individual projects. “AI funding stress is a bigger challenge for downstream beneficiaries than for the core compute ecosystem,” said Kevin Net, portfolio manager at Financiere de l’Echiquier in Paris. “Basically, the further away you get from the actual chip, the greater the risk you might see timing delays.” Warnings about funding risks have come from industry executives, including Broadcom . Chief executive Hock Tan, who said capital, rather than shortages of memory chips or manufacturing capacity, would become the biggest constraint on AI growth. Gartner has warned that more than US$3.5 trillion (S$4.48 trillion) of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as investment threatens to outpace the revenue needed to justify it. “If hyperscalers and neoclouds cannot fund their datacenter investments, that would translate into lower orders for Asia enablers like TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix,” said Vey-Sern Ling, managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. “Given how jittery the market is, the read-through would be very negative for the semi picks and shovels.” The stakes are particularly high for Asian equities, where the AI buildout has become a dominant investment theme.

events.title: Iran says two tankers catch fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: The vessels, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, used an unauthorised route, the IRGC says. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said two oil tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The first tanker hit a mine, triggering an explosion and a “fierce fire”, the IRGC said on Saturday, while the second tanker hit a mine that engulfed it “in a massive blaze”, Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported. list 1 of 3 Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again list 2 of 3 US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options? list 3 of 3 Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters Information about the ships’ names or the origin of their cargo was not immediately available. IRNA said the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route not authorised by Iran. The IRGC also claimed that while one tanker tried to cross the waterway “with US support”, the second vessel was left immobilised. Iran seized control of the Strait of Hormuz after the US-Israeli war on the country began in late February. Tehran has since demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. About one-fifth of global oil consumption transited the waterway before the war. This week, IRGC naval commander Rear Admiral Ali Azmaei warned that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile”. The United States has imposed its own naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports. Iran’s army earlier said that two tankers caught fire on Thursday and Friday in Tehran’s “prohibited zone” in the Gulf of Oman. Maritime monitors also reported two tankers struck in Gulf waters off Saudi Arabia on Friday. Last Sunday, six vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the most in a single day since the war began, according to security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the UK maritime agency UKMTO. Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month. Nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through on October 8, but only 2.9 million on October 11, according to Kpler data. The disruption has pushed up global energy prices and inflation. US President Donald Trump has explicitly ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran. “I wouldn’t use nuclear,” he told the Newsmax news site in an interview on Thursday. Trump said that he was also not considering putting troops on the ground in Iran. “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it,” he said, adding he believes a deal to end the war will be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.

events.title: Saudi-led forces try to break Houthi siege of Taiz with airstrikes

events.title: Meta says suspending No Kings account on day of action was done 'in error'
events.summary: Demonstrators hold signs during a "No Kings" protest at the South Carolina Statehouse. Sean Rayford/Getty Images The No Kings coalition held a nationwide day of action to encourage early voting. Its Instagram account was suspended in the middle of the event. Meta says the suspension was a mistake made by an automated system. Meta said Saturday that an automatic trigger is to blame for the No Kings movement's Instagram account being suspended in the midst of a nationwide effort to mobilize early voting in the midterms . The network, which bills itself as nonpartisan but arose last year in response to President Donald Trump 's actions, said its account went dark for "several hours" at the peak of its event. "Even after visibility was restored, we had no access to the account for hours," the group posted on its account. In a statement on X, Meta spokesman Andy Stone said that accounts posting, sharing, or commenting at "very high frequencies" can prompt an automated response. "That's what happened with the No Kings IG account in the lead up to today's day of action. Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error," he said in an X post. "Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize." No Kings said it wants a deeper explanation from Meta. "Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable," it said in its post. "Meta must answer for this suspension and take immediate steps to ensure it never happens again — to any account, but especially those working to inform voters and encourage participation in our democracy." The group said it held nearly 3,000 rallies across the country to encourage voters to cast their ballots early as a hedge against any effort to undermine turnout in an election that will determine the balance of power in Congress. events.title: Elon Musk is pouring money into the midterms. Here's where he's giving the most.
events.summary: Elon Musk, seen here with President Donald Trump last month, is bankrolling Republican campaigns. Bloomberg/Getty Images Elon Musk is giving reams of cash to Republicans. Most of that dough is ending up in Texas, according to financial disclosure forms. In Texas, Ken Paxton is running a tight race against James Talarico. Elon Musk is forking over generational wealth to Republicans facing tough midterm elections this cycle. Over two donations in September, Musk gave a combined $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, which has, in turn, given reams of cash to funds supporting the Republican candidate in Texas. The money, shown in new federal disclosure forms, cements Musk as a major player in Republican politics over a year after he publicly split with President Donald Trump over the latter's handling of the Epstein files (though the two have since reconciled). Republicans are facing serious headwinds over the Iran war, rising inflation, and sky-high gas prices. Polls show that American voters are largely dissatisfied with Trump's leadership and handling of the economy . All told, Musk has given about $276 million since July. Much of Musk's political donations have ended up in Texas, according to federal disclosure forms, where embattled Attorney General Ken Paxton is engaged in a mudslinging battle for the Senate with state representative James Talarico. One day after Musk notched a $75 million donation to the Senate Leadership Fund, the Super PAC gave a $75 million donation to the Texas PAC, a group aligned with Paxton. Then, also in September, another $83 million donation by Musk was matched the next day by an identical donation to the Texas PAC, according to federal disclosure forms. Talarico's campaign, meanwhile, has raised about $129 million. Musk's companies are already investing billions in the Lone Star State, as the business magnate builds SpaceX's terafab semiconductor facility outside Houston. In 2024, Musk announced that he was moving SpaceX's headquarters from California to Texas in response to Gov. Gavin Newsom's policies on gender identity. Representatives for Paxton and Musk did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday. Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, said last year that he had probably "done enough" political spending, though he left the door open. "Well, if I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I'll do it. I don't currently see a reason," he told Bloomberg at the time. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Gas company called 'rude' for not sharing decommissioning news earlier
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Secret meetings over Albany gas network held months before decommissioning announced Canadian firm ATCO owns assets around Australia but it no longer wants Albany's gas network. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) Redacted emails show ATCO Australia and the WA state government discussed the future of the Albany gas network months before customers were told it would be scrapped. ATCO will transition customers off the network over the next three years, forcing customers onto alternative energy sources. The government has ruled out taking over the network. When Hayden Jones and his wife bought an Albany laundromat three and a half years ago, it seemed a sensible investment decision. The City of Albany, 400km south of Perth, is one of Western Australia's largest regional cities, fuelled by relatively cheap and available liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Hayden Jones wants the Albany LPG network retained. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) But news earlier this year that Albany will lose its reticulated LPG gas network has put the Jones's business in jeopardy. In January, energy provider ATCO Australia announced it would decommission the Albany network over the next three years, citing aging infrastructure and high maintenance costs. Redacted emails between ATCO and the state government. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) However, emails obtained by the ABC under Freedom of Information show the Canadian-owned company and the state government had been discussing the network's future eight months before affected customers were informed. The redacted emails include a confidential briefing note sent to the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification (DEED) on May 28, 2025, under the subject line "In Strictest Confidence: Albany Gas network". They also show a meeting was held between the utility and Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson a week later to discuss the network's future. Amber Jade Sanderson said the government tried to persuade ATCO to remain in Albany. ( ABC News: Armin Azad ) Ms Sanderson said she did not receive a copy of the briefing note, but confirmed she attended the meeting. "ATCO put the view that the network was no longer commercially viable … and that they were considering making that commercial decision to walk away. "I put the government's view that we would prefer they did not walk away." Greg Stocks said ATCO should have told the city of its plans sooner. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) News of the 2025 meeting was criticised by City of Albany Mayor Greg Stocks, who said residents had been blindsided by the abrupt announcement, and should have been told earlier to assist the city in retaining the network. "I think it was particularly rude that ATCO had not informed us and all businesses that they were connecting," he said. In a statement, ATCO said any change to its licence conditions required approval by the WA's Economic Regulation Authority, prompting its meeting with the state government. "When ATCO began considering the future of Albany gas network, it was therefore appropriate to consult first with the state government," a spokesperson said. Hayden Jones's business relies heavily on LPG gas. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) But business owners, including Jones, say the consultation did not go far enough , and want to see an alternative put on the table. In August, a petition signed by more than 2,500 people was tabled in parliament calling for the state government to intercede. "Either a local supplier or the government take the network back, which is what the Albany community really wants," Mr Jones said. "They want the government to stand up, right the wrongs of the past, and take this network back into government hands." ATCO customers will have to transition to bottled gas or switch to electricity. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson said the government was not considering that option . "I understand that Albany residents are frustrated and angry that ATCO has made the decision to walk away. I absolutely understand, and I share that frustration and anger," she said. "The reality is this gas network is at the end of its technical life and would need to be entirely rebuilt. "The least-cost result is to allow customers to transition either to bottled gas or to electrification.

events.title: Assistant treasurer knew about ATO's credit card ban plans months ago
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino concedes he knew of ATO's credit card ban plans in July Daniel Mulino says the ATO was told to negotiate with credit card companies. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) The assistant treasurer says the government knew in July the tax office was considering a credit card ban following the Reserve Bank's surcharge changes. Outrage about the change from the business community forced the prime minister to step in. The issue has exposed tensions between the prime minister and the treasurer. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has conceded the government knew the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) was considering banning credit card payments in July, months before the decision was made public. The ATO's decision in late September to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1 sparked backlash from the business community, which eventually forced an intervention from the prime minister and the treasurer to underwrite the costs and allow credit cards to be accepted by the tax office until mid-2027. Mr Mulino today said he and Treasurer Jim Chalmers were first made aware of the ATO's intentions months ago. "In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options and that at that point their preference was to not accept credit cards," Mr Mulino told ABC's Insiders. "The indication we gave to the ATO was that they should continue to engage with the credit card companies, and that there should be a transition period." The admission comes after the Australian Financial Review yesterday revealed the ATO had privately informed the government about its credit card ban and presented the government with options. The ATO's decision followed changes from the Reserve Bank of Australia to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank has said was "in the public interest" and was costing consumers about $1.6 billion a year. Mr Mulino was asked why the government did not push for the ATO to continue accepting credit card payments from small businesses back in July. He said the government intervened "very quickly" after the negative fallout and insisted the government was listening. "We stepped in very quickly once the feedback came to us," he said. Small businesses were informed of the ATO's decision on September 30, a day before it was made public, and given a two-month grace period. "But the transition period, as it turned out, from stakeholder feedback, wasn't enough. And so that's where the government stepped in," Mr Mulino said. He was asked if he had any regrets about not stepping in earlier. "We've changed our position. So I've listened to stakeholder feedback, as has the PM and the treasurer," he said. "So, obviously we've changed tack and we've listened to feedback. And that's a sign of a government that is putting in place important big reforms." Mr Mulino denied the government had a "hands-off approach", saying they "didn't get into all of the details" but insisted that the ATO should continue to negotiate with credit card companies. Government backs down on ATO credit card ban The federal government will temporarily cover credit card surcharges after businesses warn that losing the payment option will put them under pressure. Earlier this month, Mr Chalmers said he was aware the ATO was "grappling" with the decision before it finalised the decision in late September, but he was not aware of the specific timeline. Mr Mulino said he engaged with government agencies shortly after the RBA's announcement in March saying they were expected to comply with the removal of surcharges. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said it was concerning these discussions were happening in July when businesses were only informed the day before it became public. "Business wasn't made aware until just hours before the surcharge ban took effect in October," he said. "This looks like a completely deficient policymaking process that took small business for granted. It cannot be repeated." The ATO initially defended its decision, saying it was not tenable for the agency to absorb the $200 million cost and that it would result in less revenue being collected and therefore less funding for government services. Taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but that credit card companies did not offer a low enough rate. The debacle, and its timeline, has also exposed some tension between the treasurer and prime minister. Mr Albanese said he intervened after receiving a text from ACCI's Mr McKellar the day before.

events.title: Mark Carney makes closing argument to Alberta against path to independence from Canada: outsiders ‘are working to break us so they can own us. Never’
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path  toward independence  in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty. With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a  trade war  and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted. “Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up. “This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said. Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence. Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies. “I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta. Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan. “He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked. Trump’s threats raise the stakes “Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary. At  Thursday’s Calgary rally  and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States. Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies. “Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said. But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province. “Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said. Some Albertans say the vote shouldn’t have been called Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.” Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high. Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism. But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote. “I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada. Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline. Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions. Political leaders unite against separation Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada. “Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said. Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection. “For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: US ambassador urges Israel to prosecute attackers of American journalist
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Trump-appointed Ambassador Mike Huckabee calls attack in occupied West Bank a ‘despicable act of terror’. United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has demanded Israel prosecute and jail those responsible for the attack on Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank. “Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Huckabee wrote on X on Saturday. list 1 of 3 Settlers set fire to mosque in West Bank as Israeli forces raid villages list 2 of 3 Israeli plan to reopen settler ‘Route 463’ threatens to isolate Ramallah list 3 of 3 Palestine weekly: Gaza marks year of ‘ceasefire’ with more Israeli killing “Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison,” he added. “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.” Levine was covering Palestinians’ annual harvest of olives on Friday in the occupied West Bank when Israeli settlers brutally attacked her and several Palestinians. Israeli settlers stormed the area, beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses. The perpetrators, armed with bottles and slingshots, “were kicking me for like 10 minutes, and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag”, Levine said. Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera that Levine “was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground.” Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. The American photojournalist underwent surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand, and was left with a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae, as well as lacerations, her daughter told The Associated Press news agency. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who wants to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base ahead of closely fought October 27 elections, claimed on Friday that Palestinians or “far-left” activists may have been responsible for the attack on Levine and other Palestinians. Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has sharply criticised Israeli settler attacks against Americans, did not identify the culprits as settlers after Netanyahu tried to sow doubt as to their identity. The ambassador, appointed by US President Donald Trump, met Palestinian-Americans in the occupied West Bank town of Turmus Aya in September to hear locals’ testimony about their experiences with pogroms. In August, Huckabee called a days-long Israeli settler siege an “act of terror”. The US State Department criticised Friday’s attack using a cautious tone on Levine’s beating, stating condemnation of “criminal violence by any party”.

events.title: ‘France, truly, is on the brink’ and just days away from a make-or-break moment in its debt crisis, analyst warns, as protests turn into riots
events.summary: Nationwide protests over the high cost of living roiled France on Saturday, adding to turmoil over public spending and debt ahead of a critical vote in the National Assembly. Rioting broke out in some cities as luxury boutiques and supermarkets were looted while public buildings were defaced and even set on fire. That followed mass demonstrations earlier this month, with students decrying run-down classrooms, missing teachers, and buildings that aren’t equipped for rising temperatures. Protestors blamed years of underinvestment in public education. At the same time, France’s looming debt has sent bond yields to the highest levels in 24 years, flashing warning signs not seen since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011. With far-right and far-left candidates in the lead to become France’s next president in the spring, markets are losing confidence that either side will take the painful steps necessary to rein in the deficit. For Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, France is suffering from a crisis of liberal democracy, a crisis of fiscal mismanagement, and a crisis of youth disaffection. “But the fiscal crisis is the most dangerous, underlying many of the country’s woes and threatening to bring it to ruin,” he wrote in a New York Times op-ed on Thursday. “France, truly, is on the brink.” The crises are also related to each other. For instance, Rahman pointed out that while France’s education spending tops the European Union average, more than a quarter of the money pays for pensions of retired teachers. Nobel laureate Paul Krugman similarly drew a straight line from France’s retirement largesse to the student unrest. Due to its very generous government pension plan, education spending has suffered, meaning France is effectively subsidizing older French at the expense of everyone else, he wrote in a  Substack post last week. France’s public debt is now a record $4 trillion, or 119% of GDP—the highest ratio since the immediate aftermath of World War II. While the pandemic as well as the Ukraine and Iran wars worsened France’s fiscal picture, President Emmanuel Macron has also pulled back from reforms meant to rein in the debt. Sébastien Lecornu, the latest in a revolving door of prime ministers, has proposed a 2027 budget that would modestly bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP from 5.4%, and faces a first critical vote in the National Assembly on Tuesday.  “If his government fails to pass the budget, the cost of servicing French debt may explode,” Rahman predicted. “France could be forced to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund and to pray for it from the European Central Bank — a humiliation for the world’s seventh-biggest economy.” The market’s distrust of France is more political than economic, fearing it has become ungovernable with the extreme left and right unlikely to make necessary changes, he added. Indeed, far-right leader Marine Le Pen has vowed to roll back the official retirement age to 62 and even previously suggested dropping it to as low as 60. Meanwhile, far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is campaigning on a plan to have the central bank simply  cancel its holdings of French debt . Such positions help explain why bond investors have sent France’s borrowing costs to sky-high levels, Rahman said. “The country, they fear, is becoming socially volatile and institutionally paralyzed.” In fact, the presidential election in May will not even be that decisive for financial markets, as a legislative election in June might fail to produce a parliamentary majority for the new president, setting up further political gridlock, he said.  France could avoid imminent catastrophe this coming week if Le Pen orders her allies in the Assembly to abstain on the budget, allowing it to pass. “That may avert, for now, the kind of meltdown suffered by Greece after the financial crash. But France is no longer in control of its destiny,” Rahman warned. An explosion in borrowing costs would signal that France is at the mercy of the bond market, which has started pricing in growing odds of a debt default . That’s similar to how the United Kingdom is effectively in thrall to so-called bond vigilantes . Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, argued in a note Tuesday that a series of convulsions would have to occur for France to get its act together and appease the bond market. That could include a no-confidence vote that leaves France with no governance from the Assembly, a Moody’s credit downgrade, a widening of street protests and violence, a sharper and contagious spike in France’s bond yield spread, and the election of Le Pen as president. The European Central Bank also wouldn’t come to the rescue quickly for fear of encouraging “moral hazard,” and other bailout mechanisms lack the firepower for an economy as large as France’s, Wizman argued. “Either way, it would seem that one would have to go through the valley before getting to the other side of the fiscal responsibility gap,” he added. “And only  after  all that transformational pain of the next few months may France find its spine and commit to austerity.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system still restricted in Ukraine
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine's use of the Elon Musk -owned SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, despite earlier signs this week that it had been fully restored. Why it matters: The current restrictions limit the Ukrainian military from using drones to intercept Russian attack drones and from using its drones to send supplies to soldiers on the front lines, Zelensky said. The intrigue: Ukrainian officials say they are still scrambling to determine whether the restrictions result from a political decision by the Trump administration or Musk. Ukrainian officials have heard different versions of what happened, with the Trump administration and SpaceX executives accusing each other. "SpaceX as a company tells us it is a technical problem. But our contacts in the company say it is coming from the White House. When we ask the White House, they say it is Elon," a Ukrainian official told Axios. Musk said in a Wednesday X post that the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. President Trump said on Friday that the White House was not involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system. Behind the scenes: The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk proposed to Trump throttling the Starlink and Starshield satellite networks used by the Ukrainian military. A source familiar with the discussion told Axios that Trump didn't push back on Elon's idea. A White House official denied the Telegraph's account. "This is totally false. As President Trump said, we didn't slow down Starlink at all, and the service is currently operational," the official said. State of play: But the service is not fully operational. Before the restrictions, the Starlink and Starshield network operated even on drones that reached 400 kilometers per hour. Now it is restricted to 161 kilometers per hour, Ukrainian officials say. Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that the Ukrainian military tested the system on Friday in cars in European Union countries. The cars drove 180 kilometers per hour, and the satellite systems continued working. But once the cars crossed into Ukraine, the system disconnected at 161 kilometers per hour. "The conclusion is that the restrictions apply inside Ukraine but do not apply in European Union countries. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelensky said. Zelensky also expressed skepticism about SpaceX's claim that the speed limit results from technical problems. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Ukraine said both systems were restricted. What to watch: On Friday, Ukraine's chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke with Trump's adviser and envoy, Jared Kushner, to discuss the Starlink issue, Zelensky said. They also spoke about holding a meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian teams next week to continue the discussions on the latest Trump administration proposal for a deal with Russia on ending the war.

events.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts drones as Egypt weighs sending help
events.summary: Forces intercepted and destroyed four drones over Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh, Eastern Province and southern region, coalition says. The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Riyadh and other regions, the latest in a wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities. “We intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South,” coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on Saturday. list 1 of 3 Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield? list 2 of 3 Yemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport list 3 of 3 Can Yemen’s government forces sustain their offensive against the Houthis? He also posted footage of what he described as the air force intercepting cruise missiles and drones and striking ballistic missile launchers belonging to the Houthis. Riyadh’s King Khalid airport has come under at least 20 attacks – including one last week that killed 13 people – since the fighting between the Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government flared in July. On Thursday, at least five people were killed in missile strikes near the presidential palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. It blamed the Houthis for the attack. On Friday, the Yemeni government said the Houthis fired two missiles at Aden’s airport , while government forces said they had advanced in Marib province, northeast of Sanaa. Saudi Arabia is backing a government counteroffensive, known as Dawn of Yemen, and has carried out air strikes on the Houthis, including on an oil facility in Sanaa. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said on Saturday he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia should the kingdom ask. Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, el-Sisi said, but it was “inconceivable” for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was harmed. “I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone. We are speaking only about defence,” he said. Egypt’s parliament is holding an emergency session on Sunday at the president’s request. Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis’ escalation. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, said Tehran supported a “comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve” the conflict. Several embassies in Saudi Arabia have restricted travel and warned citizens not to use airports. The Saudi Ministry of Education extended remote learning for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah in light of the recent Houthi attacks.

events.title: How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France
events.summary: An estimated 550,000 people took part in protests across France, demanding greater investment in education and action on the rising cost of living. The demonstrations quickly descended into violence, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked. At least 1,200 people were arrested on Saturday as riot police deployed tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds. The unrest follows weeks of student-led protests, with demonstrators joining forces to express growing anger over economic conditions and French President Emmanuel Macron handling of the crisis. In a social media post, Macron denounced the violence and said that vandals and looters will be "prosecuted and punished". BBC correspondent Adina Campbell reports from Paris. events.title: ‘I can do stuff that is unbelievable.’ Trump boasts about his self-proclaimed power and tells voters DOD will revive a Kentucky drug plant if GOP wins
events.summary: President Donald Trump touted  his power in his second go around  in the White House Saturday while rallying in Kentucky to bolster Republican turnout as his party struggles in the midterms, saying, “I can do stuff that is unbelievable.” Trump, who spoke in the city of Highland Heights to boost Republican candidates including Ed Gallrein for the U.S. House, was riffing on his decision to change how the U.S. government refers to the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. “I don’t think I could have done this in my first term. This is a much more powerful term,” Trump said. “Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first. Now, they kiss my ass.” “Well, I also changed the name of a lake in Canada to the Lake America,” he continued, referring to Lake Ontario. Trump’s self-proclaimed power is set against voter  frustration with how he’s wielded it , with tariffs and the Iran war driving up prices and more Americans seeing the president  looking out for his own interests  and not those of the country. With control of both chambers of Congress on the line, and with it the prospects of Democratic-led investigations of his administration should they win, Trump has put himself at the fore for voters, asking them to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” But Republicans privately worry that growing disapproval of his administration is a liability. Trump nominated one of his personal lawyers to serve as attorney general, ordered  military strikes  on accused drug smuggling boats, is trying to put his name on the Kennedy Center, and has  enriched himself and his family while he’s been in office. While meandering through topics onstage in Kentucky, Trump touched on gas prices, saying that the war with Iran was going to end soon — an assertion he’s made many times over the course of the nearly eight-month conflict — and that gas prices will drop to lower than previously. The crowd cheered. Facing the electoral headwinds, Trump is working to paint a portentous picture of Democrats in the final weeks before the midterms. That includes the claim that if his opposing party wins, the U.S. will “have a depression,” and that the Democratic platform includes abolishing the U.S. Senate and U.S. Supreme Court. Those are not on the Democratic Party’s platform. But Trump is trying to lump them in with the Democratic Socialists of America, which have had a few candidates win in this year’s primary elections. Trump also rehashed his  dubious promise  that if Republicans win the House and the Senate then every adult American would get $5,000. That would most likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, while exacerbating the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit. Trump added a new, seemingly conditional promise for Kentucky. That if Republicans win, he said, the Department of Defense would invest in revitalizing a drug manufacturing facility in the state. The president pulled Gallrein on stage, the Republican candidate for the U.S. House district who beat Rep. Thomas Massie in the GOP primary. Massie had aggravated Trump by pushing for the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and opposing the Iran war, and the president responded by successfully backing Gallrein in the party’s primary. Massie, however, still has a following for standing on his staunchly conservative principles, even when it meant voting against his own party. When Trump lashed out at Massie as a “jerk” and “loser” and trumpeted Gallrein as a more loyal replacement, the crowd’s response was tepid, with about half the arena clapping at Trump’s barbs and other half silent. events.title: How artificial intelligence is helping the lobster industry
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Like facial recognition for lobsters, AI technology tracing from pot to plate Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Scientists have developed artificial intelligence technology capable of recognising individual lobsters. The innovation allows traceability from pot to plate and has the potential to strengthen consumer trust — and even break into new markets. The scientists want to further develop the technology for both the processing sector and the fishery. After nearly three weeks at sea, Joe Sayers docks a boat filled to the brim with treasure — it's red, thorny and alive. "There is one in here, I know there's 220 millimetres just in the carapace … there's a couple of fish in here that are probably going to be three, four kilos, I'd say, somewhere there," he said. Tasmania's southern rock lobster industry is bouncing back after some unsteady years. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Every year, Tasmania's commercial fishers catch just over 1,000 tonnes of southern rock lobster, valued at about $90 million. While things are now on the up, it's been a tough few years for the industry, brought on by trade restrictions and a domestic market flooded with cheap lobsters. Fisher Joe Sayers says the overheads of lobster fishing are only growing. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) "Now we're up to getting a few dollars in the bank from better prices, but our costs are going up … all the time, like fuel and baits," Mr Sayers said. But for Mr Sayers, it's a way of life, and after more than 30 years at sea, he wants to hand over an industry in good shape to the next generation. Southern rock lobsters are caught measured, photographed and recorded as part of a new Lobster AI program, 01 September 2026 ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Scientists from the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS), in partnership with Fiordland Lobster Company and the South Australian Lobster Company, are trying to ensure just that, through newly developed artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Scientists Dean Giosio and Quinn Fitzgibbon photograph a lobster to see if it's in the database. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) "It's just like a fingerprint or facial recognition technology," associate professor at IMAS Quinn Fitzgibbon said. "We've used AI machine learning to look at the features on the shell of the lobster, and amazingly, we've been able to show that this technology can pick up those features and they're individual. The AI technology has been developed by Dean Giosio, Quinn Fitzgibbon and Tara Kelly from the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. ( Supplied: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies ) It's as simple as a quick snap on an smartphone. If the lobster has been photographed before, the AI recognises it, and if it hasn't, into the database it goes, joining thousands of others from across Australia and New Zealand. This lobster has been scanned before. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) The team has tested the AI under various scenarios, finding it recognises a lobster three years on, dressed up in barnacles and algae, or with a fresh exoskeleton. In time, the idea is consumers themselves will be able to photograph their dinner and know exactly where it came from. Southern rock lobsters are caught, measured, photographed and recorded. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Tackling distrust around product misplacement The technology could be transformative for exporters like Michael Blake, who processes up to 300,000 lobsters per year at his Bicheno facility. "It's the most premium-priced lobster in the world," he said. Exporter Michael Blake hopes the technology will help Tasmanian southern rock lobster reach new markets. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Scientists physically tag lobsters during population surveys, but that's not viable for the industry because tags can be removed or forged. That means once fish leave the state, there's no way of proving where they came from, and money to be made from branding a foreign lobster as prized southern rock lobster. Once lobsters are exported, they can end up in tanks with lobsters from Australia and other parts of the world. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) "The lobsters are taken out of the boxes and placed in tanks with other lobsters from other countries, as well as from Australia," Mr Blake said. He is hopeful AI could help break into new markets, like the European Union, and strengthen trust in existing ones. "Giving some of those restaurateurs overseas the confidence that this is guaranteed to come from here, will put the lobster on plates that it's currently not on," Mr Blake said.

events.title: My kids were ready for college. They weren't quite ready for adulthood.
events.summary: The author with her 3 freshman year drop-offs over the years Courtesy of the author I spent years preparing my kids for college, but I overlooked some essential life skills. I never properly taught them to clean toilets, repay debts, or recognize health problems. Now I'm trying to fill those gaps and accept that parenting doesn't end when kids leave home. Last week, a friend asked if I knew of any jobs for her recent graduate . Between his rigorous academic load, sports, and club activities that landed him in a prestigious university, he'd never held a job. "My fail," she confessed. My kids have had jobs, but I have parenting fails of my own. I'm concerned that, in the grand scheme of middle-class privileges, we forgot to teach our children some basic life skills: scrubbing bathrooms, repaying debts, and self-attunement. I crammed as much as I could into the first 18 years of their lives, but juggling my small business while parenting didn't leave time for everything. I found myself tossing last-minute advice like grapes while driving each to their respective dorms: Carry your drinks with you at all times — even to the bathroom. Know where Student Health is located. Sit in the front rows; meet your professors. Skip the jugs of BORG. We didn't teach them everything they need to survive, let alone thrive, but I'm hoping it's not too late to offer some guidance. Cleaning their toilet The bathroom might be the most inhospitable location in either of my sons' living quarters. The filth lurking below the interior rim is as confronting as the overspray of urine where the lid hinges. To protect them from chemical toxins , I reflect that I never handed my kids a cleaning wand. They'd wiped down sinks, vacuumed, and washed clothes, but the toilet was off limits. Instead, I'd taken the plastic brush into my own hand or, worse, hired a housekeeper. It should have transitioned at some age, but between my own squeamishness about cleanliness and their protests at reaching inside the bowl, I failed. I'm consoled that it appears statistically unlikely that anyone would catch a disease from their lack of sanitization, but in the interest of raising functional adults within accepted cultural parameters, I'm impressing upon them the virtues of hygiene and housekeeping as attractive to a future partner , while clamoring to provide motivation. My kids had no fiscal responsibility To teach financial awareness , my husband and I set up checking accounts and outlined budgets with our kids in their last year of high school. What we failed to do was teach them the importance of paying bills or repaying debt — imperative when adulting to secure credit, rent your own accommodations, and eventually live a fiscally independent life. We felt like we were on the right path when our kid bought his first (used) Toyota Tacoma, and we helped by providing a partial private loan to make it possible. The idea was for him to pay us back in monthly installments, no matter how small, but that quickly fell by the wayside when he felt $20 too nominal a transaction to matter. The infamous first motor vehicle purchased by the author's oldest son. Courtesy of the author He eventually paid off the entire debt in a lump sum, and we blew off his breach of our contract, but when a second kid dismissed our financial agreement, I knew we'd made a mistake. It's a lesson worth reworking in the interest of said kids' futures — perhaps we should've enforced stricter consequences for non-payment or suggested a bank loan that has natural repercussions for non-compliance? Idk, but that's my hot tip. I told them to 'read the room,' but also, they should read themselves This broad term refers to an individual's ability to assess themself in their environment, mentally and physically. I'd always advised my kids to "read the room," but now I implore them to read themselves — better. By the end of high school, I'd encouraged my kids to schedule their own doctor appointments but still played caregiver when advising them to stay home from school (with a fever) or insisting on their attendance (to avoid truancy). Collectively considered, I might have disabled their agency given that one of our kids landed in the emergency room after ignoring cold symptoms that manifested as chest pains in the middle of the night, his freshman year of college. Diagnosed with an acute case of pericarditis, his heart was stressed. He spent three harrowing nights in the hospital and continued with six months of follow-up as an outpatient; it was scary. I couldn't conceive how quickly an active young person's health had plummeted so drastically. "This must be super rare?" I asked the attending physician. "Not really, it's a textbook response to strep throat," the doctor replied. Then, turning toward my kid, he asked, "Didn't your throat feel sore?" The author with her son, recovering from complications of strep throat that led to a heart scare and three three-night hospital stay Courtesy of the author "Not really." Dropping our youngest child to start her college career on the opposite coast this fall, we kissed and hugged. "Have fun — these years are the best!" Then I added, "but it's normal to feel lonely at times. It's OK to be uncomfortable." I reminded her exactly what I probably needed to hear: "Discomfort breeds growth." And maybe that's how I'd reframe my embarrassing "fails" — as an opportunity for growth, because isn't that why we all went to college in the first place?
