events.title: In midterm races, Democrats are using the Iran war to target Republicans—even some who never served in Congress and couldn’t have cast votes on it
events.summary: In Wisconsin, a narrator complains that “groceries, utilities, everything’s getting more expensive and Congressman (Derrick) Van Orden is adding to the list. He voted for the costly  Iran war  and  spiking gas prices .” In Nebraska, Democratic candidate Chris Backemeyer says families are drowning. “And Mike Flood opened the gates. Flood voted six times for Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war, flooding us with higher prices on groceries, gas, cars and medicine, costing us a thousand dollars more a year.” And in Iowa, a group called Vote Vets Action Fund said Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson voted five times for the Iran war, “giving us record prices for gas and fertilizer.” Those ads are but a few examples of how Democrats and aligned advocacy groups are using an  unpopular  war as they challenge Republicans, aiming to win back power in the House and Senate. It’s the culmination of a strategy Democrats launched in the spring, when they began to repeatedly bring up war powers resolutions aimed at ending the conflict. The votes had little practical effect, but forced lawmakers to go on record and take a stand. Now those votes are being highlighted in campaign ads across the country, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which charts media spending. In some cases, the Republicans targeted have never served in Congress before, so they couldn’t possibly have voted on the various war powers resolutions. Even then, Democrats are portraying them as destined to be rubber stamps for President Donald Trump when it comes to the war. Tying the war to the cost of living The Associated Press analyzed data on broadcast and cable ads aired from Sept. 1 through Oct. 14 in the most competitive midterm races. The analysis focused on House and Senate races rated as either tossups or leaning Democratic or Republican by the Cook Political Report. A smaller number of streaming ads were also examined. At least half of the 50 races featured Iran-related ads, most of which included household cost-of-living messages. All told, the ads aired on TV more than 43,000 times since Sept. 1, costing an estimated $42 million. The AP used both AdImpact’s own issue designations along with additional analysis of the ads’ language to identify them. Of the 65 unique Iran-themed ads identified by the AP, 61 of them stressed household cost-of-living messages such as rising prices for fuel and other items. The Republican playbook Republicans are largely ignoring the Iran war in their ads. Their best strategy is to go after Democratic weaknesses so voters say “this guy is worse,” said Ron Bonjean, a Republican strategist. “In the end, you’re trying to get as many Republicans out to vote for you as possible and bring over some independents,” Bonjean said. “And talking about the Iran war is really not a winning message because you’re playing on the Democratic turf.” The major themes addressed in the Republican advertising since Sept. 1 are taxes and crime, followed by issues tied to character, healthcare and immigration. Some Republicans have sought to distance themselves from the Iran conflict outside the airwaves. In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate  Mike Rogers  has said the “war with Iran needs to end — and end quickly.” His opponent, Democratic nominee  Abdul El-Sayed,  has run ads saying that a billion dollars a day is going to a war “we have no business fighting” and he was running to “invest our tax dollars here in Michigan.” In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins emphasized in a recent debate that she voted nine times to end the conflict, prompting Democratic challenger Troy Jackson to say she voted five times to “make it happen.” In all, the Senate has voted 14 times on resolutions seeking to halt or restrict Trump’s military action against Iran. The House has held six such votes since the conflict began in late February. In the  latest House vote , seven Republicans ended up siding with Democrats in voting to end the war. That includes four Republicans seeking reelection in highly competitive districts: Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn in Iowa. Barrett and Fitzpatrick had voted previously to remove U.S. troops from hostilities, but the yes votes were the first for  Miller-Meeks and Nunn , reflecting the growing weariness with the war. Where Iran ads are most prevalent While the Iran war ads made up about 5% of the total TV spots aired across the competitive races, some contests leaned into the topic heavily. The highest concentration was in California’s 48th Congressional District in the San Diego area. Roughly a third of the 12,000 aired ads touch on Iran. Democrats are seizing on a remark that Republican Jim Desmond made in the early days of the war, in which he said “no pain, no gain” as part of an interview on Real America’s Voice. He also said in that interview he believed the higher prices were just “a spike” and would come down once the U.S. eliminated Iran’s nuclear capability. “No pain, no gain?” asks an ad from Democratic candidate Marni von Wilpert. “Tell that to a family filling up their gas tank.” Desmond and the National Republican Congressional Committee responded with an ad that doesn’t mention Iran but criticizes von Wilpert for raising taxes and fees when she was on the San Diego City Council. In contrast, the ad says Desmond fought to lower costs and supports suspending the gas tax. Not far behind in Iran-related ads are Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, now held by Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans, and Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, an open seat. Roughly a quarter of the ads in those districts touch on Iran. Both are highly competitive races. Meanwhile, some 4,000 Iran-themed ads have aired in Ohio, or about 4% of the total in one of the nation’s  most expensive contests . Nearly all were from Democrat Sherrod Brown’s campaign and leaned heavily on pocketbook themes. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Photos: No Kings rallies in US urge midterm voters to cast ballots early
events.summary: Thousands gathered at events throughout the country on Saturday, building on two years of No Kings marches. Rallies organised by the No Kings network opposed to United States President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the US, with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections. No Kings has more than 3,000 events planned across the US. The planned events, this time dubbed “No Kings: Vote Early”, were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency. “It’s a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard,” organisers said in a statement. By advocating for voting early, the “No Kings” organisers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance once election day rolls around. A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft. At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the November 3 general election. “The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he said. “You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a superhero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.” Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. His administration sued California election officials Thursday , asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. On Friday, the Department of Justice warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. Earlier that day, Democratic Senators Alex Padilla of California, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Dick Durbin of Illinois wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche, demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

events.title: Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands took to the streets for separate demonstrations, putting pressure on governments across the EU. Hundreds of thousands of Europeans have taken to the streets in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries. Saturday’s wave of unrest in Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal has put pressure on governments across the European Union. list 1 of 3 Albanian police fire rubber bullets as protests against Rama escalate list 2 of 3 Tear gas and unrest as hundreds of thousands protest for reforms in France list 3 of 3 Buildings and cars set on fire as cost of living protests rock France France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with more than 550,000 people joining demonstrations, according to the Ministry of Interior, and police facing off with protesters across the country. The marches, which followed weeks of student protests, degenerated into clashes, looting and fires after violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets, as well as attacked police vehicles and officers. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were hurt. “It’s a miracle the toll wasn’t higher,” he said as he visited officers deployed in central Paris. Dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg, the French news agency AFP reported. Whole streets in the capital “have been devastated”, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said. A fire set by masked protesters in Limoges largely destroyed the more than 140-year-old town hall, while city halls in Marseille and Lille were broken into and vandalised. In Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office. President Emmanuel Macron said on X that those responsible would be “prosecuted and punished”. In Belgium’s capital, Brussels – which has already seen weeks of protests by students against university registration fees – police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters, whom they accused of launching missiles at them and setting fires. In Liege, a smaller city east of Brussels, police also deployed water cannon to break up demonstrations. Police did not say how many people attended. Meanwhile, in the Portuguese capital of Lisbon, an estimated tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost of living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled ⁠⁠since 2017, while rents for new leases have increased nearly as much. Portuguese Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos ‌‌Abreu ‌‌Amorim said on Friday that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”. Protesters said their leaders are “out of touch” with the problem. In Milan and Bologna, Italian police reported that, alongside peaceful cost-of-living rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers. Italian media reported several injuries and arrests. Although protests in the other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of EU law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera. “France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said. He said Saturday’s protests may not be the last in many of these countries and new hotspots could emerge. In Greece, Germany, and Austria, the “early stages” of a movement are emerging, with mobilisation expected “in the coming week”, he said. They are not a single movement, he explained, but several protests happening at the same time, with some “shared grievances”: underfunded education, rising living costs and, for students, uncertain prospects after graduation. The unrest comes at a crucial time for Europe, Alemanno said, as the continent prepares for an “unprecedented super-cycle of national elections” in the coming 12 months, with votes scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland. “Inevitably, all these protests, all these mobilisations, are going to be at the centre of the political conversation,” Alemanno said.

events.title: From the navy to bullion trading: Start-up founder builds wealth through precious metals, discipline
events.summary: Ian Chan invested a significant portion of his personal savings and profits from previous investments to start precious metals trading company Big Bullion in December 2025, along with financial support from his family. SINGAPORE – Former naval officer Ian Chan enjoyed his time at sea, although he sometimes struggled with seasickness. “I eventually decided not to continue along that path, which was a difficult decision because serving the nation was something I genuinely wanted to do,” he said. The 25-year-old subsequently invested a significant portion of his personal savings and profits from previous investments to start precious metals trading company Big Bullion in December 2025, along with financial support from his family. The company has generated about $1.5 million in revenue thus far, comprising $1.2 million from investment-grade gold and silver bullion and the remainder from buying back precious metals jewellery for refining. Big Bullion is expected to become profitable by December 2026. However, getting the business off the ground came with its own challenges, from establishing relationships with reliable suppliers, to sourcing gold and silver inventory, to developing hedging strategies to manage fluctuations in bullion prices. “The experience has taught me the importance of managing business finances carefully, particularly cash flow and working capital,” said Chan. The final-year student at NUS Business School added that he hopes to make investing in precious metals more accessible to younger Singaporeans through social media and educational content that explains how gold and silver pricing, premiums and buyback values work. “Ultimately, our goal is not just to sell precious metals, but also to help customers better understand what they are buying, how pricing works and how physical gold and silver may fit into their broader financial plans,” he said. Chan is engaged to his 25-year-old fiancee, who also helps him with his business. Q: Do you invest? If so, what do you invest in and why? Apart from precious metals, I also invest in a broad range of stocks, including exposure to the US market through indexes such as the S&P 500. Equities give me exposure to businesses around the world and the potential for long-term capital growth. I also believe liquidity is important. Cash gives me the flexibility to meet short-term needs, manage unexpected expenses and take advantage of opportunities without having to sell investments at an unfavourable time. Q: What is your biggest or most valuable asset right now? My business is one of my most valuable assets, alongside my gold and silver holdings. Building a business has also taught me that an asset’s value is not always immediately reflected in a bank balance. It can lie in the relationships, systems, knowledge and opportunities built over time. Q: What is your approach to growing your money? I believe younger investors with longer time horizons can generally consider taking more investment risk, provided they understand what they are investing in and can withstand potential losses. At the same time, taking risk does not mean concentrating everything in one asset. Diversification is important because different assets behave differently under different market conditions. Above all, I believe consistency matters. It is tempting to keep searching for the next big opportunity, but building wealth often comes down to investing regularly, controlling costs and allowing time for compounding to work. Q: What was your first exposure to investing, and what was your first investment? My first investment was at the end of national service, when I put about $200 into the S&P 500. It was a small amount, but it gave me a starting point. Q: What has been your biggest financial mistake? One area I could have managed better was my use of Singapore’s tax-advantaged savings schemes, particularly the Central Provident Fund and Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS), where additional contributions may have been appropriate for my circumstances. The right CPF or SRS contribution depends on factors such as eligibility, tax bracket, liquidity needs and long-term plans, so it is not simply a matter of contributing as much as possible. Q: What has been your best financial decision? One of my best financial decisions has been consistently spending below my means and investing at least 20% of my income, even when it was tempting to spend more or pause investing. I have dollar-cost averaged into investments over approximately seven years, including diversified US equities and precious metals. This has helped me develop discipline rather than trying to predict the perfect time to enter the market. I have also been grateful that I learnt the importance of insurance planning early. Arranging appropriate coverage while younger helped me secure protection before potentially facing higher premiums or changes in insurability later on. Q: Moneywise, what were your growing-up years like?

events.title: MapQuest now shows you Flock and other license plate reader cameras on your route
events.summary: A new MapQuest feature allows users to find license plate reader cameras in their area. St. Louis Post-Dispatch/Contributor/Getty Images; Business Insider MapQuest is pulling the curtain back on automatic license plate readers. Users can now locate Flock Safety and other surveillance cameras on MapQuest's app. Critics of the tech have raised privacy concerns and potential misuse. MapQuest, the OG software to find your way from point A to point B , is taking on the surveillance state. The free mapping service unveiled a new feature for its mobile app on Thursday that allows users to turn on a "surveillance layer" on a map to locate known automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, along their route. MapQuest says the app can identify cameras developed by Flock Safety , Axon Enterprise , Motorola Solutions, and PlateSmart, among others. "The Roads Have Eyes!" the company said in its BlueSky post announcing the new feature. The Roads Have Eyes! 👁️ Turn on the Surveillance Layer in Map Options to see known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other outdoor surveillance cameras. [image or embed] — MapQuest ( @mapquest.com ) October 15, 2026 at 6:49 PM MapQuest's General Manager Doug Berger said drivers using the service inspired the company to add the feature. "We build around what drivers ask for, and showing surveillance camera locations is one of our users' top three requests," Berger told Business Insider in a statement." License plate readers capture images of vehicles and then use machine learning to turn details such as license plate numbers, car make, color, and model into searchable data. They're commonly found at intersections, parking lots , roadways, highways, and neighborhood entrances, businesses, and private properties. Law enforcement agencies initially embraced license plate readers to help them locate vehicles and identify suspects. Retail outlets have also used Flock cameras as part of their security efforts. A major backlash against the cameras, however, has led stores, police, and towns to dial back their use. Critics say the cameras raise privacy concerns and that the data they collect can be misused or shared with federal immigration officials. Some people who've opposed the cameras have staged protests, launched petitions, and even forcibly removed them. The city of Tempe in Arizona said in August it shut down its Flock Safety camera network and planned to terminate its contract. Other towns followed suit. "These cameras have helped our police officers do their jobs, and we don't discount that," Tempe Mayor Corey Woods said in a public statement at the time. "But the risk of misuse is too great. We have to be able to provide public safety in a way that maintains the trust of our community. For Tempe, that means taking these cameras down." Flock says its license plate readers do not use facial recognition and that customers — meaning the ones putting up the cameras — can control access to and sharing of the data collected. Amid growing backlash, the company has tightened its privacy safeguards , including reducing the time data is retained from 30 days to 7 days. "They are built to focus on the vehicle involved in an incident and the details that can help distinguish it from other vehicles on the road," Flock told Business Insider in August. MapQuest first launched in the late 1990s, allowing users to map out a route and print directions. The release of Google Maps eventually obliterated the service. As it tries to stay relevant, it has jumped at opportunities to leverage prevailing public discourse. In August, MapQuest briefly topped app stores after it — unlike Google — rebuffed President Donald Trump's executive order to rename "Lake Ontario" to "Lake America." The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday. Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates. Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%. Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.” One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.” In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized. Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining. The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. events.title: My daughter and I drove 2,000 miles to college. It was the best goodbye I could've asked for.
events.summary: The author and her daughter drove 2,000 miles to drop her off at college. Courtesy of the author My daughter and I took the scenic route from Oregon to her college in Missouri. We camped near Yellowstone, explored Wyoming, and visited South Dakota landmarks. The trip gave us precious time together before she started her independent life. After buying a car for my daughter to take to college, the problem was getting the little Mazda from Portland, Oregon, to Fulton, Missouri. Maria and I are fun in the car, but awful at driving long distances. We checked the miles, over 2,000, and groaned. "Are we doing this?" I asked. "Remember Eugene?" We laughed, thinking about the time after an exhausting day, we couldn't manage the usual three hours from Eugene, Oregon , to Portland without stopping every 10 to 15 minutes. We took turns saying, "Your turn," as we blasted cold air and chomped Good 'n' Plenty licorice to stay awake. Eventually, we napped at a rest stop. I finished the drive and let Maria sleep. We took the scenic route to college "Let's make it an adventure," Maria said when we were debating whether to take the scenic route. She knows I love sleeping in a tent and waking up outdoors. Being in nature would ease my aching heart, already missing her. I savored our time before we even started. We mapped our route, picking the long way. In Yellowstone, we tented next to a motorhome complete with a satellite and TV. We cracked up as we popped up our two-person tent in the RV's shadow. In the morning, it was a quick coffee and on to gawking our way through the park, pointing at bison, moose, elk, deer, wolves, and more. At a geyser view spot, a tourist tried to touch a bull moose with a huge rack of horns while onlookers poised their phones. We made so many memories together We drove across Wyoming with its wide-open spaces and the prettiest blue skies. Then camped at Custer State Park, our tent site flanking a river. In the morning, we plopped on a log and sipped cowboy (unfiltered) coffee. "So much better than flying," I said, surprising myself. Our awe was mild at Mt. Rushmore , where we snapped bad tourist pictures, pretending to squish the presidents' heads between thumb and index finger as a curly-haired woman in white pointy Keds glared at us. The author and her daughter made of the trip an adventure. Courtesy of the author Then, onto Crazy Horse : a massive monument of Crazy Horse, the Lakota leader, still being carved out of the mountain. I cried at its mass, its beauty, its story. For scale, Mt. Rushmore could fit in the finger that points to his people's land. Next was the iconic Wall Drug, where we stretched our bodies, then drove on to the Corn Palace . "All corn?" I asked. Yes, beautiful, detailed murals crafted of corn and other grains covered the Moorish building. The road trip made me less sad to see her go Endless signs in Kansas enticed us with the World's Largest Prairie Dog, a live five-legged cow, plus rattlesnakes. Even though the prairie dog turned out to be a 15-foot-tall, four-ton concrete statue, it topped our list for fun roadside attractions and included a bonus rattlesnake "pit" in a gift shop where rattlers slept in terrariums. The cashier's nametag said Suzy. She hit the tops of the cages with a cane, startling the snakes to shake their rattling tails. We jumped too. "It's OK," I told Suzy, my hand up in the universal sign for stop. "Let them rest." "You paid to see 'em," she rasped, whapping another terrarium as Maria gave her the side-eye. We held our belly laughs in until we reached the car. The author and her daughter camped throughout their trip. Courtesy of the author We stopped at rest stops and gas stations. Drank sparkling water (me) and soda (her). Snacked on chips and Wheat Thins. Took rinse showers at campsites. The only time we drove semi-sleepily was through Kansas with the obligatory, "Are we there yet?" And "Can you drive?" It wasn't as bad as that haul from Eugene home, but the straight flat is hypnotizing. "My turn. I got you," Maria said, tightening her ponytail and her resolve. I saw her on the cusp of her grown life as she drove the last leg, singing full tilt, our playlist a mix of Garth Brooks, Earth, Wind & Fire, The Chicks, and more. Willie Nelson sang us across the country. We played "On the Road Again" every morning, every time we restarted, every time we crossed a state line. Whenever I hear "Making music with my friends" it's my daughter I think of. Once we reached Fulton, Missouri, I knew I could fly home without my girl. We were both ready. While it was bittersweet to drop my dream-chasing kids — first my son, then my daughter — at college, that year my excitement for her overshadowed my sadness. We'll always have the rattlesnakes. We've laughed about them ever since. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘How many canaries have we killed in the coal mine?’ — Wall Street debates if the latest AI bubble warnings are another head fake or the real thing
events.summary: Since the advent of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022, the list of possible indicators that the AI boom was about to go bust is long and keeps getting longer, leaving Wall Street asking each time if the end is finally near. For instance, whenever AI chip giant Nvidia saw its market cap cross the $2 trillion, $3 trillion, $4 trillion or $5 trillion milestones, bears sounded the alarm. The borrowing binge by AI hyperscalers and their astronomical capital spending plans raised more red flags. The DeepSeek shock in early 2025 triggered another freakout as the Chinese AI model stirred doubts about the necessity of all that capex. Also last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s admission that an AI bubble exists and Michael Burry’s bearish bets represented more red flags. This year, the Iran war, the South Korean stock market’s meltdown, and “circular” funding deals between AI companies added to the fears. But earnings continued to soar, and stocks eventually rebounded to set record high after record high. Of course, the persistence of traders to keep doubling down on AI could also be a sign of a bubble. Many on Wall Street also acknowledge that the good times will come to an end at some point. The only question is how long to ride the AI bets without leaving money on the table. Now there’s a new reason to wonder if it’s time to cash out. The current AI angst centers around whether the trillions of dollars in AI spending will pay off sufficiently, dragging down debt-laden companies like CoreWeave. The neoclound computing firm saw its stock tumble and credit default swaps surge recently. For Dan Greenhaus, strategist at Solus Alternative Asset Management, CoreWeave isn’t a canary in the coal mine that signals the AI bust is imminent. “How many canaries have we killed in the coal mine over the last three years as everybody has latched on to every new sign of weakness so to speak as evidence that the bull market was about to end only to see the broad market, both tech and otherwise, go on to make new highs?” he told CNBC on Friday. “So I don’t know that I would read any more into what’s happening now than I would have or did any of the other headlines.” To be sure, borrowing costs have jumped as the Iran war and oil prices sent bond yields to the highest levels in more than 20 years. The Federal Reserve is also hiking rates again to rein in stubborn inflation. That’s put more scrutiny on the riskier areas of the AI boom, which has grown increasingly reliant on issuing debt via the bond market. But Greenhaus pointed out that CoreWeave’s unsecured debt has been especially targeted, calling it “the riskier of the riskier AI buildout play.” Meanwhile, earnings from AI chip suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor indicate the broader demand environment remains robust. At the same time, he also doesn’t expect companies across the AI ecosystem will be able to keep financing themselves indefinitely as rates go higher. “I don’t know whether this is the breaking point or another 25 or 50 basis points higher is the breaking point,” Greenhaus explained. “But as rates move higher, the more speculative tails so to speak of the buildout are going to be called into question, and right now that’s CoreWeave.” For its part, CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said markets can “misunderstand and act irrationally” and told employees in a memo that the company’s deal backlog is more than enough to sustain its debt obligations. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang also backed CoreWeave, which counts the chipmaker as a shareholder, saying it does not need a financial backstop. “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” he told Bloomberg . “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.” Others on Wall Street also see strong demand for AI and think the recent selloff is yet another buying opportunity. Still, even eye-popping revenue estimates may not be enough to support sky-high spending. On Wednesday, Gartner warned AI data center owners need to generate a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030 to cover capital spending, financing costs, and a 12% return. But total enterprise and consumer AI revenue that’s headed to data centers will only be $3.6 trillion at most, putting more than $4 trillion in asset value exposed to write-down risk through 2032. On Friday, analysts at Bank of America said in a note that the AI investment boom is following a classic capital cycle, which usually end in disappointment “even though the underlying technology often lived up to expectations.” Typically, early profit margins tend to be high, driving overinvestment and excess capacity while also attracting more competition. In AI’s case, competition has already ramped up, especially from Chinese open-weight models. On top of that, business spending on AI has started to dip, as higher token volumes fail to offset lower prices for tokens. “This monetization disappointment in the face of intense competition is precisely the failure mode seen in past capital cycles,” BofA added. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions, Zelenskyy condemns it as 'wrong'
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump invoked the Graham Act’s national-interest waiver to suspend new duties on Russian goods and major Russian energy buyers. The moves drew praise from a Russian envoy and criticism from Democrats and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The waiver came two days before the law’s implementation deadline and follows a separate temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine. "... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X . "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people." President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving key parts of the new U.S. sanctions on Russia. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order. The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham , a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina. Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas. Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders. Zelenskyy said he expects Trump to waive other sanctions on Russia, too. "Sanctions relief will continue," he posted on X. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately." The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran. Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort. The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran. High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. "The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X. "The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added. But Trump's opponents have criticized the move. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver. "Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy had warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry." Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

events.title: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as protests against Rama escalate
events.summary: Five days of clashes rock Tirana as students join a wider movement demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Police in Albania have fired rubber bullets at antigovernment protesters in the capital, Tirana, as violent clashes intensify over demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The clashes continued on Saturday for a fifth consecutive day after high school and university students joined a broader movement against Rama, whose governing centre-left Socialist Party has held power since 2013. list 1 of 2 ‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama list 2 of 2 Albania’s PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for protests The unrest has brought growing anger over education, unemployment and alleged corruption into a wider confrontation with the government. Protesters threw stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police near Rama’s office and elsewhere in central Tirana. Some set cars and rubbish bins alight, creating burning barricades across streets. Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges as demonstrators pushed against security lines. The AFP news agency reported that officers used rubber bullets for the first time since the demonstrations began. National police chief Skender Hita confirmed their use at a news conference on Saturday, saying they had been deployed “in a limited manner”. The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare said nine protesters and four police officers received medical treatment on Saturday. Hita said 167 people had been arrested over five days of unrest, while 132 officers had been injured. Seven police officers were also suspended pending investigations into allegations that they had exceeded their authority. Rama, who is serving his fourth term and has refused to resign, visited businesses damaged during the unrest on Saturday. He promised to listen to students and protect their right to demonstrate, while warning against further destruction. He also accused his conservative political opponents of encouraging the violence. The students have complained about expensive university fees, poor educational facilities and limited employment opportunities, alongside allegations of government corruption. At the start of Saturday’s demonstration, protesters set fire to a suitcase and threw it into the Ministry of Education’s courtyard. AFP reported that the gesture symbolised their determination not to leave Albania in search of better opportunities. “We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country,” journalism student Sinan Billa told AFP. The student demonstrations have added to months of antigovernment rallies organised by the Flamingo movement, which began as a campaign against a luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast. The project is linked to an investment company founded by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. The movement has since widened its demands to include Rama’s resignation amid allegations of corruption against his government. The unrest has also spread beyond Tirana. Local media reported that protesters in the coastal city of Durres damaged a post office and blocked roads with burning barricades, extending the confrontations beyond the capital.

events.title: Trump's Russia waiver draws instant bipartisan backlash
events.summary: Top Republicans and Democrats alike lined up Saturday to condemn President Trump 's decision to waive recent sanctions on Russia , calling it "irresponsible" and "a deal with the devil." Why it matters : Trump already faces a bipartisan effort to overturn his Russian diesel deal when Congress returns after the election. Now he may have to deal with even broader outrage over sanctions Congress approved just a month ago. Driving the news: Late Friday night, Trump issued an executive order waiving implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed in September. The act would have imposed broad sanctions not only on Russia, but on other countries buying its oil. What they're saying: Democrats forcefully criticized Trump's decision. "By giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote . "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. Republicans were equally unsparing. "We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up. We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine," Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) wrote . "I have requested a classified briefing on the rationale for this decision." "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled." One soon-to-depart congressman , Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), hinted at the trouble Trump may face when Congress returns. "Congress has a lame-duck session. The President has an agenda: supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc… I think the agenda is dead. Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus," Bacon wrote . For the record: The White House defended Trump's decision. "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests." What to watch: The question now is just how hard Congress will push back when it returns in a few weeks.

events.title: Hiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue sky
events.summary: As the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastened It was a swelteringly hot afternoon in south-west Myanmar on 21 May 2024. Tropical thunderstorms, showers and highs of 36C were forecast for the area around the Irrawaddy Basin. High above, monsoonal heat and humidity were building into a vast convective column of water vapour, a towering cumulonimbus cloud soaring up to 35,000ft (more than 10,500 metres) into the air. From the ground, it would have looked like something from a children’s picture book – a soft, fluffy white mass. But for Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 passing just above, it was anything but benign. In the cabin of the Boeing 777, passengers were being woken up for breakfast with three hours to go on the journey from London to Singapore. For the 210 travellers on board, the past 10 hours had been uneventful. The seatbelt signs were off. Some were milling around, others were using the toilets, and cabin staff were preparing trolleys for service. At 2.19pm and 23 seconds local time, moderate turbulence shook the plane for 17 seconds and the seatbelt sign was switched on. Then, as one passenger described it, it was “like a grenade had gone off”. In just 4.6 seconds, any passenger not strapped in hit the roof with 1.5 times the force of gravity and was thrown back on the floor in an instant. Passengers reported hearing people screaming in agony, blood streaming down faces, with overhead panels broken by the force of bodies hitting them. One person was left dead and 79 were seriously injured. The turbulence had lasted just over 21 seconds. While SQ321 was an extreme case that made global headlines , turbulence is the leading cause of injuries to passengers and crew in non-fatal accidents, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Figures from the Federal Aviation Administration record about a dozen serious injuries a year from turbulence across the US alone. It can be caused by a multitude of factors, including geographic features such as mountains – the top 10 most turbulent routes are all over either the Andes or the Himalayas. Some forms, such as the type caused by mountains and wake turbulence, which is caused by other aircraft, are fairly well understood and avoided. Pilots have always had to contend with the sky’s speed bumps as part of the job. But the threat of turbulence across the world is increasing due to the climate crisis. Not only will pilots need to contend with the frequency and severity of these episodes rising, they’re facing a future that includes a large surge in clear-air turbulence – an invisible, largely undetectable turbulence that comes, quite literally, out of the blue. Richard Woodward is a former Royal Australian Air Force test pilot and Qantas A380 captain who served the airline for 32 years. He has flown routes all around the world and has seen more than his fair share of difficult conditions, including flying over a cyclone (it was surprisingly smooth and the radar “painted it beautifully”). But Woodward says airlines and the aviation industry are increasingly aware of the threat posed by global heating. “There’ll be an increase in the severity of thunderstorms and storms in general because, as the planet warms, the amount of energy inputting into these events will become massively greater,” he says. Thunderstorm or convective turbulence – the cause of the SQ321 incident – creates strong updrafts, then strong downdrafts as the air and water vapour cool. It may be encountered several thousand feet above clouds and as far as 20 miles (more than 30km) on either side. This can be particularly dangerous, Woodward says, given that “there’s more energy in a typical thunderstorm than there is in a nuclear weapon”. That massive amount of energy can be seen in lightning – which sometimes even reaches into space, Woodward says – but it also manifests in turbulence. More heat, and greater differences between hot and cold areas, will supercharge already powerful thunderstorms. It’s a problem that pilots and passengers have encountered in Australia. In the same month as the SQ321 episode, a Qantas Boeing 737 encountered severe turbulence while on approach to Brisbane airport after entering a storm cloud at 11,400ft. Three cabin crew, who were not seated at the time, were injured; one was left with a broken ankle. Another crew member with an undiagnosed concussion returned to work on several subsequent flights without medical attention. The Australian Transport Safety Board report was highly critical of the airline’s response, saying the crew member “returning to work with an undiagnosed concussion likely compromised [their] ability to perform safety-critical tasks”. Qantas has since overhauled its safety protocols for crew injuries.

events.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well. events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Attacks hit several parts of the Strip as UNICEF reports more than 340 children killed since ‘ceasefire’ began a year ago. Israeli drone attacks have killed at least six Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, according to Palestinian medical and emergency workers, as deadly raids continue despite a year-old “ceasefire”. The attacks on Saturday were in northern, central and southern Gaza, with one of the latest reported deaths near Jabalia refugee camp. list 1 of 3 The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu list 2 of 3 Israeli raids and arrests in southern Syria push population to the brink list 3 of 3 As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing A Palestinian man was killed and several others wounded when an Israeli drone struck a group of civilians near al-Faluja cemetery, west of Jabalia, reported the Palestinian Wafa news agency, citing medical sources. One Palestinian was killed and several injured when an Israeli drone struck the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, Wafa said. Earlier, two people were killed and others wounded in an attack in the Tuffah neighbourhood of northeast Gaza City, according to staff at al-Shifa Hospital. Witnesses told Al Jazeera that the people hit were returning from the burial of an earlier attack victim. Another person was killed in a drone attack in eastern Gaza City, al-Shifa Hospital said. In central Gaza, staff at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital reported one person killed and another injured in Deir el-Balah. In an update issued on Saturday, Gaza’s Health Ministry said 1,511 Palestinians had been killed and 5,375 injured since the United States-brokered “ceasefire” was announced on October 10, 2025. In an update covering the preceding 48 hours, the ministry reported six deaths and 43 injuries across the strip. It said 74,469 Palestinians had been killed and 175,492 injured since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023. The continuing toll on children was highlighted on Friday by UNICEF, the United Nations children’s agency. Speaking to reporters in Geneva, spokesman Ricardo Pires said more than 340 children had been killed since the ceasefire began. He said seven children had died in attacks over the previous two weeks, with at least 33 others seriously injured. UNICEF said about 800,000 children remained displaced, many in tents or unsafe buildings as winter approaches. The violence comes as Gaza’s population faces growing restrictions on where to live. Mapping published by Al Jazeera on October 12 showed Israeli forces control or restrict access to about 65 percent of the territory. The “Yellow Line”, initially established to mark Israeli military positions after a partial withdrawal under the “ceasefire”, has been pushed further into Palestinian areas, the report said. The remaining accessible area is home to 2.1 million people. On Friday, Gaza’s Health Ministry warned that more than 1.4 million Palestinians were projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse for the rest of the year.

events.title: My 2 friends and I had babies within 3 weeks of each other after 25 years of friendship. Our group chat became a lifeline.
events.summary: The author (center) has been friends with two women since their years together at boarding school. Motherhood, she said, has brought them closer. Courtesy of Shea Karssing. Our friendship formed over questionable decisions, break-ups, hangovers, and, eventually, the messy business of becoming adults. Then, three baby girls born in three cities over three weeks started a completely new chapter. Our connection became our parenting lifeline, proving that the best friendships grow with you. "What a night!" "I barely slept." "I don't even know what time I went to bed." The same statements can have very different meanings in different stages of life . My friends and I used to worry about where everyone was at 2 a.m. Now, we worry about whether everyone's baby has pooped that day. Laura-Kate (Lauks), Kirsten (Kirst), and I met 25 years ago at an all-girls boarding school in South Africa, then partied our way through university and early adulthood. For years, our biggest problems were nursing sore heads with painkillers and junk food, who was dating whom, where we were going that weekend, and whether anyone had taken a particularly unflattering photo. Then, the three of us had babies all within three weeks of one another, reaffirming our bond and allowing us to evolve together in new and exciting ways I never imagined. The author (center) said that life took her and her friends in different directions, but motherhood helped them bond in a new way. Courtesy of Shea Karssing. Real adulthood happened Lauks got pregnant unexpectedly, bravely navigating the challenges of being a semi-single mom with a husband who works abroad for up to three months at a time. In the same period, Kirst and her American husband settled in the US, and I was undergoing IVF treatment. We all had our own challenges. Fast forward a bit, and Lauks told us she was expecting another unplanned surprise . It was a contrast to my own fertility journey, which had been a roller coaster of disappointments, including a failed embryo transfer. I was about to undergo a second transfer when she gave us the news over group text. Lauks lives in a town about an hour from me. It happens to be on the way to my fertility doctor. On one drive home, soon after sharing her good news, I stopped to see Lauks to congratulate her. I was also six weeks pregnant at the time. I remember sitting there in the cafe trying to get the words out: "I'm pregnant." Cue the ugly crying. Of course, my next phone call was to Kirst in the US. Little did I know that she had some news she was itching to tell me too. All three of us were pregnant at the same time. The tone of our WhatsApp group changed immediately After comparing and complaining about our pregnancy symptoms for months, one baby arrived, then another, then another. We all arrived at motherhood differently, but we each welcomed a baby girl into the world within three weeks across three different cities (and two continents), and our friendship acquired an entirely new vocabulary. We had once bonded over crushes, kisses, and hangovers. Now, we talked about latching, snot-sucking, and the intricate details of every strange rash. The conversations may have been less titillating, but somehow, they were even more intimate. Our WhatsApp group became a kind of 24-hour maternal helpline. "Does this look normal?" Reply at 3 am: "Yes, unfortunately." We sent memes when we were too exhausted to form sentences. We celebrated first smiles and first rolls. We talked about periods, pimples, sex, husbands, and everything else that apparently becomes acceptable conversation once you've been friends for 25 years. Then, the group chat blew up with more surprises Earlier this year, Kirsten let us know that baby number two was on the way. This time, it was me bubbling over inside, dying to tell them that I had gotten pregnant naturally. In August, Kirst gave birth to a baby boy, and my baby girl arrived in September. Although we haven't been in the same room since Kirst moved to the US three years ago, we remain as close as ever, if not closer. My girls are my cheerleaders, doulas, online health advisors, and a massive reason why I've stayed sane (enough) as a mother. They've shown me the power of long-term friendship and the ways women can lift each other up. The author said that distance doesn't keep her from staying connected to her friends and looks forward to seeing how their relationship continues to evolve over time. Courtesy of Shea Karssing. In another 25 years, we'll be in our 60s I can't help but imagine what another 25 years will do to our friendship. We'll be in our 60s, and the kids will (hopefully) be fending for themselves out in the world. Along with the gray hairs and wrinkles, our priorities will have probably changed once again. After the first 25 years, I've learned that the best friendships don't stay the same, they grow with you. So I know my besties will still be there for me, just with entirely new things to commiserate over, cry over, and kill ourselves laughing about. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The tactics used by companies to push pregnant women out of work
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts How pregnancy discrimination is pushing Australian women out of the workforce When Abby McCawley found out she was having a girl, she sent a message to her coworkers to share the exciting news. "Everyone around me was so happy, including the people I worked for and the people I worked with," she said. Abby was five months into her role as a rental property manager at Ray White Brunswick in Melbourne's inner north. After taking two days off work to manage morning sickness, Abby returned to her desk in the office and discovered something odd. She couldn't log onto her computer. Moments later, Abby's boss called her into his office and terminated her employment. Abby McCawley believes she experienced pregnancy discrimination. ( Four Corners: Ron Foley ) "I was shocked, I was upset … I thought about the baby. "I just thought, 'I haven't done anything wrong, why am I being let go?'" Abby said she had never received warnings she wasn't performing. More than 100 women have told Four Corners they lost work after becoming pregnant or having a child. Some were employed at Australia's biggest companies, and nearly a quarter worked in the public sector. Together, the cases reveal the problem is far bigger than a few bad bosses. After analysing dozens of cases, Four Corners has established a collection of tactics used to push mothers out of the workforce, revealing an unwritten playbook used by employers. Fired after being publicly praised by the company on social media In the weeks before Abby was let go, she had no idea her job was at risk. Then, in her first trimester, she asked to work remotely for a few hours to manage morning sickness. Her request was denied by the office manager. Instead, Abby was told a new policy required employees to give a day's notice to work from home. "It [was] quite disappointing, because it's obviously not something that you can predict," she said. Still, Abby felt secure in her job and wasn't worried. A week before Ray White Brunswick terminated Abby's employment, the real estate agency publicly praised her on Instagram. Ray White Brunswick endorsed Abby McCawley on its Instagram page. When she was fired, Abby said she was told it was partly due to a company restructure. She took her employer to the Fair Work Commission seeking compensation, but mediation failed, so she is now suing Ray White Brunswick in the Federal Court. Her lawyer, Laura Blandthorn from Solidarity Solicitors, alleged Abby had experienced "very clear, direct discrimination based on her pregnancy". She said Abby was initially told her employment was terminated due to an "office restructure", then was later advised it was due to "performance reasons". Laura Blandthorn represents Abby McCawley. ( Four Corners: Ron Foley ) Ray White Brunswick's director Jamil Allouche declined an interview with Four Corners. In a statement, he said: "Abby's employment was terminated for the reasons that we discussed with her at the time her employment ended. "Those reasons related to her behaviour in the workplace, reported to me by other employees and observed by me as the decision-maker. "As the matter is currently before the court, I am not able to comment further, and I will allow the process to take its course." Mr Allouche did not respond to further questions about what that behaviour was. Lawyer Susan Price, from the Working Women's Centre NSW, has represented women facing pregnancy discrimination for decades and said in other cases, criticism of a new or expectant mother's performance in the workplace was common. Susan Price says some mothers are still treated differently at work in Australia. ( Four Corners: Ron Foley ) "You do see what I describe as a real shift in attitude towards a worker once they've come into the workplace and announced they're pregnant," she said. "It's almost like that worker has now been identified as a problem and things that were absolutely fine before, start to get criticised, their performance gets managed." Twenty-one women told Four Corners they had been let go after becoming pregnant, only to find someone else had taken their job, and in some cases under a different title. It's a practice lawyers call a "sham restructure". Zana Bytheway, executive director of employment rights legal centre JobWatch said it could sometimes happen to women on maternity leave. "They may find their job has been made redundant, but it's often a construct," she said. "Often they found that their actual position … is still there.

events.title: Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest oil reserves and sends 90% of its crude exports to the U.S. — It will vote on a first step to leaving Canada
events.summary: For decades, Alberta separatism was a fringe cause. On Monday, voters in Canada’s oil heartland will decide whether to take the first step toward a referendum on leaving the country. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is not voting to leave Canada on Oct. 19. Instead, voters will decide  whether the province  should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future  referendum on separation . Alberta Premier Danielle Smith , who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said that support for starting the separation process, which was around 23% in a recent poll, is “still too high for my liking.” Alberta has long feuded with the federal government over oil and federal power. Liberal prime ministers  Pierre Trudeau  and, decades later, his son  Justin  became deeply unpopular in the province over energy policy. Justin Trudeau’s government  imposed a national carbon tax  and other climate measures that Alberta leaders said hurt its oil industry. Yet separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote,  former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney  said. Then came the pandemic and  the Freedom Convoy , which paralyzed parts of Ottawa, the Canadian capital, and blocked major Canada-U.S. border crossings. “They needed a new cause,” Kenney told The Associated Press. “And it naturally morphed into separatism.” Pandemic-era restrictions supercharged separatism Jeff Rath, a leader of the independence movement, said federal vaccine rules preventing unvaccinated Canadians from flying were his breaking point. “If Trudeau won’t let me leave Alberta, I’m just going to pick up my whole province and go,” Rath recalled telling a friend. “COVID was really the straw that broke the camel’s back.” “A lot of people were radicalized by the convoy,” he said. The 2022 Freedom Convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a  broader revolt against pandemic restrictions . Kenney said people mobilized over anger at globalization, vaccines and pandemic restrictions, while social media allowed previously isolated activists to find one another and organize. “They found each other and they found a cause,” Kenney said. Kenney said the movement also became more professional, building organizations, raising money and drawing in political operatives with campaign and fundraising experience. He also sees substantial overlap between separatist activists and people who support Russian President Vladimir Putin or believe conspiracy theories about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kenney stressed he was describing activists, not typical separation voters, whom he characterized as frustrated Albertans sending Ottawa a message. Kenney said the MAGA movement has been “inspirational” for some separatist activists. He said they “tried to infiltrate with at least some success” the United Conservative Party he founded. Smith replaced Kenney in 2022 after appealing to United Conservative Party members angry over COVID-19 restrictions. “Literally, you can look at the players,” Kenney said of the convoy and separatist movements. “It’s the same people.” Carney finds unusual support in Alberta Prime Minister Mark Carney  has made getting Alberta oil to new markets a national priority and backs a  proposed pipeline  to the West Coast. His more business- and energy-friendly policies, along with his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and 51st-state rhetoric, have made the federal Liberal leader unusually popular in conservative Alberta. Kenney, one of the most prominent conservative critics of Trudeau’s approach to Alberta, said Carney “speaks as an Albertan,” understands the province’s grievances and aspirations, and is moving in the right direction on energy. Rath called Carney a “formidable opponent,” saying “every major politician” in Alberta and Canada is against the separatists and acknowledged an uphill battle. He said he would be “thrilled” with more than 30% of the vote — well short of a majority. “Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life,” Carney said. “We have to be strong and we are stronger together.” Activists go to Washington Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States, and separatists have taken their campaign directly to Washington. Rath confirmed he and other independence advocates met with U.S. State Department officials three times and presented a document outlining what an independent Alberta could offer the United States. Rath claimed people involved in the meetings were going directly to the White House and that a possible oil pipeline through the U.S. to the Pacific was “literally a topic of our last meeting with the U.S. State Department.” The State Department said that “The Department regularly meets with a wide range of representatives. The vote is a decision for the people of Alberta.” Kenney called the outreach “bonkers,” saying people with “zero democratic mandate” were discussing with a foreign government “the status of a separate state that does not exist.” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta “a natural partner.” Future of separatism Keith Wilson, another Alberta independence leader who was lead counsel for the 2022 convoy organizers, said separatists see the vote as a way to give Alberta more leverage in dealing with Ottawa, even short of independence. “That’s right, because it’s called leverage. It’s called negotiation,” Wilson said. He said he would accept substantial structural changes to Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa short of independence. “I don’t think it will recede,” Kenney said of the separatist movement in Alberta. Even 10% to 20% support, he noted, would far exceed separatists’ historic vote share. If low turnout pushed them toward 30%, “they’re going to be even more emboldened.” “That’s not a threat to Canada,” Kenney said. “But it is a threat to the conservative movement.” Alberta is not Canada’s only national-unity challenge. Quebec voters returned  the separatist Parti Quebecois  to power Oct. 5, although  support for independence  remains around 30% and its leader has said he will not hold a referendum while Trump is U.S. president. Quebec voters have twice rejected independence, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
