events.title: I lived in LA for 20 years. It took moving my 3 kids to a small Arizona town to find what I'd been missing.
events.summary: Jen Podany moved her family from California to Arizona. Courtesy of Jen Podany Jen Podany raised her three children in a busy Los Angeles neighborhood where traffic limited their independence. After moving to a small Arizona town, her kids can ride bikes and play with neighborhood friends. She says their new lifestyle reminds her of the freedom children had growing up in the 1980s. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jen Podany , founder of Bluestone Sunshields. It has been edited for length and clarity. Near the end of 2024, my family of five had once again escaped Los Angeles for the quiet we found 10 hours south in Snowflake, Arizona . We'd been doing it for years, renting an Airbnb in Snowflake, a town of 6,000 in the middle of nowhere, switching off amid the miles of empty land. It had started as a stopover on our way to visit my husband's family in New Mexico . We fell in love with the town, and from then on, we'd visit whenever we needed to get away from the busyness of LA. In Snowflake, we felt like we could catch our breath. Our souls calmed each time we arrived and ached to stay each time we left. We put an offer on a house Back in LA, specifically Burbank, the five of us — my husband and our three children , whom we homeschooled — lived in a duplex made up of two connected apartments. We lived in one of them, which had two bedrooms and one bathroom. From the other apartment, my husband and I ran our two separate businesses. Jen Podany put an offer on a house in a small town. Courtesy of Jen Podany The duplex was in a neighborhood near a busy street, and we had to be cautious about letting the kids go outside to play because of the cars. I was always holding someone's little hand when we were out, just in case. You could hear planes flying back and forth into Burbank Airport. As our kids and businesses grew, we felt increasingly confined. Then we saw a house on the market in Snowflake, and I felt in my bones that we should put in an offer. It was a four-bedroom house surrounded by land, chickens, cows, and a crazy turkey. We could buy it and have our own place to stay when visiting, rather than always renting an Airbnb. We bought the house for about $500,000, and on our first visit to stay in it in January 2025, none of us wanted to go back to Burbank . We knew then that we'd make Snowflake our home. And so we did. We moved from Los Angeles to a town of 6,000 people In so many ways, our life looks exactly like life in LA . Our routines have remained the same. Every morning, just like in LA, we start our day at a coffee shop. Except in Snowflake, there's only one place to go instead of 20 choices. We work, we homeschool, we eat our meals, and we go to sleep — just like we did in LA. Jen Podany moved her family from California to Arizona. Courtesy of Jen Podany But by transplanting our lives to a quiet town, we all feel calmer and more peaceful. Personally, my nervous system has regulated. In LA, I felt like the world was constantly coming at me, like I was being bombarded and reacting to everything around me. Here, I feel like I'm in the driver's seat, with a clear head. Not only has it been good for my well-being, but it's also been good for my business. The move has given me the mental space to think bigger. It's led to greater creativity, paving the way for business growth. My kids have an 80s childhood My kids love Snowflake, too. I didn't have to convince them about the move. They have the freedom to be out of the house without worrying about cars and crime. Just a bike ride away are other kids with whom they are often found playing. I think kids grow up quickly in cities, and living here, I feel like my kids get to just be kids. It's like going back to being a kid in the '80s, and I love that for them. The house is bigger, so we aren't living on top of each other, but they've also got endless outdoor space to explore. Even though I lived in LA for 20 years, we never experienced friendship and community as we have in just over a year in Snowflake. Jen Podany says life in "mountain time" is slower. Courtesy of Jen Podany We can't leave the house without seeing someone who wants to stop and talk. Everyone here is on "mountain time" — slowing down. No one is rushing around, head down, looking at their phones, too hurried to have a conversation. Everyone is present and friendly. My husband and I still occasionally have to go to LA for work, and each time we come back home to Snowflake, I take a deep breath and know we made the right decision to relocate our family. events.title: Trump waives new Russia sanctions in the "national interests"
events.summary: President Trump waived new sanctions on Russia late Friday night, saying it was in the "national interests" to hold off on the sweeping levies under the Graham Act that he signed just last month. Why it matters : Trump is easing American pressure on Russia despite a bipartisan chorus calling for him to do the exact opposite. It comes a week after his surprise deal to let Russia sell diesel internationally, which Republicans have condemned as loudly as Democrats. It also puts Republican candidates making their final midterm sprint in the position of having to defend the president's warmer relationship with a country voters overwhelmingly see as an American enemy . The latest: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky lamented Trump's decision in a post to X Saturday morning. "This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he wrote, amid fresh Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Driving the news: The White House released the text of an executive order late Friday night detailing the implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The bill, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), imposed broad new sanctions on Russia and countries that do business with it, including buyers of its oil. The order notes that the law allows the president to "waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty." "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order. What they're saying: Republicans and Democrats alike blasted the waiver. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled." The big picture: The waiver caps a historic week in recent U.S.-Russia relations, where Trump abruptly eased pressure on multiple fronts. Whether it was the diesel deal, or a fight over Ukraine's ability to use Starlink to defend itself against Russian munitions, or a public denial of Russian involvement in the Iran war, Trump has spent the last few days shifting America's position on an old foe. By waiving the Graham Act's so-called secondary sanctions, Trump will also avoid putting fresh pressure on China and India, major buyers of Russian oil. The bottom line : The louder the bipartisan anti-Russia chorus gets, the more Trump doubles down on pulling back the pressure. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reactions. Ben Geman contributed.

events.title: U.S. debt interest payments hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in fiscal 2026 — faster than total federal spending, revenue and GDP growth
events.summary: The federal government’s fiscal year ended last month, and the final tally offered another stark warning about the trajectory of U.S. debt. According to Treasury Department data released on Friday, the federal budget deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, 12% worse than the $1.78 trillion gap in fiscal 2025. That came as revenue increased 3% to $5.4 trillion, lagging behind the 6% bump in spending to $7.4 trillion. Social Security and Medicare were the biggest line items, but in third place was interest payments on the national debt, topping defense spending and Medicaid. Gross interest costs for fiscal 2026 came in at $1.36 trillion, Treasury data show, with an average interest rate of 3.53%. That’s more than double the rate in 2021, just before the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle to rein in inflation. Net interest payments rose 8% to $1.05 trillion, outpacing increases in total spending, revenue and GDP. In fact, it exceeds real GDP growth of about 2% as well as nominal GDP growth of about 6%. Fiscal 2026’s net interest costs translate to about $2.9 billion a day, and the Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimated they represent 3.2% of GDP, breaking the previous record set in 1991. With gross U.S. debt at $40 trillion, publicly held debt at 100% of GDP, and borrowing costs up, interest payments are projected to be the fastest growing portion of the federal budget in the coming years. At the same time, the debt burden is being increasingly exposed to market volatility that threatens to make interest costs even steeper. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been issuing more short-term debt to finance the deficit and is retiring long-term obligations. Now, about one-third of publicly held debt, or more than $10 trillion, is due to mature within the next 12 months, meaning the federal government must roll it over at today’s higher rates. In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected annual debt interest expenses will reach $2.1 trillion by 2036. But then President Donald Trump launched the Iran war, which sent oil prices and bond yields soaring. The 10-year Treasury yield is now above 5%, blowing past the CBO’s forecasts for 4.1% this year, 4.2% in 2027, 4.3% from 2028 to 2031, and 4.4% from 2032 to 2036. Treasury Department If bond yields remain about 1 percentage point above the CBO’s estimates, interest costs will surge to $2.8 trillion, or 5.9% of GDP, by the end of the decade, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.  “Higher interest begets more debt, and greater debt begets higher rates and higher interest. Eventually, the whole thing could come crashing down,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said last month. “That’s why Washington needs a fiscal intervention now, before it’s too late. The President, the Treasury Secretary, and Congressional leadership need to understand the severity of this issue. There are no easy fixes, and we can’t just wish this problem away.” But so far, there’s no sign of much willingness to tackle spending or revenue. Trump has even called for a $5,000 “dividend” check to Americans if Republicans win the midterm elections and is already handing out “rebates” to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees. Meanwhile, Bessent has argued that heating up the economy further can get the debt under control. “With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.” But CBO Director Phillip Swagel said last week that faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check . While stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, it’s not that simple. Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs. Assuming interest rates of 4% to 5%, Swagel estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8%, and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6% in order to stabilize the debt. That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%. “So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” he said. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are political choices.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
events.summary: The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said. Lee said semiconductor demand still far exceeds supply, even as producers expand capacity. Semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition. The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday. "For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded." His comments come after semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks like SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants like Nvidia . Chip stocks have fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said. On Thursday, an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper , a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to a CNBC translation . events.title: Investors are buying up vast tracts of timberland across U.S. in one of market's longest-term bets
events.summary: Institutions have been buying timberland at the rate of one million acres a year, according to Bank of America. But lumber prices have been on the decline and profiting from timber can take many years, current owners warn. It isn’t as passive of an investment as it seems, either: hunting, illegal logging, wildfires, pests, disease, and land values all need to be monitored. When the economy and the market look shaky, gold and government bonds are the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber. The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage. Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, including younger Americans priced out of the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term. "Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy. "Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said. Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' producer price index for logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially. Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor. Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said. For example, he said, demand for wood pellets used in bioenergy, while controversial , has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand from recreational and lifestyle buyers , providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting. The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation. Timberland managers dominate acquisitions Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue. According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently. Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said. According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall. South Carolina Forestry Commission data show statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%.

events.title: I'm a Colorado local. If I had one day to show you my state, I'd skip Denver and take you to a city just west of it.
events.summary: I've lived in Colorado for over 10 years. If you really want to get a taste of the state, try visiting the city of Golden. milehightraveler/Getty Images As a Colorado local , I love bringing first-time visitors to the state to Golden instead of Denver. It's a short drive from downtown Denver with beautiful mountain views and a walkable downtown. There are great places to eat alongside mountain views, hike, and enjoy the scenery in Golden. I've lived in Colorado for over a decade. If I had just a single day to show someone what I love about the state, I wouldn't take them to our capital city, Denver. Instead, I'd bring them to the much smaller city of Golden. Golden gives has a little bit of everything for visitors: mountains and hiking trails, a creek running through town, a historic downtown made for wandering on foot, and plenty of places to eat and drink. It's located just about 15 miles west of downtown Denver, or about a 25-minute drive, and typically less than an hour's drive from the Denver International Airport . Here's why I love bringing out-of-towners to Golden — and where I'd take them when they visited. I'd start the morning with coffee at a family-owned shop. Sogo Beans and Boards is one of my favorite morning stops. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall Golden has several coffee shops, but I'd start my perfect day here at Sogo Beans and Boards. The family-owned coffee and skate shop is just minutes from downtown. I love that Sogo air-roasts its fair-trade coffee and makes its own syrups and pastries. Its plant-filled room, free Wi-Fi, and garden patio make it easy to linger over a latte, and it's the kind of independent shop that makes a morning feel unhurried. We'd spend lots of time outside, which is easy to do in Golden Hiking North Table Mountain Park is one of my favorite ways to see the foothills around Golden Courtesy of Lexi Marshall The city makes it easy to go from a coffee shop to a trail without a long drive. For a leisurely morning, I'd rent an e-bike and follow the paved Clear Creek Trail, which winds alongside the water through parks and greenery. For more of a workout, I'd hike North Table Mountain, where the initial climb stings but rewards you with sweeping views of the city and surrounding mesas. Riding the Clear Creek Trail is a great way to see Golden by e-bike. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall In warmer months, tubing on Clear Creek is another way to take in the town's outdoor culture and scenic views. If I had more time, I'd take the short drive from town to visit Golden Gate Canyon State Park, a beautiful place to enjoy aspen groves and mountain scenery. Come winter, the same park is a serene place to snowshoe through snow-covered trails. The Golden Mill is my go-to for lunch The rooftop patio at The Golden Mill has mountain views. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall After working up an appetite, I'd head to The Golden Mill, a food hall and community gathering space along Clear Creek. It offers several food concepts — from sushi and tacos to fried chicken, barbecue, and New Zealand-style ice cream — which means a group with different tastes can all leave happy. More than 50 self-pour taps offer beer, wine, cider, and more. The best part is the setting. Large creekside and rooftop patios have mountain views, which makes it an ideal spot to settle in after a morning outside. My sister and I recently spent a morning there for rooftop yoga led by a local teacher, then walked around town afterward before returning for lunch. My sister and I spent a peaceful morning in Golden. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall It was peaceful, and it reinforced what makes the place work: It feels less like a traditional restaurant and more like somewhere you can spend a few hours eating, drinking, and watching Golden go by. The yoga is a summer series that typically returns in May, and the event lineup rotates with the seasons. Past offerings have included rooftop barre and Keg Conditioning, a workout that uses empty kegs as equipment. Downtown is made for wandering Washington Avenue is lined with locally owned boutiques, galleries, and Western outfitters, and a seasonal Saturday farmers market adds to the scene. Kayakers can play at Clear Creek Whitewater Park and beer fans can tour the Coors Brewery. Coors began brewing beside the creek in 1873. One year later, the Colorado School of Mines was established nearby. It's part of an industrial past you can still sense as you walk. I'd leave some of the afternoon unscheduled, too. Part of Golden's appeal is simply walking along the creek, looking up at the foothills, and stopping wherever something catches your attention. Golden is proof that the best trips aren't always the flashiest Golden is just as beautiful in winter as it is in spring, summer, and fall. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall All of the above is ultimately why I'd choose Golden for someone's first taste of Colorado . Denver has plenty to offer, but Golden gives you a concentrated version of the state I'd want to share with a first-time visitor: mountain views without a long mountainous drive ; outdoor adventure alongside a walkable downtown; and enough food, beer, and local character to fill the day. Sometimes it's not the most extravagant destinations that create the most meaningful memories. Some of my favorites in Golden have been the simplest, like that quiet morning with my sister. After more than a decade here, that combination of ease and charm still feels like Colorado to me. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3 , the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip. Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades. The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click. Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate. It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app. That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach. If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings. The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.) The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149. The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green. Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2 , which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out. The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Software’s new consolidator gets big vote of confidence from Berkshire
events.summary: Italy's Bending Spoons has emerged as a major player in tech M&A, and is now moving aggressively to snap up out-of-favor software names. The holding company's stock price shot up this week after Berkshire Hathaway bolstered its investment, putting in more than $300 million. "This is what private equity firms were planning to do but they got their nose bloodied," said Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight. At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote. Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway . Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion. "Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement. The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio. For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the " SaaSpocalypse ." "You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore." Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus . Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo , AOL and Eventbrite in 2025. The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07. Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price. Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions. Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied." "They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020. Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years." As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.

events.title: Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and scary – Chinese AI
events.summary: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge. Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence. In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by. The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries. Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level. It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again. Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square . A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule. Then came AI and the state discovered complete control. Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to. Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished. For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world. Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology. Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions. Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights. Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents. There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need. Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented . But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option. As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation. He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.

events.title: 'Dead money’ for a decade: Why this hedge fund approach may deliver an advantage over bonds
events.summary: Investors may want to rethink their bond allocation and opt for managed futures exposure. DBi's Andrew Beer suggests the popular hedge fund strategy could deliver a modern twist to traditional 60/40 portfolios . "[Bonds have] been dead money for the entire decade," the firm's co-founder and managing member told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "I fell in love with a strategy called managed futures because tactical is really good. Be nimble when other people's [portfolios] aren't." Beer contends the managed futures strategy, historically only available to hedge funds, could counterbalance stocks better than bonds during periods of volatility , which has been moving higher due to recent worries surrounding debt and the artificial intelligence trade . His reason: Managed futures exchange-traded funds can go long and short across global markets to position early against turbulent market events. "You want something that has low correlation to both stocks and bonds, and something that will do well in crises," Beer said. "It's very, very hard to find a better hedge fund strategy than managed futures to accomplish that." He helps manage the iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy ETF (DBMF) . The fund replicates the performance of leading managed futures hedge funds inside a low-cost, liquid ETF, according to the firm's website. "There's an existential crisis right now in strategic asset allocation and the model portfolio world," Beer said about the 60/40 approach. "I love my bonds … [but] I'm not making it a 40% allocation for something that is not adding to the rest of my portfolio." As of Thursday's close, Beer's ETF is up almost 19% so far this year, according to FactSet data. However, managed futures may not be a replacement for bonds . According to NovaDius Wealth Management's Nate Geraci, bonds still have a place for diversifying a portfolio. "I call fixed income the most challenging area in investing right now," the firm's president said in the same interview. "[Alternatives] fit in the sleeve of a well-diversified portfolio that includes stocks and bonds. But I don't think you just give up on the bond side of the equation." Geraci added that investors should understand how alternative investment strategies like managed futures ETFs could interact with the rest of a portfolio. These funds can outperform during volatile markets, but they may also have periods of underperformance. "You have to let that work out over the long-term," said Geraci, who is also an ETF Institute co-founder. "To me it's just a balance. It's all about diversification."

events.title: States sue OpenAI, saying it gives life to ‘cyberhacking agents’ while ChatGPT hurts children and deceives adults
events.summary: At least eight states  are suing  artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit. The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said. At the same time, the lawsuits contend that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up  with artificial intelligence . “OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement. The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models — or “cyberhacking agents” as one lawsuit called them — that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions. In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls “misaligned models” and that it had found nothing close to the  rogue incident discovered in July  when an AI agent hacked into another AI company. States join together in lawsuits The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia. Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.” In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends. The states say that the risks and harms — to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents — were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit. “Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit. ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits. The AI landscape is evolving It’s possible all of the allegations in the states’ lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT  designed for teenagers , with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats. Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous. A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI’s protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product  don’t work as intended  and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens. Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit. In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an  $18 billion landmark legal settlement  that ended a trial over teen  social media addiction  and settled claims filed by nearly every state. Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures. OpenAI is making a similar appeal. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.” OpenAI also said it works with external experts who review its policies and ChatGPT’s behavior. ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said. Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said. But Laura Zimmermann, Common Sense Media’s director of youth AI research, questioned the value of OpenAI’s statistics. For one thing, ChatGPT can do a student’s homework in seconds, so even 15 minutes can have a big impact on a teenager’s development, Zimmermann said. She also questioned whether OpenAI knows which users are teenagers or children, given that her organization’s testing found that ChatGPT couldn’t or didn’t detect which user is a child. events.title: The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, and the energy portion goes up $50 a week, top economist says
events.summary: More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and  adding to the cost  of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the  midterm elections approach . Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the  fighting disrupts  Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores. Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September  jump in wholesale prices  suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated. The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said. Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead: Filling up fuel tanks is noticeably more expensive BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September. WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or  45% above its prewar level , and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said. Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to  overall inflation  by raising the cost of moving goods. WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz  remains dangerous  and constrained, prolonging  uncertainty over oil supplies  and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild. Higher airfares are hard to escape too BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association. WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have  raised ticket prices and fees , trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics. WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down. Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates. Any growth in grocery prices pains Americans after multiple years of food inflation BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase. WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices  can be volatile , and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs. Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%. Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after  multiple years of food inflation . Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier. WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers. A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries. Rubber meets the road when it comes to shoe prices BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year. WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%. WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027. “Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said. Transportation costs add up throughout product supply chains BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel. WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices. events.title: Low-cost clinic helps pet owners with vet bills
events.summary: Christine Gardner described support from the clinic as "amazing" A reduced-cost veterinary clinic has treated 160 pets in its first 11 days, according to the RSPCA. The animal charity's Medway West branch has launched to offer cut-price care for the pets of people on low incomes or receiving benefits. "Your pet would come first. You'd have a bit of toast yourself and pay out for your pet," said Chatham cat owner Christine Gardner. "Having somewhere like this is amazing." She told the BBC it was "just really good to have something nearby that I can get to" with her six cats. Angela Adams said her pets were her "babies", adding: "I would rather starve than they starve." She said she had eight cats, two rabbits, four guinea pigs, two African land snails and a tortoise, and that she did not know what she would do without the animals, as she was unable to work for health reasons. "It's very expensive. Seven of my cats were due for vaccine this month and you can imagine the cost of that," she told the BBC. "That's a lot of money." "I've had friends messaging me struggling, so this place is brilliant for people." The RSPCA's Imara Ó Niocail says some people can longer afford to care for their much-loved pets RSPCA branch account manager Imara Ó Niocail said that "a lot of people who were more than capable of affording to have these animals" were no longer able to care for them due to the cost of living or a change in circumstances. "We would like to keep the animals at home with the owners and treat them there," Ó Niocail told the BBC. The low cost clinic meant that pet owners in Medway could "seek the treatment that they need and then take the animals home", without having to pay the full vet costs , she added. Medway West branch manager Kevin Morton said the charity's centres were "full-to-bursting" with animals and some people "give their animals up because they can't afford to look after them". "Some people might think that if you can't afford to feed it, then don't have it, but if it's your only companion you have, they can keep people going," he said. The branch has supplied 18,909 food items, 1,294 treats and 919kg of biscuits so far in 2026 through its pet food bank. events.title: When AI and robots work together, Anthropic says these jobs are at risk. Should gardeners worry?
events.summary: A gardener tends a flowerbed. cbarnesphotography/Getty Images Anthropic examined what might happen when AI and robots are combined. That could put more hands-on jobs, including gardening, in the path of automation, Anthropic warned. I'm skeptical that robots can handle the messy reality of pulling weeds. Remember when Anthropic's AI jobs report suggested gardeners were among the safest workers because AI couldn't pull weeds or tell a rose from a dandelion? In practice, I'm skeptical. For instance, anyone who's spent time working in a garden knows how hard it is to identify the right plant, kneel in awkward spots, and pull a weed out properly by the roots without damaging everything around it. Robots are improving. But if you've ever watched one tackle a messy real-world task, you'll know there's a long road between a research chart and reality. events.title: A welcome recovery milestone for Pope Leo after cancer surgery

Catch up quick: The Vatican announced Leo would be having surgery to remove a nodule from his lung on Oct. 11, and later said the surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung. The Vatican confirmed the surgery was successful on Tuesday, and later said that Leo was walking around, eating normally, and that his blood tests and chest X-rays were normal. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center, and if caught early, survival rates are very high. Zoom out: His hospitalization and subsequent cancer diagnosis struck fear into Catholics across the world, who offered him prayers and well-wishes as he recovered. For example, a group in Chicago, the first American Pontiff's hometown, created a care package for Leo featuring get-well cards and a Chicago White Sox blanket. events.title: My husband and I have different definitions of 'financially responsible.' Building a house is forcing us to compromise.
events.summary: My husband and I bought land, and are starting the process of building a house. Lisa Leslie When it comes to money, I'm a big budgeter, and my husband prefers taking risks. Now that we're building a house together, our differences are causing some disagreements. We've learned to stay flexible and balance each other's approaches. My husband and I have very different ideas about financial responsibility . When we're feeling stressed about money, my instinct is to run the numbers and account for every financial what-if. He's a big-picture dreamer who sees what something could become and is more willing to say, "We'll figure it out." His attitude has paid off before. He had the vision for our first home, which we bought for under $100,000 and recently sold for a decent profit after 13 years of renovations. I know some of the best things we've done together wouldn't have happened without my husband's willingness to take a chance, but our differences have still caused some friction over the years. Now that we're building a new home together, we're trying to balance my need to plan for the unknown with his belief that we'll find a way forward. After 13 years, we took a risk and sold our home We sold our home and bought land in a part of Maine we love. Lisa Leslie For 13 years, we'd lived in the same place. My husband had moved frequently as a child, and he wanted his two daughters to have a consistent place to call home. Leaving this house behind was bittersweet, but my oldest stepdaughter had just bought her own house, and my younger one was heading off to college. We were ready for what came next. We could have bought an existing house needing renovations. Instead, we found land in southern Maine that felt worth taking a risk on. We've always loved the area. My family has an annual reunion there, where we spend a week at the beach . Our new property will hopefully give us that lifestyle without the summer crowds: It's more than 2 ½ acres with hiking trails next door, a nearby kayak and paddleboard launch, and the ocean just a short drive away. We decided to go for it, and by the end of August, our old house was nearly empty. My younger stepdaughter left for college on a Wednesday, we moved the rest of our things to a rental on a Thursday, and officially sold the house that Friday. Every estimate comes with an 'unless' If excavators hit ledge, our costs could go up. Lisa Leslie In September, we began building our 1,500-square-foot house. We're now paying $3,000 a month for a rental home — with a construction loan on top of that — and keeping track of a lot of numbers, from lumber and labor to excavation, plumbing, electrical, permits, and finishes. My husband is doing most of the construction himself, which is what makes this project possible. If we had to pay for all of the labor, we probably couldn't afford to build right now. However, that's not to say this hasn't been a very stressful time. We think we've accounted for everything, but every estimate has an asterisk: Unless lumber prices go up. Unless a contractor's price changes. Unless we hit ledge — that is, solid bedrock beneath the soil that can be expensive to excavate. We might have to rethink the foundation or adjust the entire plan once we see what's underground. I find that uncomfortable, but my husband doesn't. We're leaving room to adjust We've made some compromises, and we'll likely have to make more. Lisa Leslie My husband can picture what this property could become over time, and has big dreams for it. He wanted a garage, a small cottage where our family could stay when they visit, a little more space, and nicer finishes in some areas. I kept bringing us back to what we could afford right now, and how much we wanted to keep in savings rather than put everything into the house. After a lot of discussion, we decided to start small. We're building for the life we have today, while — at his request — leaving room for the one we might want tomorrow. The garage and cottage can wait. For now, we're focusing on getting the house right without stretching our budget too far. That means staying flexible. For instance, my husband wants a finished basement , and I agreed, knowing this would give us the option to add a third bedroom down the road. Though the cost difference between a basement and an unfinished crawl space isn't huge upfront, hitting ledge could put us thousands — or even tens of thousands — over budget. We're willing to give the basement a shot, but if excavation costs start climbing, we may have to scale back to a crawl space and save the extra bedroom for another day. We have a plan, but we know it might change once we get further into the build. I'll keep making the spreadsheets and asking for the numbers. He'll keep looking at the big picture and reminding me why we decided to do this. This project, and my husband, have taught me that financial responsibility isn't necessarily about eliminating every risk, but knowing which risks are worth taking and staying open to changing course. events.title: Trump's student loan overhaul could lead to more bankruptcy filings, former judge says
events.summary: After nearly three decades as a bankruptcy judge, Sarah Sharer Curley details what she calls the unfairness of the legal process in her new book, "The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America." "We allow the financial markets to take innumerable risks, yet we refuse to allow an individual to be forgiven for choosing to pursue an advanced degree," Curley wrote. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. In Judge Sarah Sharer Curley's nearly three decades presiding over bankruptcy cases, some were especially painful to witness, she said — such as the 73-year-old woman who stood before her in 2012 with a student loan balance of more than $584,000. The debt dated back to the 1970s and had grown throughout the woman's public sector career, Curley writes in her new book, " The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America ." She had "never made a lot of money," Curley said, and by the time she sought debt relief, the woman was living in poverty, with Social Security as her only income. Even so, strict bankruptcy laws can make it nearly impossible to discharge student loans . Curley, the first woman appointed to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arizona, said it was a familiar story. CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Curley retired in 2014. CNBC spoke with her this month about her new book, in which she describes a legal system that often fails to give indebted Americans the second chance it promises. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. 'People are subject to many unexpected events' Annie Nova: What do people get most wrong about those who file for bankruptcy? Sarah Sharer Curley: People assume that individuals who file for bankruptcy are committing fraud, trying to hide assets and cheating creditors. Nothing could be further from the truth. AN: And so why did people end up in your court? SSC: People are subject to many unexpected events. People can't always plan adequately for the next earthquake, hurricane or natural disaster. But usually, it's someone losing a job. It could also be an illness that becomes chronic with medical costs that increase dramatically over a short period. Student loans is another area of concern. Universities are charging more for basic degrees, as well as graduate programs. The cost of medical school over four years can be more than $400,000. AN: You write that many people who file for bankruptcy are not unemployed; they're just living paycheck to paycheck. What does this tell us about our economy and labor market? SSC: Despite the increase in wages that most economists tout, many people are working as independent contractors. They receive few benefits and have few rights. The company is not responsible to them. Other individuals may be working for a company but find the wages or benefits are insufficient. Many people are forced to work for several employers to meet their needs on a weekly basis. Although unemployment may be low, the quality of the employment is also low. AN: The story in your book about the woman in her 70s with the six-figure federal student loan balance really stood out to me. What happened in her case? SSC: The federal government would not agree to any settlement. I was the one who would have to decide whether her debt would be discharged or not. But the case law I had to follow was not in favor of discharging student loan debts. So, I didn't have a lot of flexibility in granting her relief. However, I gave her credit for seven years of public service helping out troubled teens in San Diego County, since people who are in certain types of public service only have a 10-year repayment period. That meant that she'd need to repay the debt for just three more years. AN: Wow. Why wouldn't the federal government agree to any settlement with her? SSC: The federal government retains law firms to represent it in bankruptcy court, allowing the law firms to have a certain amount of discretion as to how to proceed. As a result, some law firms are aggressive in the positions that they take. In the case of the woman in her 70s, the law firm attorneys didn't believe her when she said she had no assets and was on Social Security.

events.title: Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping
events.summary: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women Y ou may be familiar with rule 34 of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women. See, for example, Meta’s “ pervert glasses ”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers have filmed themselves trying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they are harassed by strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg did not feel the need to apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology. Then there is the Flock license plate tracking system, which has been abused by an extraordinary number of law enforcement officers to track the locations of their exes or other women they are sexually interested in. And, of course, there are the AI image generators, which have been used to create deepfake pornography of women and girls. According to a 2023 report , “deepfake pornography made up 98 per cent of all deepfake videos online, and 99 per cent depicted women”. Now, there’s a new toxic tech trend to worry about: livestreamed robogroping. Police in Cologne, Germany, are currently investigating an incident in which a humanoid robot controlled by two teenage males touched a 16-year-old girl’s buttocks and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Footage of the groping robot, which was wearing human clothes and a fake mustache, was reportedly livestreamed by the two males online. The robot in question has now been confiscated by the local police, who seem a little befuddled by the whole thing. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” a police spokesperson told the Associated Press, adding it was “new territory for us”. It may be new territory but I can guarantee you that this won’t be the last time we hear about an incident like this. Getting your hands on an AI-powered humanoid robot is still a lot more expensive than buying a pair of smartglasses, but the technology is rapidly becoming a lot more accessible. Earlier this year, a school in New York made headlines after announcing its new teaching assistant would be a humanoid robot called Sally, made by a company that makes realistic sex dolls. Outrage over the announcement forced the school district to halt its plans , but it’s only a matter of time before we see humanoid robots in schools. Indeed, in a report published last year, Bank of America predicted that, as costs go down, we will see mass adoption of humanoid robots from 2035 onwards. By 2060, they expect there to be 3bn humanoid robots, which will replace 20% of the workforce in the industrial sector and 50% of the workforce in the service sector. As the industry develops, expect corporations to ensure that their profit-maximizing robots have more legal protections than the humans they may harm. This week in Philadelphia, for example, a woman was arrested after allegedly blocking the path of one of the annoying Uber delivery robots that are now ubiquitous in the city. (The fact the police intervened is absolutely wild to me as a Philadelphia resident, considering they rarely seem interested in doing their jobs.) A growing body of case law has found that police officers are not under any legal obligation to protect citizens who are not in their custody. Yet they seem surprisingly keen on protecting robots. Our brave new world, everyone! I’m afraid pervert glasses are just a small glimpse of what’s to come. By 2060, robogroping may be as commonplace as catcalling is today. You can pay $7,500 to take dating lessons from a man accused of rape Braden Eric Peters, who goes by the nom-de-influencer Clavicular, shot to fame for smashing his face with a hammer in order to beautify himself. Bonesmashing, as it’s called, is part of a toxic trend called looksmaxxing , which involves people (largely young men) going to extremes to increase their “sexual market value”. When not bonesmashing, Peters gets into regular trouble with the law. Most lately, he was charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts last month; his attorneys have denied the allegations. Nevertheless, it seems that there are people out there willing to pay $7,500 for a week at Camp Looksmax, a new venture in which Peters coaches attendees on confidence and dating.

events.title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
events.summary: A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California . The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor. But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable. Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers. This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county : rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost. “I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.” Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies. With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions , Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return. What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community . Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects. It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in. “This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.” From strip club owner to datacenter developer When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both. Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee. Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio.
