events.title: This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power
events.summary: This article was originally published by Canary Media . America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation — from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants . But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors. Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming. Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low , in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required . On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory . However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocked tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards. For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps — all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations. “This is low -hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe , a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, sa ys of the technology. What are variable frequency drives? Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air . But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy. VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent , says Neal Elliott , director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy. All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email. “We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” sa ys Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002. Electric Motors in Nearly Every Factory Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant — whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving — was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues. But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott sa ys . Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters. Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing up-front costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, sa ys Zack Valdez , senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers. “If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he sa ys . And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system. The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid — giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers. VFDs Slash Motors’ Electricity Use Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers. “If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” sa ys Kirk Anderson , director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee. Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the buildout of gas turbines and power plants. “Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he sa ys , referring to a growing effort b

events.title: 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year
events.summary: Work How a 70-year-old beekeeper is keeping his family honey farm afloat: 'It's a legacy that I feel responsible for' Work His gas station speakeasy brought in about $5 million in one year: Behind the hidden door, it's still the 'roaring twenties' On The Job NYC's 'Baklava Guy' brings in $20K/month selling Turkish pastries Psychology and Relationships What we lose when kids can't connect, IRL How I Made It Hidden bar in gas station business brings in about $5 million a year Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generation antique seller, had no prior experience with farming when he bought a small farm in Clarence, New York, in 1993. Nobody thinks he's out of his gourd now. Schultz, 74, is the owner and operator of The Great Pumpkin Farm , a seasonal attraction about 15 miles northeast of Buffalo that draws over 100,000 visitors each fall. The Great Pumpkin Farm brought in $2 million in annual revenue in 2025, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It — and it's open just seven weeks a year. This year, the farm is open to visitors between Sept. 19 and Oct. 31, and they're not just coming to buy pumpkins. With a $20 weekend admission ticket, fall enthusiasts can ride the farm's pumpkin-themed train, explore its giant corn maze and compete in pie-eating contests, among other attractions. Halloween is big business for Schultz and other seasonal business owners. Halloween-related spending is expected to reach $13.5 billion in the U.S. in 2026, according to a consumer survey by the National Retail Federation published in September. Among the 74% of Americans celebrating the holiday this year, 42% said they plan to carve a pumpkin. At The Great Pumpkin Farm, "attendance is increasing just about every year," according to Schultz. During the fall, "there are people that come here almost every weekend," he says. "They love it so much, they just keep coming back." A giant pumpkin put them 'on the map' Schultz, who runs an antique store and an antique auction business year-round, says he was inspired to start his farm after visiting a pumpkin patch in upstate New York in the early 1990s. That farm had "muddy parking lots and not a whole lot of restrooms," he recalls, but there were "a zillion people" walking around and buying pumpkins. "I looked around and I said, 'I could do this, better than this,'" Schultz says. So when the old cow farm next to his antique store went up for sale, he bought the 85-acre property for approximately $650,000, he says. With the help of other local farmers, Schultz learned how to grow his own gourds, and The Great Pumpkin Farm officially opened in 1996. But Schultz had even bigger plans for his farm. That same year, he asked Ray Waterman, founder of the World Pumpkin Confederation , an organization dedicated to growing giant pumpkins and squash, to host his annual World Pumpkin Weigh-Off at The Great Pumpkin Farm. Schultz bought prize indemnity insurance, which covers the cost of contest and promotion prizes, and offered $50,000 to anyone who brought in a pumpkin that weighed 1,000 pounds or more. He took out ads in papers "across the country" to promote the weigh-off. The winning pumpkin, grown by a couple from Lowville, New York, broke the world record at the time at a whopping 1,061 pounds. "We were in magazines and newspapers all over the world," Schultz recalls. "That put us on the map right off the bat." The Great Pumpkin Farm still hosts a weigh-off event every October, and this year's heaviest pumpkin weighed a whopping 1,908.5 pounds, almost double the weight of the 1996 winner. Hay rides, pumpkin cannons and more These days, Schultz focuses less on growing gourds — to keep up with demand, he purchases most of the farm's pumpkins from nearby farms. But The Great Pumpkin Farm's 50-foot pumpkin pyramid, which is visible from the road, is still the first thing that incoming visitors see. According to Schultz, the farm stocks over 25,000 pumpkins each year. Weekend visitors pay $20 per ticket, which covers admission for both days. They can access a vast range of activities including hayrides, pie-eating contests, magic shows, a giant slide, live music, train rides, a kid-friendly "boo barn" and pumpkin pedal kart rides, just to name a few. For an extra fee, visitors can try the farm's amusement rides, pumpkin cannons, zombie paintball train, carnival games and Buffalo Bills-themed corn maze. Alongside the farm's bar and bakery, Schultz hosts festival food vendors whose offerings range from barbecue to specialty grilled cheese sandwiches. "You can come out here and spend the day and still not have done everything," he says. Weekdays require no admission charge, and are more low-key. Visitors can purchase pumpkins, visit the Halloween store, bar and bakery, and enjoy the outdoor playground, petting zoo and hay maze.

events.title: Berkshire shares buck market sell-off, rally to highest since Buffett said he would step down as CEO
events.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Portfolio Tracker (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.) Berkshire Hathaway shares closed Friday at their highest level since Warren Buffett told shareholders at the May 2025 annual meeting he planned to step down as CEO at the end of that year . The day before that Saturday surprise, both the Class A and Class B shares had closed at all-time highs. Over the next three months, they lost more than 14% of their value as investors worried a " Buffett premium " was dissolving. It's been more than a year since their post-meeting low in August of 2025, and the recovery has not been a straight line, but BRK.A ended Friday at $798,000, just 1.4% below its all-time closing high of $809,350. The B shares finished at $532.02, also 1.4% under their all-time closing high of $539.80. A loss Thursday broke a 10-session winning streak that added 5% to Berkshire's stock prices but they rebounded with gains of more than 1% Friday. CNBC Pro thinks investors may be happy Berkshire is spending some of its big cash pile under CEO Greg Abel, with $4.5 billion of buybacks in Q2 , investments in Alphabet , Taylor Morrison Home , Lennar , (although there haven't been any buys of that stock since October 2), and now, Bending Spoons . (More on that below). It also notes Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields believes higher short-term interest rates are helping to lift the shares. Berkshire still has roughly $360 billion in cash, "a good symbol of continued patience under the new CEO," and those higher rates mean "they'll be making more money" on that money. In addition, its insurance operations have benefited from a quiet hurricane season so far. Higher oil prices are good for its $19 billion stake in Chevron , which closed Friday at an all-time high after gaining almost 36% since the start of July. Berkshire's energy-related subsidiaries are also getting a tailwind. And recently, Berkshire may be getting a boost as investors shift away from high-flying AI and tech stocks and turn to "old" economy names . For example, Coca-Cola , a long-time Buffett favorite and now a $37.6 billion holding , also closed Friday at an all-time high, perhaps with some extra help from KFC's switch from Pepsi to Coke . It's up 34% year-to-date. Berkshire's position has gained $2.4 billion since last Friday, overtaking Alphabet to become the third largest stake in its portfolio. (See the full top 10 below.) Berkshire's B shares have cut their June 1 deficit of 17.5 percentage points versus the S&P 500 by almost two-thirds. They are now 6.0 percentage points behind the benchmark for the year. Atypical bet on 'buzzy' Italian tech company is big win ... so far Berkshire Hathaway's surprising bet of close to $1 billion on Bending Spoons is paying off big, at least in the short term. The Italian company, which began trading on Nasdaq in the U.S. in July, buys cast-off internet names like AOL, Evernote, and Vimeo, uses AI to cut costs, and deploys the savings to make more acquisitions. In late July, CNBC Pro said , "Wall Street is buzzing," and "analysts ... see big gains ahead." The tech stock is decidedly not a typical Berkshire value play , trading at a large multiple to its earnings. But before Wall Street's open Wednesday morning, a Bending Spoons news release revealed Berkshire is investing a "further" $330 million in the company by purchasing 10 million newly issued shares at $33 per share in a private placement . That was already an almost 12% discount from Tuesday's closing price of $37.86 and the news sent Bending Spoons shares even higher . They hit an intraday high of $58.56 before closing up 41% at $53.46 on Wednesday. Bending Spoons shares are up 24.3% over the three trading days since the revelation, after giving up a chunk of their earlier gains in Friday's tech sell-off to end at $47.07. That's a solid 42.6% higher than Berkshire's $33 purchase price for a profit, on paper, of nearly $141 million. But what's that "further" in Bending Spoon's statement? The release also disclosed, apparently for the first time, that Berkshire invested $600 million at Bending Spoon's IPO more than three months ago. The release doesn't specify how many shares Berkshire bought in July, and Bending Spoons wouldn't confirm my math, but assuming Berkshire paid the $29 per share IPO price, that initial purchase would have been almost 20.7 million shares. That puts Berkshire's holding now at close to 30.7 million shares, which would be worth more than $1.4 billion at Friday's close, a gain of 55.3% for its overall investment of $930 million. Bending Spoon's release also says the "new investment brings Berkshire Hathaway's ownership to 4%.

events.title: Trump ratchets up the chaos in an October barrage
events.summary: President Trump is carrying his insatiable appetite for controversy into the most unforgiving stretch of the electoral calendar, fortified by a decade of political survival. "Bottom line, it's gonna all work out. You know why? It always does," Trump told reporters this week. Why it matters: Gone are the days of a single "October surprise," swallowed by a familiar barrage of scandals, provocations and shattered conventions that have persisted in the closing weeks of Trump's final midterm election. The big picture: Axios has documented Trump's steady demolition of presidential norms in his second term, from the transition through his first 100 days and first year in office. This year, even the threat of losing Congress — and with it, much of his ability to pursue his agenda over the next two years — has done little to temper the pace or audacity of Trump's presidency. Consider the first 15 days of October alone, and the succession of controversies that might have shaken the foundation of a more conventional presidency: Raid on a political opponent: Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home and seized her phone as part of an investigation aimed at stripping the sitting member of Congress of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deporting her, the Wall Street Journal reports. Omar denies wrongdoing. Calls to shoot leakers: Trump declared at an Arizona campaign rally that officials who leak sensitive military information "should be shot," invoking an earlier era when he claimed the government routinely executed leakers. Concessions to Vladimir Putin: Trump eased sanctions ⁠ on Russian diesel, demanded the ouster of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and pressured Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries. Late Friday night, Trump waived sweeping new Russia sanctions ⁠ under a bipartisan law named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed just last month. Taxpayer-funded political ads: Trump spent millions in taxpayer dollars on campaign-style ads promoting his presidency, until a federal judge ordered them halted. He then directed his MAGA Inc. super PAC to finance future spots, drawing a separate complaint alleging violations of campaign-finance law. Federal crackdown on the press: The Justice Department launched an antitrust investigation into ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC after the networks suspended White House pool coverage to protest Trump's ban on three news organizations. $5,000 election promise: Trump pledged to send every adult American a $5,000 check if Republicans retain control of Congress, explicitly tying more than $1 trillion in proposed federal payments to the outcome of the midterms. DOJ intervention in the midterms: With voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California to block 20,000 ballots from suspected noncitizens — the latest escalation in a sweeping campaign to affect American elections. Grisly social-media posts: Trump posted footage of a man being fatally mauled by a tiger, followed by a montage of animal attacks set to upbeat music and an AI-generated video of himself wrestling and embracing a tiger. $333 million in ballroom donations: Secret records obtained by the Washington Post revealed the corporations and billionaires bankrolling Trump's White House ballroom, including donors who benefited from government contracts, regulatory decisions and a presidential pardon involving a family member. The other side: Three October episodes forced Trump into rare retreats — largely of other people's making. A televised execution: Trump scrapped the plan to livestream a convicted mass murderer's execution by firing squad after bipartisan outrage. An ambassador's downfall: Trump forced Kimberly Guilfoyle — who was engaged to his son for four years until 2024 — to resign as ambassador to Greece after reports that she solicited $100,000 from a political donor to cover personal credit-card bills. Guilfoyle denies wrongdoing. A five-day press secretary: Trump ousted Katie Zacharia amid scrutiny of her legal credentials and a widely criticized debut. Axios reports Trump was blindsided to learn that Zacharia — whom he had introduced as an attorney — had never passed the bar exam. What they're saying: Far from seeing October as a month of political peril, the administration is celebrating it as a continuation of Trump's record. "Since Day One of his administration, President Trump has boldly and consistently fulfilled on his campaign promises to protect national security, make America beautiful, secure the border, crack down on crime, ensure free and fair elections, and make life more affordable," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told Axios. "October is shaping up to be another incredible month," she added. Between the lines: Trump has spent a decade defying political gravity. But the economic strength that helped insulate him during his first term has given way to a deepening crisis of public confidence. A Fox News poll released Wednesday put Trump's approval at 36% — his lowest in either presidency — including a devastating 22% for his handling of inflation. In the same Fox poll, government corruption narrowly surpassed inflation as the issue drawing the most extreme concern from voters. The bottom line: Trump is treating a moment of maximum political vulnerability like business as usual, betting that the instincts that carried him this far won't fail him now.

events.title: The 20 global cities with the best quality of life
events.summary: European cities rank highly in quality-of-life rankings. MEDITERRANEAN/Getty Images Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index ranked cities around the world on their quality of life. US cities ranked highly for economics, but fell short in the quality of life category. European cities dominated the quality of life list, while only one US city made the top 20. Cities in the US rank high globally in terms of economics, but they have some ground to cover in quality of life , according to a new report. For its 2026 Global Cities Index, economic advisory firm Oxford Economics ranked 1,000 cities across the globe based on five categories: economics, human capital, environment, and quality of life. Every category is viewed from an economic lens, even quality of life, where indicators include income equality and housing expenditure, among others. "The Global Cities Index records the progress cities are making across a comprehensive range of metrics," Mark Britton, managing director of city services at Oxford Economics, said in the report. "Sitting alongside our forecasts and scenario models, its ability to highlight how paths change under different conditions and its capacity for comparability shows you not just where cities stand today, but also where they are heading." The overall list features several US cities in the top 20 — eight, to be exact, with New York taking the No. 1 spot. However, when highlighting quality of life specifically, only one US city made the cut. Quality of life, which accounts for 25% of a city's overall score, wasn't a bright spot for the US, but plenty of other cities excelled in that category. events.title: SM Lee calls for renewed tripartite ties to safeguard port jobs amid AI, trade headwinds
events.summary: Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong called on unions and leaders at the PSA to work with the Government to help workers adapt through continuous reskilling just like in the past. SINGAPORE – Protecting port workers from being left behind by technological disruption and shifting global trade patterns requires a strong, forward-thinking partnership between unions, port management and the Government. Making this comment at the Singapore Port Workers Union’s (SPWU’s) 80th anniversary dinner on Oct 17, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong called on unions and leaders at the PSA to work with the Government to help workers adapt through continuous reskilling, just like in the past. Only with upskilling will workers be able to take on higher-value, technology-driven roles and safeguard their long-term livelihoods. “As in past waves of transformation, we must not leave workers to face these changes alone. More than ever, we will need a strong and well-led SPWU, working closely with a competent and innovative PSA management team, to secure PSA’s success, and workers’ livelihoods,” said SM Lee. “This is the way to build a disciplined and skilled workforce with a strong Singapore core, and secure for them a fair share of the fruits of their labours.” The port industry in the past has undergone several rounds of transformation as technology advanced , with the change from manual stevedoring and operators controlling yard cranes, to remotely operated automated guided vehicles. Each time the jobs changed, the PSA retrained workers to take up new roles, while the union leaders persuaded workers to adopt a flexible mindset and upgrade themselves, said SM Lee. He was speaking to over 600 attendees that included union leaders, members and management representatives at The Ritz-Carlton, where he was also conferred the SPWU Honorary Membership for his longstanding support and commitment to the industry, union and tripartism. The union, which was first established in 1946, currently represents over 10,000 members from various organisations such as PSA Corporation, PSA International and several port logistics companies. Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong speaking at the Singapore Port Workers Union’s 80th anniversary dinner on Oct 17. Apart from competition from other ports that are catching up quickly with digitalisation and automation, SM Lee warned that the industry itself currently faces supply chain disruptions, climate change, and geopolitical tensions that affect all shippers and port operators. “Green fuels such as ammonia and methanol will require new processes, skills and safety protocols, (and) rapid advances in AI, autonomous technology, sensors and robotics are already dramatically transforming port operations,” he said, adding that repetitive physical tasks such as coning and de-coning may be done by embodied artificial intelligence in the future. These comes with new challenges and new opportunities, such as higher-value tasks that are less demanding and completely new roles that do not exist yet, such as in sustainability management and alternative fuel options. Reaffirming the Government’s commitment to supporting this transition, he called for a renewed tripartite compact to safeguard jobs, deepen worker expertise and ensure all port employees share fairly in the benefits of future growth. Singapore’s port handled 44.66 million shipping containers, or twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), in 2025 – its highest on record – eclipsing the 41.12 million in the previous year. Tuas Port, when port operations are fully consolidated there by the 2040s, will have a capacity of 65 million TEUs, said SM Lee, adding that this was unimaginable back in 1965. “To outsiders, the past six decades look like an unbroken string of successes,” he said, adding that mutual trust had only been forged through a laborious process of organisational change and personal adjustment. He cited the launch of new port locations – such as Keppel, Brani, Pasir Panjang and Tuas – that required workers to adjust to new working environments and commute arrangements. “Tuas, in particular, made commuting significantly longer,” said SM Lee, adding that PSA made extensive transport arrangements, while the union helped workers adjust to the new work locations. Bus services to Tuas South have also been increased through the union’s participation in a tripartite committee with PSA management and government agencies, said SM Lee, adding that the authorities are also studying the feasibility of a Bus Rapid Transit system . PSA’s loss of several major shipping clients to the Port of Tanjung Pelepas in the early 2000s also led to retrenchments and wage cuts, said SM Lee. SPWU negotiated hard with PSA management to secure the best possible deal for the workers who had to leave, while keeping sight of the bigger picture. But when PSA made a strong recovery, it made a gain-sharing payout to its workers in 2005.

events.title: 6 easy and delicious Ina Garten dishes you need to make this fall
events.summary: Ina Garten's recipes will keep you cozy this fall. Scott Kowalchyk/CBS via Getty Images I've made dozens of Ina Garten's recipes, and some of her dishes are perfect for fall. Garten's chicken chili is quicker and lighter than your traditional chili recipe. And her weeknight Bolognese and rigatoni with sausage will keep you cozy as temperatures dip. This year's descent into fall has been more of a crawl, but I think we're all ready for some cozy weather. And what better accompaniment to a classic rom-com and your favorite sweater than a dish by Ina Garten ? The "Barefoot Contessa" star has built a whole career on recipes that are easy and comforting. I've made dozens of Garten's dishes , so I decided to look back and find a few that I think are perfect for this busy season. From a Bolognese that's ready in 30 minutes to a cake packed with the flavors of autumn, these are Garten's best fall dishes. Ina Garten's breakfast sandwiches will energize you for chaotic fall mornings. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The start of fall is so hectic. Work ramps back up, school is back in session, and the prep and stress of the holidays begin to creep in. Travel-friendly and loaded with protein, a breakfast sandwich is just what you need. And Garten's version only requires five ingredients: English muffins, whole milk, avocado, bacon, cheddar cheese, and eggs that you can cook in the microwave. The microwave eggs are surprisingly creamy, and the sandwich is deliciously filling. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Everything in Garten's breakfast sandwich works so well together. She recommends using thick-cut applewood-smoked bacon, which provides a crispy contrast to the soft eggs. Spreading the avocado on the bottom adds both flavor and nutrients, and I love the tanginess of the sharp white cheddar. If you're making this sandwich for more than two people, I recommend cooking the eggs on the stove rather than in the microwave to save time. But this is a great recipe to teach your kids so they can make breakfast on their own. And if you're a college student, you could easily whip this up in a dorm. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's bacon, egg, and cheddar sandwich here. Making a huge batch of Garten's homemade chicken stock has been my fall tradition for years. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I began testing Garten's soup recipes in 2023 and knew something was missing after I kept using boxed stock. "Store-bought is fine!" might be Garten's most famous catchphrase, but she believes homemade chicken stock is akin to "liquid gold." "Nothing available on the market has the depth of flavor or richness of stock you've made yourself," she wrote in "Go-To Dinners," her October 2022 cookbook. "It contributes such great body and aroma to so many dishes. Plus, having a big pot of chicken stock simmering away on my stove just makes me feel good." Garten's stock is packed with flavor because it involves simmering three roasting chickens for hours alongside carrots, onions, celery, parsnips, garlic, and plenty of herbs. There's no flavor left in the chicken once the stock is ready. If you'd rather save the meat for meals, you can always take the chicken out once it's cooked through and continue to simmer the aromatics. I also recommend freezing chicken bones so you always have some on hand for more stock. The recipe makes enough stock to last through the winter, and it provides the base for so many delicious soups. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe provides nearly nine quarts of stock, and you can store it in the freezer for up to six months. My absolute favorite Barefoot Contessa soup to make with the stock is Garten's chicken pot pie soup , which I whip up anytime my fiancé and I are craving a bowl of comfort. Her ravioli en brodo is a delicious twist on chicken noodle, while her Italian wedding soup is light and bright. If you want to switch things up from soup, you can also use the stock to make Garten's one-pot chicken and orzo — another delicious meal for chilly nights. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's homemade chicken stock here. Garten's chicken chili is a lighter twist on the traditionally hearty dish. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten served traditional chili for two decades at the specialty food store she ran in the Hamptons before becoming a cookbook author and Food Network star. When Garten decided to switch up the chili and use chicken instead of beef, it became even more popular than the original recipe. The dish also features red and yellow bell peppers, fresh basil, and a variety of seasonings, including chili powder, ground cumin, and red pepper flakes. Garten serves the chili topped with green onions, cheddar cheese, corn chips, and sour cream. When I first made Garten's chicken chili for some friends, they said it made them feel "so warm and cozy." Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The tomatoes and spices build a rich broth, and each bite of chicken is so tender and juicy. It's also a great dish for hosting because you can lay out the toppings in individual dishes, allowing everyone to personalize their bowl to their own preference. Plus, who doesn't love a bowl of chili on football Sunday? Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's chicken chili here. Garten's weeknight Bolognese is ready in 30 minutes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider My pasta cravings always hit when temperatures start to dip. And during this busy season, Garten's weeknight Bolognese is a perfect fit. The recipe includes ground sirloin, crushed tomatoes, heavy cream, Parmesan cheese, and fresh basil, but it's designed to be adaptable and pantry-friendly. Garten says you could easily swap the sirloin for any ground meat and skip the cream and basil if you need. And while she recommends using orecchiette, any dried pasta will work with this recipe. My family couldn't get enough of Garten's speedy Bolognese. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider It's pretty incredible how much flavor Garten manages to create in a dish that traditionally simmers for hours on end. The rich sauce bursts through every bite of the small pasta shells, which I personally loved for this dish, and the freshly grated Parmesan cheese on top makes it feel extra comforting and indulgent. "It's a very meaty, very hearty pasta," my dad said before declaring that the dish was "perfect." We loved the dish so much that it earned the second spot in my ongoing ranking of Barefoot Contessa pasta dishes . Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's weeknight Bolognese here. If you're searching for a cheesy pasta with little clean-up, Garten's one-pot dish is the perfect fit. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The rigatoni pasta is paired with sausage and fennel, plus some onion, garlic, heavy cream, freshly grated Parmesan cheese, and a few additional ingredients. events.title: Exclusive: Musk tells Isaacson "AI and robots" will need to fix deficit
events.summary: Elon Musk tells biographer Walter Isaacson in a new podcast interview that the fizzled DOGE experiment, which the SpaceX and Tesla CEO once headed, proved there's "no way we were gonna solve the deficit from within the government." "The only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots," Musk tells the author for a new podcast series, " The Builders with Walter Isaacson ," premiering Tuesday. "We're not gonna solve it by trying to save our way there." Why it matters: Musk's comments to Isaacson — author of the definitive 2023 biography, " Elon Musk " — admit that DOGE was a flop, but point to the chance that some future administration will take a new stab at the problem using ever-more-capable AI. Zoom in: Musk said the appetite to cut spending "is not there at the presidency, the House, the Senate or the judiciary. Basically, no one in authority in the government whatsoever — with maybe a few rare exceptions [like the] Rand Pauls of the world — actually wants to reduce spending." "Maybe if the president made that his primary goal, we could do that," Musk added. "If you try to solve the deficit and stop wasteful spending, you make a lot of enemies. President Trump likes to be liked. He doesn't like people calling him, being upset about ... some funding being stopped." Musk admits he "kinda got carried away, basically" and that he wound up being "gone for too long" from his companies. "What I should have done," he added, "was be more in the background ... and probably only had it last for a month or two" rather than the four months he was formally in the White House. "I should have gone back and focused on AI a little sooner than I did." When Isaacson asked Musk if his time in the West Wing had been too seductive, in a way, Musk replied: "It was, a little bit. I mean, it was kinda cool 'cause ... I'm just there in the Oval Office while all these, like, big momentous decisions are being made." Asked about the time he brandished a chainsaw onstage at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) a month into Trump's second term, Musk said: "That was a weird weekend." Pressed to elaborate, Musk said: "Let's let sleeping dogs lie or whatever." The big picture: Isaacson warned this week that Steve Jobs and the other great creators of the personal computer age would be cautious about autonomous AI agents not tightly connected to human control. Isaacson includes his warning in the new preface to an updated edition, published this week, of his sweeping 2014 history of the digital age, " The Innovators : How a Group of Hackers, Geniuses, and Geeks Created the Digital Revolution." Behind the scenes: Isaacson tells me he launched "The Builders" because he wanted to press the builders of this new AI age on these dangers and hear in their own voices what motivates them. "Musk is an amazing engineer who is pushing us forward with Starship, Starlink, Neuralink, and autonomous EVs," Isaacson said. "But as I describe in my biography, I think he is too prone to darkness and conspiracies when it comes to politics and people. His complexities come through in the interview, as I hope they do in the biography." What's next: Isaacson's podcast series, created by media company Kaleidoscope , includes conversations with Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, Fei-Fei Li, and Dario and Daniela Amodei. A series preview says the tech legends "open up about their ambitions, what frightens them, how they think about humanity, and what drives them to build so big and so fast. The conversations are intimate, charming, and sometimes chilling." Listen to a trailer for "The Builders."

events.title: Black voters test the socialist left's ceiling
events.summary: Black voters may determine whether Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) can build on breakthroughs in the 2026 elections. Why it matters: This year's primaries showed that DSA's path runs through older Black voters who wield enormous influence in Democratic primaries — particularly in the South — but have been slower to embrace insurgent candidates. By the numbers: Black Democrats are more likely to like than dislike leaders who identify as democratic socialists, but nearly two-thirds remain neutral toward them. 21% of Black Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents told Pew Research Center they like such leaders, compared with 11% who dislike them. Another 65% were neutral. Among Black Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 23% of those ages 18–49 like leaders who identify as democratic socialists, compared with 20% of those 50 and older. State of play: Angie Nixon's upset win in Florida's Democratic U.S. Senate primary made the Black state representative the first DSA member to win a major-party statewide nomination. Her politics blend labor organizing and civil-rights protest: The former union organizer fought voting-rights battles with sit-ins and a bullhorn and opened a bookstore amid Florida's school book bans, hosting Black-history workshops and organizing groups. Her vote share rose in precincts with younger and larger Black populations, an Axios analysis of election results found. Donavan McKinney's Detroit victory also showed a DSA-backed candidate can break through in a center of Black political power. The DSA-endorsed state representative defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar 51.9%-48.1% in Michigan's 13th District, pairing deep Detroit roots and a legislative record with labor and local support. Yes, but: A July Redbox Research poll for A Fight Worth Having found former Rep. Cori Bush (D-Mo.) leading Rep. Wesley Bell (D-Mo.) 52%–20% among voters under 35 and 46%–36% among those 35–49. But only 19% of the Black likely-primary electorate in the poll was under 50. Bell ultimately defeated Bush 59%-37%. Zoom out: Nationally, 39% of Democratic-aligned adults under 30 like democratic socialist leaders, compared with 26% of those 50 and older. In 2016, an NBC analysis of 25 state exit polls found Bernie Sanders beat Hillary Clinton 52%-47% among Black voters under 30. In South Carolina's 2020 primary, Black voters made up 56% of the electorate, and 69% of Black voters over 45 backed Joe Biden, according to Edison exit polling . Between the lines: New America's Theodore Johnson tells Axios older Black voters often impose a "viability hurdle" before taking a chance on candidates. Johnson said younger Black voters can be "central" to an insurgent coalition but "insufficient" without broader support. What they're saying: Darius Jones of the National Black Empowerment Action Fund warns against reading frustration with establishment Democrats as socialist conversion. Younger Black voters are "increasingly impatient with the pace of results," he said, but that is "not a wholesale endorsement of the DSA in any way." Marcus Board Jr. , a political science associate professor at Howard University, said DSA's difficulty connecting class politics to race is "definitely a hurdle." The other side: DSA says it is "committed to growing our membership into a more diverse, multiracial, multigenerational movement" by organizing around Black workers, child care, housing and food security.

events.title: Bank of England governor walks out of IMF summit in protest against Russia
events.summary: Andrew Bailey among finance leaders to leave session in Bangkok when Russian finance minister addressed group The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has taken part in a walkout of finance leaders who left an International Monetary Fund meeting in protest against Russian involvement. Bailey joined counterparts from France, Germany and a number of Scandinavian and Baltic countries who left the session in Bangkok when the Russian finance minister, Anton Siluanov, addressed the group in Russian. The Bank of England confirmed that Bailey took part. The president of the German Bundesbank, Joachim Nagel, said nearly half of all delegates took part in the joint departure when Siluanov started speaking. “The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat told the Reuters news agency. “We cannot normalise relations with Russia.” The walkout was acknowledged by the chair of the IMF’s steering committee, the Saudi finance minister, Mohammed al-Jadaan. Al-Jadaan said: “We came here for a reason, and we achieved ⁠it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters.” Germany had warned against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage. Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers this year. The US has been supportive, with the treasury undersecretary Erin Browne telling Reuters that Washington supported Russia’s presence despite concerns from European countries. The meeting in the Thai capital heard that the global economy was showing remarkable resilience despite Russia’s war against Ukraine, and in spite of the issues around the strait of Hormuz caused by the US’s and Israel’s bombing campaign. However, al-Jadaan added that there was no room for complacency, amid public debt levels and high bond market rates. A statement from al-Jadaan after the IMF meeting said: “The global economy has weathered the latest in a series of shocks better than expected, but buffers have been eroded, and resilience cannot be taken for granted.” He added: “Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security.”

events.title: My partner and I don't share a bank account, and we still won't after our wedding
events.summary: The couple has been together for four years without merging bank accounts. Courtesy of Catherine Work My fiancé and I have been together for four years and have never had a joint bank account. We're transparent about our incomes, savings, and spending, and we've never had a fight about money. We plan to pay for our wedding together, but we won't combine our finances after we get married. My parents have a shared bank account and kept all their large purchases in both their names, so I thought sharing an account would be my financial destiny, too, if I ever got married. I didn't question it until recently. Now, my partner and I are getting married in just a few months, and we don't plan to combine our finances. After four years together, we've never had any accounts or cards in both of our names. The closest we ever got to that was me using his credit card on a payment app when we were in Vietnam because mine didn't work. We both contribute to rent and household expenses. We pay back the other person our half of large purchases like flights and hotels, but we don't keep a tab of who owes who what (a nice change from my previous romantic relationships). We've always been open about money We were upfront about our income, debt (or lack thereof), and our mutual desire to live below our means from day one. After about three years of dating, we told each other how much we have in savings. We continue to be transparent about money and agree on the vast majority of each other's purchases — it helps that we're both very frugal. We've built up trust over the years, and we'll continue to offer up personal financial information when we want to, knowing we have privacy. Neither of us has the login information for the other's bank, but we know we can always ask how much the other is earning or spending. I thought the next step was a shared bank account with two credit cards — I assumed that's what love and commitment meant in an economic way. We kept asking ourselves how having both our names on one account would improve our lives, and we kept coming up blank. I also didn't want to waste time filling out paperwork or calling my bank for something I wasn't even interested in. Keeping finances separate works for them. Courtesy of Catherine Work Our system works for us We've lived together for almost four years and never had a fight about money. I have some financial anxiety, and I think having a shared account might actually make that worse. Since my fiancée makes more and pays for more, I regularly check in to see if he's still OK with that. We approached our wedding, our first big purchase together, the same way we plan travel — with Excel, conversations, and making sure we stay under budget to cover unexpected costs. My fiancée bought our rings, and I bought our flights (we're getting married in Denmark). We both agreed to contribute the same amount of money to the wedding. Every payment we make for the big day goes into a spreadsheet, and at the end of all our purchases, if one of us has spent significantly more, the other will make the next large purchase. Keeping our financial stressors low is also made easier by the fact that we won't plan to have kids or pets, or make any large purchases like a house or a car. Taking care of our parents is the only thing that might one day impact how we view our financial setup. Another thing we agreed on from the start was that we wanted a pre-nup . Not sharing a bank account and having a pre-nup might not sound romantic (or like we can't share) to some, but if anyone were to look at our purchases, they'd immediately see we do spend our money on each other—just with separate accounts intact. We haven't fought about money, and I'd like to keep it that way I know I'm going into a marriage with dignity and respect. My future husband won't get a notification if I spend over $100, he won't be able to review a bank statement at the end of the month to see how many ice creams I've treated myself to, and we won't know how much the other person spent on a Christmas present. We'll never have to ask the other person if we can spend money or fear that our separate emergency funds will be depleted by the other. My parents shared a bank account, and they often fought over money — one thing I promised myself I'd never do with my future spouse. Keeping our finances separate has worked so far, and I believe it'll continue to after we're married. We're both open to changing our minds one day, but until we have a good reason, we're very happy having separate accounts, together. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The EV Bust Creating a New Battery Boom
events.summary: Factories built to supply America’s electric-vehicle boom are getting a second life making batteries for the power grid. As EV demand weakens and electricity demand from data centers and new factories strengthens, battery makers are shifting toward stationary storage, but the new market still relies on federal incentives and a supply chain that remains partly dependent on China. The shift is visible at TransGrid’s Atlas projects in Arizona, where the contractor Qcells is using LG Energy Solution’s US-made battery cells. (Source: Bloomberg)

events.title: From 3,000 feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze
events.summary: In our second in a series on high-end UK manufacturing, we visit the artisans producing rich clients’ bespoke luxury cars ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales They are the plaything of kings, presidents and A-listers, with Rolls-Royce enthusiasts ranging from the Sultan of Brunei to Rowan Atkinson, from King Charles III to Kermit the frog . And at the carmaker’s factory in Goodwood, West Sussex, special requests from customers get more indulgent every year. An interior lined with 3,000 iridescent feathers, or a built-in champagne cooler , or a car built in homage to its owners’ dog, have all become part of the job. Even with a fast-growing team of artisans and engineers, the company is stretched, and soon it will nearly double the size of its factory as part of a £300m investment by its owner, BMW, which it said at the time of the announcement was part of “securing our future here in the UK”. Behind much of the demand is a new kind of client, who is younger than ever and with a fortune built in technology, says Julian Jenkins, Rolls-Royce’s director of sales and brand. The average buyer is now just 43 – down from 56 in 2010. “Never has there been so much wealth created so quickly at such a young age,” he says. Bespoke, high-value customisation is becoming an increasingly valuable pillar of UK manufacturing, which still makes up about 9% of the UK economy despite the years of deindustrialisation that Andy Burnham has vowed to reverse . This week, the wider sector helped drive a surprise expansion of GDP in August, after growing 0.8% month on month. On a tour of the Goodwood factory, an inner door panel is emblazoned with a bitcoin symbol, hinting at changing tastes. “The industries – cryptocurrency, AI and tech – are where we see some of these young entrepreneurs finding their way very quickly to Rolls-Royce,” Jenkins says. “They are very specific about what they want.” Another car, built for a wealthy American couple, was devoted to their Labrador, Bailey. The dog’s face was pieced together on a rear panel using more than 180 individual slivers of wood, which was a four-month project, with paw prints engraved in the doors for good measure. Clients nowadays, Jenkins says, “are creating something in their image”. Four models make up the current Rolls-Royce range: the Phantom, starting at £441,000, the nearly three-tonne Cullinan SUV, from £345,000, the Spectre electric car, from £333,000, and the cheaper Ghost, from £290,000. But the average Rolls-Royce sells for about £500,000, up from about £300,000 a decade ago, driven largely by customisation work. A heavily personalised car can cost 25% more than the standard price, and seven-figure sums are “not unusual”, a spokesperson says. “The limits are set by the client,” Jenkins says. “We’ve seen some extremely complex and intricate commissions, and some of those can take multiple years. With that, there is value that comes as a consequence.” It is a vision Rolls-Royce’s founders could scarcely have imagined for a company that staked its early reputation on reliability. The business dates back to 1904, when Charles Rolls, an aristocrat and racing driver, met Henry Royce, an engineer, at the Midland Hotel in Manchester, and agreed to sell every car the latter could build. By 1907, Autocar magazine called the Silver Ghost, an early model, the “best car in the world” after completing the gruelling Scottish Reliability Trial without a single mechanical fault. Now, Rolls-Royce has its own entry in the Collins dictionary, as a byword for “anything considered to be the very best of its kind”. Its longest-running model, the Phantom, celebrated its centenary last year. An expansion into aero engines during the world wars made it a manufacturing powerhouse, but later financial collapse forced the government of the time to nationalise the company in 1971. The car business was split off and sold to the engineering firm Vickers. Rolls-Royce, the FTSE 100 aerospace giant , still shares the same logo. In 1998, BMW bought the right to put the Rolls-Royce name on cars, and in 2003 opened the Goodwood factory, promising to triple annual production from about 2,000 cars a year. Two decades later it succeeded, when output peaked at 6,032 cars, falling back to 5,664 last year. Would the Rolls-Royce engineers whose Merlin engines powered the second world war Spitfire have guessed the company name would end up in German hands? “Rolls-Royce motorcars is very much a British company at heart,” says Chris Brownridge, its chief executive. However, he admits it benefits from “synergies” with BMW, such as “battery technology research and development, access to wind-tunnels and other major facilities”. The expansion at Goodwood comes as carmakers are under significant strain from Chinese competition, soaring industrial energy costs and US tariffs.

events.title: I'm a career coach for Gen Z workers. Here are some unspoken workplace rules every new hire should know.
events.summary: Laura Massetti, a career coach for young workers, said that Gen Z workers struggle with unwritten rules and need professional training. Courtesy of Laura Massetti Laura Massetti spent 15 years leading teams and saw Gen Z workers struggle with unwritten rules. Massetti said Gen Z workers need training on communication, judgment, and follow-through. As AI levels technical skills, Massetti said human skills can help early-career workers stand out. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Laura Massetti, founder of Real Work Ready, which helps early-career professionals develop workplace skills. Massetti has more than a decade of experience in the corporate world, leading sales and marketing teams. The essay has been edited for length and clarity. I spent 15 years in the corporate world, leading sales and marketing teams. I loved mentoring early professionals , but I often found myself thinking: My goodness, I wish I could make this process go quicker. I never only look at whether someone could do the work. It is more about whether they could communicate clearly, exercise good judgment, and follow through. As a career coach for young workers , I know there are things that you, as an employee, get judged on that no one actually puts inside the rubric. We expect people to figure them out over time, but in reality, someone has to teach them. Gen Z needs feedback in a workplace that expects people to figure things out I don’t think that Gen Z is unready for work . I think no one has taught them what to do. This generation grew up with a cellphone in their hands. They’d post something on Instagram and get 10 likes. They’re used to instant feedback: Tell me what I need to grow. That’s not how the workplace is built. We have annual reviews. You learn through experience; you learn the hard way. Young workers are digitally fluent, which makes this generation incredible for so many reasons. But growing up digitally, compounded by the pandemic, left gaps in opportunities to practice face-to-face interaction. Now they’re entering workplaces with other generations, and those generations set the rules. Meanwhile, AI is taking on tasks that used to help people develop. We learned shoulder to shoulder with someone. How are new hires supposed to learn if we’re outsourcing those opportunities? You’re being judged on things no one puts in the rubric There are areas you’re being judged on that no one actually puts inside the rubric, including communication and clarity , prioritization and judgment, your ability to follow through, professional presence and credibility, ownership and reliability, and organizational awareness. It’s not just about how you communicate. When you enter the workplace, do you know how to get stuff done? How aware are you of the organization you operate in? You need to understand when to use email, when to use Slack, and when to stop by someone’s office. You can’t walk in and assume you know the rules. In one new-hire program at a company with about 100,000 employees, a manager told me that someone had pinged the CEO on Slack to request a skip-level meeting. Mind you, that would’ve been probably 10 skip levels. Poor thing, he had no idea. No one had told him that wasn’t how you reached out to the CEO in that organization. I’ve also seen people show up to meetings unprepared, without what they needed or knowing how to follow up. Dressing appropriately is something I had to learn on my own. About six months into my job, I wore a full black business suit to a meeting in Miami. It absolutely did not match the environment. I was way too formal. Match the client’s environment and match how they dress. The other day, I saw someone meeting their manager in a suit jacket over a basketball jersey and shorts, but wearing loafers. Your job is to show your manager that they can trust you to be professionally present and to deliver. Managers have a responsibility here, too. When we say, “They’ve been here for two years, and they’re just not getting it,” we need to ask ourselves: What aren’t they getting? What am I judging them on that I haven’t clearly explained? Practice the human skills that will set you apart My company now offers a six-month program that combines online training with weekly role-playing of workplace scenarios. We practice things like how to react when you receive feedback. The goal is to give people experiences they might otherwise wait years to encounter. My advice to every fresh graduate and those entering the workforce is that, at a time when AI is making skill sets equalizers , you will need to define how you’ll be different. Technical skills are still incredibly important. But how do you communicate, exercise judgment, execute an idea, and get people’s buy-in? I’ve never made a hiring decision based on technical capability alone. It’s mostly about whether I can trust that person. Knowing the ins and outs of coding is one thing. Being able to speak to a boardroom and convince people of an idea is another ability you can bring to an employer. Those are the skills I believe will make all the difference. events.title: I downsized from a 3-bedroom to a 2-bedroom when I got married. There's one thing I miss.
events.summary: The author and her son moved into her husband's 2-bedroom townhome. Courtesy of Ashley Archambault When my husband and I got married, we had to decide where to live. My son and I ended up moving into his 2-bedroom home. There are a few pros, but we didn't consider how much we'd miss having a guest room. When my husband and I got married, we each had our own homes. I had a one-story, 3-bedroom home, while my husband had a 2-story, two-bedroom townhome . At first, we compared the pros and cons of each house. For instance, my house had a large yard, which can be a perk size-wise, but lawn maintenance was a chore. While my husband was willing to move, we ultimately chose his house, mainly because it was so close to his job. I knew from experience what a blessing an easy commute is, and I didn't want him to have to give it up, so we decided to consolidate. My son and I moved from our 3-bedroom home to my husband's 2-bedroom townhouse. I was giddy when we got married, and thinking more about moving in together and planning our wedding than the long-term realities of living in a smaller home. The lack of an extra bedroom was an issue we didn't foresee My son and I still occasionally miss our old home, but I don't regret selling my home and moving in with my husband. The worst part of downsizing has been no longer having a guest room. I mainly used the third room in my house as an office, but the bedrooms at my husband's house were large enough that there would be room for an office in ours. And my son would still have his own bedroom, so we didn't realize how much we'd miss the extra bedroom until it was too late. It's nearly impossible for us to have anyone spend the night or a weekend with us I'd mostly thought of the extra room as my office, and didn't consider that we also used it as a guest room. Now, without it, it's difficult to have anyone over for the night. We have a few options, but none of them are appealing to anyone, including our potential guests. When I had my own home, it was so easy to have friends visit for the weekend, because I could offer them a room. Having space for guests is a privilege I didn't realize I'd miss. I can still offer the chance to stay, but when someone takes us up on it, my husband and I feel kind of awful the whole time. We've had guests overnight and offered them the couch pullout or the air mattress. But despite our best efforts, everyone feels a little awkward because our guests have no privacy without an actual room of their own. Sometimes, we've thought of offering our bedrooms — or at least one of them — while my son would get displaced to the living room on an air mattress. He honestly loves doing that anyway, because he thinks it's like a sleepover , but the problem comes in the morning. Our downstairs space is pretty much just the living room and kitchen, so when someone comes downstairs in the morning, whoever's sleeping on the giant air mattress — whether our guests or my son — will inevitably be woken up. In our next home, having an extra bedroom will be a requirement My husband and I both miss having guests, as he could also have more guests over before my son and I moved in. We don't like that we don't feel we can offer loved ones a place to stay, or that when we do, the best we can offer them is an air mattress or my 12-year-old's bedroom. In addition to wanting to have more company over, my husband and I have aging parents . We don't want to find ourselves in a situation where one of them needs living assistance, and we don't have the space. There are a few things we want in a forever home, like a more spacious kitchen, of course, and a giant garden in the back, but having a guest room again is at the top of our list. events.title: I was diagnosed with breast cancer a year ago. Please stop calling me a fighter.
events.summary: The author, shown with her family, was diagnosed with breast cancer in October of 2025. Courtesy of the author A year after my breast cancer diagnosis, I'm rejecting the "fighter" and "warrior" labels others put on me. I'm tired of the pinkwashing that feels like it's turning a terrifying disease into a cheerful marketing campaign. I'm grateful for my care and the people who supported me, but I don't need to find a silver lining or turn my experience into an inspirational story. I was diagnosed with breast cancer a year ago, and with Breast Cancer Awareness Month underway, I have a confession that feels almost sacrilegious: I hate breast cancer culture . I hate the "fighter" and "warrior" labels I didn't ask for, and I especially hate the over-the-top pink branding that I see so much. I didn't ask to join this club. I didn't want to lose my hair to chemo or have my breasts amputated . I didn't choose to worry about whether my kids and relatives might also develop this horrible disease. And I hate pink; I always have. I'm grateful for my treatment and that I've weathered it all relatively well. I just feel pissed that this was my lot in life. As I reach the anniversary of the day my "before" split into the "after," I don't know what I'm supposed to call myself now. "Fighter" doesn't feel right. "Warrior" definitely doesn't, and "survivor" is complicated. The author said she doesn't like the "warrior" or "fighter" labels often given to those being treated for breast cancer. Courtesy of Kate Loweth. I didn't choose to fight cancer I understand that people mean well when they call someone a fighter. They want to acknowledge what she's enduring and remind her she's strong. Pink ribbons and awareness campaigns can raise money and encourage screenings, and those are all wonderful things. But in the rush to turn cancer into a story about courage and hope, there's little room for the less inspirational feelings: anger, resentment, exhaustion, and fear. I didn't fight cancer in the way people seem to imagine. I showed up for appointments, followed my doctors' recommendations, and endured treatment because I wanted to live. I didn't have some extraordinary reserve of bravery. I didn't get to opt out. What was the alternative? The author, shown with her daughter while getting treatment, said she would happily trade every bit of perspective she has gained for the life she had before her diagnosis. Courtesy of Kate Loweth. I didn't earn a special title by going through chemotherapy. I was a person with a disease who wanted to get better. Sometimes I was scared. Many days, I was exhausted. Sometimes I was just trying to get through the day. I'm over the pinkwashing of breast cancer And the pink. Everywhere, pink. Pink products, pink merchandise, pink marketing campaigns. Sometimes the branding feels like a cheerful coat of paint over a genuinely terrifying experience. Cancer isn't cute. Losing your breasts isn't a lifestyle rebrand or a "free boob-job." Buying a pink water bottle doesn't necessarily make anyone feel less alone in a hospital room. I don't begrudge anyone who finds comfort in a pink ribbon or a community of fellow patients . My problem is with the expectation that breast cancer should come packaged with a neat, uplifting message. What if I don't want to embrace this experience? What if I don't feel grateful for the lessons it taught me? I'd happily trade every bit of perspective I've gained for the life I had before my diagnosis. Finishing treatment doesn't mean everything's over There's no clear finish line. Treatment ends, and everyone wants to celebrate that you've made it through. You want to celebrate, too. But you're also left processing what happened to your body, what you've lost, and what the future might hold. As much as I try to go back to my "before" life, I'm constantly holding my breath, waiting for the other shoe to potentially drop. Before cancer, I didn't spend much time thinking about my identity . I was busy being a mom, wife, sister, daughter, and working woman. Now, I'm still figuring out how much space cancer deserves in my life. I don't want every conversation to be about my health. I don't want people to expect me to inspire them simply because something terrible happened to me. I'm grateful to be here, but I'm still angry I'm grateful for my doctors, the people who showed up for me, and the advances in medicine that gave me treatment options. I'm grateful that I've come through this in relatively good shape. But I can appreciate the care I've received and still be furious that I needed it. As I reach this anniversary, I don't need a label to make my experience meaningful. I don't need to turn cancer into a lesson or find a silver lining in every awful moment. I don't need to be inspirational. If you want to support someone with breast cancer, you don't have to call her a fighter. Acknowledge that what she's going through is hard. Offer an ear or, better yet, a DoorDash gift card. Let her feel however she feels. As for me, I'll mark this anniversary with gratitude, anger, uncertainty, and the knowledge that I'm still here. That's enough. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
events.summary: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors “I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare. It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader. But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy. One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors. Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast. In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”. And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings. A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation. It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease. Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.” One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said. Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic , OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory. He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation. But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats. “I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said. “The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.” The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing , believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.

events.title: Apple to 'work hard' to fulfil iPhone Duo deliveries as orders overwhelm stock
events.summary: Apple has said it will "work hard" to fulfil demand for its much-anticipated foldable iPhone Duo , as orders overwhelm supply and cause delivery dates to be pushed back. The device, the California-based company's long-awaited entry into the foldable market, was introduced alongside Apple's iPhone 18 Pro last month and is the first new major hardware release under chief executive John Ternus. Apple began accepting online orders for the Duo on Friday, but customers were reported to have quickly seen delivery estimates being pushed back from November to December and, as of Saturday, towards the end of January. In the UAE, Apple's online platform shows a delivery estimate of January 22, similar to its US and UK sites, applying to all four storage capacities and two colour options. It is unclear whether there are earlier or later dates in other areas. By contrast, delivery estimates for the iPhone 18 Pro are about two to three weeks. The period after a new iPhone is launched usually presents longer lead times, but those are eventually whittled down – in later periods to as little as a week – after the launch hype has eased. “The preorder demand for iPhone Duo ... has been nothing short of extraordinary," an Apple representative said in a statement to The National on Saturday. They added that the company aimed to get the devices to users "as quickly as possible". Online orders will continue while the company "looks forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores worldwide", the representative said. Considering the appetite shown by consumers, the delays could also be a positive signal for Apple's foldable – its debut device after the market went mainstream nearly a decade ago. It could also be a sign of further growth in the category, especially after Samsung Electronics reported record orders for its latest Galaxy Z foldables , which were introduced in July. Apple does not break down order and sales numbers. Counterpoint Research last month said the company was expected to sell about six million Duos this year owing to the strong demand potential driven by its “bold” pricing, which is just $100 above its main competitor, the refreshed Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8. Observers had expected a higher price point for the iPhone Duo. Sales could now hit about 14 million, adding about $28 billion to the company's revenue for the 2027 fiscal year, Bloomberg Intelligence estimates. The iPhone Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599.
