events.title: SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
events.summary: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier. Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.” Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast. Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate. Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder . Thanks for having me. I’m looking forward to it. I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it. It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion . They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here? It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar. The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more. Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company. I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that. But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it. Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did? When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage. Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial. Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial network. Now they finally realized, “If I’m going to offer mobile service, I need some form of a terrestrial network.” At the same time, the telcos are not going to help them out. They’re not going to give them a wholesale agreement. Then when they go back and say the companies that had the lowest churn, what is the fundamental value you need in a terrestrial network? It’s low-band spectrum. Why? It travels further, you can get better coverage, and you have that connectivity. So getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network. That’s why the stocks reacted, because people finally came to terms with the fact that Elon is actually going to build a terrestrial network. events.title: Famous Larrimah pub shuts after bikies visit sister venue on 'charity run'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts World famous Pink Panther pub shuts doors after bikie raid on owner's other venue The owner of the world famous Larrimah Pink Panther Hotel has closed the venue after what she describes as government "harassment". ( ABC News: Kristy O'Brien ) The owner of the NT's Pink Panther pub in Larrimah has shut its doors following a police raid on the owner's other venue. NT Police say they have charged three men with drug and weapons offences after members of the Outlaws bikie gang stopped at the Stuarts Well Roadhouse. The three men are due to face the Alice Springs Local Court in January while alleged liquor licence breaches have been referred to Licensing NT. The owner of the Northern Territory's famous Larrimah Pink Panther Hotel and the Stuarts Well Roadhouse has shuttered both businesses following a police raid regarding "a visit" by the Outlaws bikie gang this week. In a statement released yesterday, an NT Police spokesperson said investigators had searched the Stuarts Well Roadhouse "and an adjoining property" after a tip-off alleging breaches of the venue's liquor licence. They said officers searched the property on Wednesday and allegedly found an unsecured firearm and ammunition, 214 packs of illegal cigarettes, six unlawfully imported OC spray canisters and $3,800 in cash. Police allege a search of the Stuarts Well Roadhouse and "an adjoining property" resulted in the seizure of an unsecured firearm and ammunition along with 214 packs of cigarettes. ( Supplied: NT Police ) Police charged a 59-year-old man with unlawfully possessing a Schedule 8 drug and a 33-year-old man with breaching his firearms licence conditions. They also charged a 71-year-old man with manufacturing, selling or purchasing a prohibited weapon, with all three due to face the Alice Springs Local Court in January next year. The spokesperson said the alleged liquor licence breaches had been referred to Licensing NT. 'Corrupt cops', government 'harassment' Following the raid, the owner of both venues, Laura Ragless, took to social media to announce they were each "officially closed". "Don’t bother coming the government harassment and all has taken its toll sorry," she wrote. "We will always respect our supporters but no longer can take the government harassment the convicts running this country." Stuarts Well Roadhouse owner Laura Ragless has labelled charges laid following a raid on the business as "trumped up". ( ABC News: Hamish Harty ) On Tuesday, Ms Ragless posted pictures to the Stuarts Well Roadhouse Facebook page showing members of the Outlaws motorcycle gang attending the pub on the Stuart Highway south of Alice Springs. "A little rain and wind can’t stop these legends from hitting the road," she wrote. "Great to see the crew rolling into our roadhouse today! "Thanks for stopping by, guys. Ride safe and enjoy the journey!" In a separate post on Wednesday, Ms Ragless denied any wrongdoing and suggested the Outlaws had been on a "charity run". "Accused of illegally selling cigarettes and gun charges when I don’t even have guns anymore," she wrote. "And to top it off Stuart’s well [sic] locked down by corrupt cops that can’t even produce a warrant enough is enough." In another post this morning, Ms Ragless claimed the charges were "trumped up" and the tobacco products were "personal cigarettes not sold in or around the roadhouse". Under NT law, licensees and staff are required to direct outlaw motorcycle gang members to leave the premises if they refuse to remove "any clothing or items that identify their club". In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries told the ABC animal welfare officers had conducted an unannounced inspection of the Larrimah Hotel on Thursday after receiving "reports regarding animals". "No animal welfare concerns were identified pursuant to the Animal Protection Act 2018 at the time of the inspection," they said. Larrimah Pink Panther Hotel owner Laura Ragless says she closed the pub by choice. ( ABC News: Neda Vanovac ) "The Animal Welfare Branch assesses all reports received and undertakes enquiries where appropriate. "It will continue to monitor and assess information in accordance with its normal operational processes." Ms Ragless also took to Facebook on Wednesday to defend her treatment of the business's resident saltwater crocodile, Sneaky Sam. Sneaky Sam has been the Larrimah Pink Panther Hotel's resident croc for years. events.title: Up in the air: Tesla's 'flying' Roadster raises more questions than answers
events.summary: Elon Musk 's Tesla Motors has flaunted a new flying car – well, sort of. Mr Musk touted it as “something that you haven’t seen in any movie” but it's not exactly Back to the Future stuff. However, the stunt seems to offer a glimpse of the future of transport. It's a great idea, but several points need clarity before road-and-air-legal cars become a reality. What happened Late on Thursday, Texas-based Tesla introduced the redesigned Roadster, the electric vehicle maker's original model. It was a long-awaited unveiling for the new version of the car after production ceased in 2012. The Roadster was “launched” off a curved ramp, flipped over in mid-air and landed with the help of built-in thrusters designed by Mr Musk's other major venture, SpaceX. The car was also made to fly and barrel-roll over a line of Tesla vehicles, including its electric cars, Semi Truck and Cybertruck, although it seemed to take off vertically as it neared the first vehicle rather than launching well before. The latest Roadster, which is set to go into production in 2028, is billed as going from zero to 100kph in a second – significantly faster than the first-generation model, which achieved that speed in under four seconds. What's inside At the event at SpaceX's hub in McGregor, Texas, Mr Musk said the new Roadster used an “advanced ultra-high pressure air tank”, with 10 nozzles that carry about 250kg of air, which can recharge by itself without the use of any propellant. Air tanks are critical in vehicle systems, as they are key components for brakes, suspension, tyres and thrusters. In the space race – one of Mr Musk's closely-watched endeavours – they are very high pressure to support propulsion. The Roadster's air tank will “literally puff itself up and be able to do these manoeuvres whenever you'd like”, Mr Musk said. However, the thruster-powered Roadsters will only come in limited-edition models and there will not be any street-legal versions. Legal questions That means not everyone can, at least not yet, “fly a car”, let alone perform barrel-rolls and kick-flips with the upcoming Roadster – especially as laws on the vehicle are both very tight and vague. In the mid-2010s, US regulations had stated that flying cars would need two licences – one for the road and one for the air. The very niche nature of flying cars – whose technologies are still very much in their infancy – makes it difficult to assess rules by region. Whoever drives the flying car is another issue. A notable example of this was the AirCar, which was granted an airworthiness certification by Slovakian authorities in 2022. Its maker, Klein Vision, subsequently said its operator would need a pilot's licence – not just a driver's licence – to operate it. Mr Musk acknowledged this, saying, “I'm not sure if it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.” However, he emphasises that with the new Roadster, “we can go further … this will be an actual car on the roads”. Insurance and air space Then there's the thought of having to load a car with compressed gas, which can cause explosions and raise alarm bells for owners and insurers. “[It's] a tremendous feat of engineering. It’s hard to argue otherwise,” said David Thomas, director of content marketing at US software developer CDK Global. “I’m not sure where you fill up a car with that. And it’s unlikely anyone will insure it either.” And after ensuring any flying car is safe and legal, commercialisation is also a big question, said George Agathangelou, general manager and executive director of Cyprus-based financial services firm Teroxx. “Would drivers need aviation certification or a pilot’s licence? What happens to liability, insurance and airspace restrictions,” he said. “Imagine explaining to your insurer that you didn’t rear-end another vehicle, you attempted to fly over it.” Yes, it's real Tesla isn't the first to unveil such a vehicle: in 2021, Britain's McMurtry introduced the Speirling, an electric hypercar using powerful fans to generate downforce. Tesla's approach is different as it combines suction with thrusters. Mr Musk made sure that there was an audience to witness the Roadster stunts in Texas and ensure people would not claim it was AI. Analysts at Chinese logistics company Raman Technology noted that it was “not antigravity magic, [as] it integrates aerospace technology inside an electric vehicle”.

events.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness. Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing. It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line. The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt. It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.” By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.” Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges . But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.” Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership. Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.” When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand , for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.” He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out). Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “ Wahl Street ,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience. “I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding, “I can’t understand that philosophy.

events.title: The humble chickpea has just boomed in value
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chickpea prices hit $1,000 per tonne as importers rush to lock in supply Aussie chickpea prices are on the up. ( ABC Everyday: Heidi Sze ) Chickpea prices have skyrocketed to $1,000 per tonne. Several countries are rushing to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan. Australia's chickpea production is forecast to be down more than 50 per cent this season. Australian chickpeas are in hot demand, with delivered prices surging this month towards $1,000 per tonne in some regions. It is a significant jump from earlier in the year, when the market was trading closer to $600 per tonne. Grains Australia Pulse Council chair Peter Wilson said it was a great result for growers. "We haven't seen $1,000 per tonne since 2024 , so it's significant. It's a great price," he said. Chickpea prices have gone up considerably this month. ( ABC Landline ) So what is driving the sudden price surge for Australian chickpeas? Mr Wilson said it was due to a combination of factors. "There's a lot of volatility globally right now, which is creating enormous turbulence in logistics and supply chains, which is keeping buyers on edge," he said. "We're also seeing the impacts of El Niño, which looks to have left parts of India with lower-than-average rainfall from the monsoon, which has caused their local chickpea prices to rise, which is pushing everything along." The season's first delivery of chickpeas to the Mt McLaren receival site in Queensland. ( Supplied: Marc Johnston/GrainCorp ) Mr Wilson said there were several nations wanting to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan, which starts in early February. "Ramadan creates peak demand for a lot of our pulse crops [like chickpeas], and we see buyers wanting to have product pre-positioned at least one month ahead of Ramadan," he said. "So we're seeing some urgency from buyers trying to get product onboard vessels for key destination markets such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and the UAE, so it's in the market and ready for that Ramadan demand." In its most recent crop forecast, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES) predicted Australian chickpea production would fall by 52 per cent "to just over 1 million tonnes in 2026–27" due to significant cuts to area planted and expected lower yields in the major growing regions of northern New South Wales and Queensland. ABC Landline has been told that forecast may be "optimistic" and the overall crop might be even lower, which is another reason why there is some buyer urgency at the moment. Prices are expected to ease as harvest supply increases. New season chickpeas arrive at the receival site at Yamala, Queensland. ( Supplied: Fred Smith/GrainCorp ) North West Queensland chickpea grower Lucas Findley said he was pleased with his harvest, yielding about 1.2 tonnes per hectare. Although he had already forward-sold most of his chickpeas at a lower price, he said it was still exciting to see the market rally. "High prices are always good for any commodity and I'm happy for anyone who can take full advantage of these prices," Mr Findley said. "We'd sold around 75 per cent of our chickpea crop prior to this recent price rise at a good price that we were happy with. "But we still have around 25 per cent of the crop available to take advantage of the stronger prices, which will be a very nice finish to the season." Hummus is made from cooked, mashed chickpeas. ( ABC News: Wesley Mitton ) Mr Findley grows about 1,300 hectares of chickpeas as part of his grain and cotton rotation in Julia Creek. His chickpeas will be exported out of the Townsville Port, which is gearing up for its second-ever dry bulk shipment of the pulse. Last October, more than 38,000 tonnes of chickpeas were sent to India and Pakistan in a first-of-its-kind shipment from north Queensland, sourced from growing regions including Richmond, Julia Creek, Maxwelton and Marathon. This year, the port will also export sorghum for the first time, which Mr Findley said was "fantastic". "It just shows that people are supporting the expansion of North West Queensland farming more and more," he said. Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview . events.title: Travel booking platform Klook Technology files to withdraw US listing
events.summary: Klook joins a growing list of companies that have deferred IPO plans in 2026, including smart-ring maker Oura and nuclear services company Holtec. Klook Technology has filed to withdraw its US IPO plans on Oct 16, saying “this is not the right time to proceed with an IPO” because of market conditions. Reuters said US IPO activity has slowed as higher bond yields, a restrictive policy outlook and geopolitical uncertainty have made investors cautious. The Hong Kong-based travel platform, founded in 2014, said revenue rose 24% to US$417.1 million in 2024 and bookings are on track to exceed 80 million in 2026. Travel booking platform Klook Technology on Oct 16 filed to withdraw its US initial public offering (IPO) plans amid market volatility. “Given current market conditions, Klook has decided this is not the right time to proceed with an IPO,” a company spokesperson told Reuters. “We will continue to evaluate the right time for a listing.” IPO activity in the US market has softened in recent weeks as higher bond yields, a prolonged restrictive policy outlook and geopolitical uncertainty have made investors more cautious. Klook joins smart-ring maker Oura and nuclear services company Holtec among a growing list of companies that have deferred IPO plans in 2026 as volatile markets continue to curb investor appetite for new listings. The Hong Kong-based company had filed for a US IPO in November 2025 , and at the time disclosed a 24% jump in 2024 revenue to US$417.1 million (S$534 million). Founded in 2014, Klook offers bookings for tours, attractions, transport and other travel experiences across a wide range of locations globally. It competes with global platforms such as Booking.com, TripAdvisor, China’s Trip.com and South Korea’s Yanolja. “Our business continues to grow, with total experiences booked on track to exceed 80 million this year,” the spokesperson said. Klook was aiming to list its shares on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol “KLK”. REUTERS

events.title: Katie Zacharia ousted as White House press secretary
events.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted Friday after just five days on the job, according to two senior Trump administration officials. Why it matters: Zacharia will be the shortest-tenured press secretary in modern history, with her first and only week in the White House marked by speculation about her legal credentials and criticism of her first press briefing. Trump told reporters Friday that he had urged Zacharia to "reconsider" the job, saying: "The news has been so nasty to her. I've never seen anything like it actually. And I said to her, 'honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider." "POTUS is a big fan of Katie's, and what POTUS said to the reporters is exactly what he said in private," a senior White House official said. Driving the news: Zacharia was seen as a surprise pick when Trump announced her hiring on Oct. 9. She started work the following Monday, Oct. 12, and gave her first — and likely only — press briefing the following day. In that press conference, she was visibly shaky and nervous and left the president unimpressed, a White House official told Axios. Trump was also "blindsided" when he learned she wasn't an "attorney" as he had posted on Truth Social when he announced her hire. Zacharia tried to do damage control after a Wall Street Journal report that she wasn't licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. She told Fox News that she failed the exam and never retook it, since she was moving to China But her interview explanations weren't seen as up to snuff by Trump, the source said. Background: Zacharia's hiring was solely a Trump decision, one furthered along with the strong input of his personal assistant Natalie Harp. Zacharia flew out Thursday to Washington, slipped quietly into the White House without seeing any friends in the media or administration and had a good meeting with Trump. On Friday, Trump offered her the job on the spot. Contrary to other reports, Trump told Chief of Staff Susie Wiles his decision. Wiles, who did not know Zacharia before, raised no objections because she knew the press secretary job is a personal one for the president, another administration source said. Before hiring Zacharia , Trump wanted to hire former Fox News host Maria Bartiromo, two administration sources said, but she signaled she was not going to take the job. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings was in contention but wasn't offered the job. Behind the scenes: Zacharia's arrival concerned some staffers who feared she wanted to replace them. Zacharia denied this and tried to put their minds at ease. A White House official told Axios that Zacharia and her family are having dinner tonight with Vice President Vance and Vance's family at the VP's residence at the Naval Observatory. "The warmth for Katie goes well beyond the president," the official said. What we're watching: Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy said he spoke with Trump on Friday and that the president is in "no rush" to name a replacement for the press secretary. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout. Go deeper: Trump press secretary explains failed bar exam Barak Ravid contributed to this story.

events.title: Work starts on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Regional Development and Planning The 4.5-star hotel will offer almost 100 rooms. ( Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council ) Work has started on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years. A recent report into the region's accommodation needs showed it was 800 beds short every night. Construction on the new hotel on Airport Drive is due to finish by the middle of next year. It has taken two decades, but Bundaberg's next hotel development is underway. Four hours north of Brisbane, the city is a key tourism destination for the southern Great Barrier Reef but has not attracted significant short-term accommodation development in 20 years, according to Bundaberg Regional Council. The 4.5-star, three-storey hotel, situated across the road from the Bundaberg Airport, will offer 97 rooms. Mayor Helen Blackburn said the demand for accommodation was constantly growing. "The hotel demand study showed us that we were 800 beds short every night in our region," she said. "This is just one step towards bridging that gap." Cr Blackburn said it had been difficult to attract hotel developers to the region due to the current stock of aging motels. "Those older motels sell their rooms at a cheaper rate, which then doesn't give investors the confidence to think that if they build a new hotel, they can get the price for the rooms that they need," she said. Developer MVP said the new hotel would refresh the hospitality offering in Bundaberg. "We hope that it will be a destination of choice for travellers to the region and will bring more travellers to the region," a spokesperson said. Construction is due to finish by the middle of next year. ( Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council ) The hotel has been funded by investor MyState Limited, with chief executive Brett Morgan saying the demand was clear. "Every time you go down the street in Bundaberg, there's no-vacancy signs everywhere," he said. Mr Morgan said the hotel would also create about 50 ongoing jobs. Bundaberg Tourism chief executive Duncan Littler said the development would cater to leisure and business travellers. "Already, there's more than 750,000 people that choose to visit the beautiful Bundaberg region each year and they stay for more than 2 million nights," he said. "We hope that investments like this will also encourage other [tourism] operators, potentially even airlines, to consider investing in the region." Brett Morgan, Helen Blackburn and Duncan Littler have welcomed the project. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Cr Blackburn said other accommodation applications were in the pipeline but did not elaborate. "We have definitely been encouraging accommodation providers in terms of hotels, student accommodation and even aged care accommodation to set up in our region because we know that we need that here," she said. Construction on the Airport Drive hotel is due to finish by mid-2027, with the first guests expected later next year. events.title: Darwin accountant trades tax for cane toad taxidermy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'More to life': Darwin accountant trades numbers for cane toad taxidermy Mithram Selvaratnam transforms cane toads into souvenirs sold at Darwin's Mindil Markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) There are 531 dead cane toads in Mithram Selvaratnam's Darwin backyard freezers. By Christmas, some will be wearing Santa hats. The former accountant runs an unusual souvenir business, which sees him doing everything from sandblasting and whitening crocodile skulls to gutting and stuffing dead toads. Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam now sells taxidermy cane toads and crocodile products at Darwin's markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) It's a far cry from the life he envisioned for himself when he left Malaysia to study accounting in Australia 16 years ago. "When I grew up it was all about the rat race," he said. The decision to leave it all behind came to Mr Selvaratnam after working full time as an accountant in Melbourne. "I was doing that corporate life, 9 to 5, stuck in the office, and I just felt like there was more to life," he said. Christmas-themed cane toads are being prepared for the festive season. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Word of Mr Selvaratnam's dilemma got out to his Darwin-based aunt, who offered an unexpected solution. For decades she had been selling curries at the iconic Mindil Markets and a neighbouring stall had put his Territory souvenir business up for sale. That was in 2017 and the transition from spreadsheets to stuffed toads hasn't always been smooth sailing. Mr Selvaratnam was initially purchasing the toads from a taxidermist in Queensland, but when the supplier decided to retire, he was left with two choices — give up the business or take matters into his own hands. Grace Ray works on a taxidermy cane toad at Mithram's Leanyer work space. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) "Before I started doing this, I could barely pick a toad up," he said. "But I thought, we have plenty of toads in the Territory, an abundance of supply, so I'll just make them myself. "I went [to Townsville] and put myself through a two-day bootcamp of learning how to do it." It was through gritted teeth and pinched nostrils that Mr Selvaratnam learnt to gut, tan, stuff and dry the warty pests before painting them with varnish to make them "look pretty". Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam couldn't even touch cane toads until he underwent 'taxidermy bootcamp'. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Armed with his new-found knowledge, a head torch and gloves, Mr Selvaratnam began scouring golf courses and gardens hunting the pests. Community 'toad busts', like the one held recently at the Territory Wildlife Park , can provide hundreds of dead toads to Mr Selvaratnam in a single night without him having to lift a finger. Territory Wildlife Park ranger Luke Hare says toad busts aim to reduce the numbers of the pests while also educating the community of their dangers. "Cane toads produce significant risk to a lot of our native species," he said. "A lot of our natives can't tolerate the toxins cane toads have, so when they eat the cane toad, or try to eat them, often it will kill them." Mr Hare estimates that there could be hundreds of thousands of cane toads running rampant in the wildlife park on Darwin's outskirts. For Mr Selvaratnam, the park's latest haul of 531 toads has come just in time for his end-of-year Christmas orders. Soon, newly minted santa hat-clad critters will join their rum-drinking, ukulele-playing and occasionally X-rated counterparts. The recent toad bust has filled the freezers at his Leanyer workshop. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) But cane toads aren't the only unwanted creatures finding a second life in Mr Selvaratnam's backyard. Among the tanning equipment and taxidermy tools are chest freezers full of crocodile heads. "I started with the toads and the skulls came about a year after that," he said. Crocodile teeth and skulls are also turned into souvenirs. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Mr Selvaratnam had initially been buying the skulls from a supplier, but in a case of deja vu, retirement once again threatened his supply chain. "This time I didn't go down to Queensland to learn, I just got him on the phone and he ran me through it, and from then, on experimentation, really," he said. The skulls are a by-product from crocodile farms in the Territory, and along with croc teeth, buffalo heads and other leather goods, they make up the rest of Mr Selvaratnam's unlikely livelihood. He's also recently been experimenting with other forms of taxidermy including the Territory's iconic barramundi.

events.title: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
events.summary: The Treasury Department said the U.S. budget deficit came in at nearly $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year. The U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress. The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday. It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official. With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001. Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week. Social Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025. Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025. Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion. Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year. In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile. "Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August. President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional. The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers. The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

events.title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
events.summary: Treasury yields remain above 5%, pushing mortgage rates toward 7.5%. The deficit was $1.99 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% from last year. AI investment is increasing competition for capital. Divided government will likely take meaningful deficit reduction off the table. Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield . The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market. If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields. But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump 's term. There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP. Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates . If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits. The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years. "My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth. AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , a research group that advocates for balanced budgets. GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy. Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election. In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep.

events.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
events.summary: Apple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The price of the first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max. Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup. Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.

events.title: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
events.summary: Democratic candidates hold the fundraising edge across key Senate races and 13 of 21 House "Toss Ups" analyzed by CNBC. Republican super PACs are offsetting those gaps with record outside money, led by a $272.9 million quarter for the Senate Leadership Fund. Elon Musk emerged as the cycle’s biggest known individual donor, pouring more than $276 million into federal groups, including a major effort to help Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race. One of the last big campaign-finance snapshots before the Nov. 3 Election Day is now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats. On one side, Democratic candidates have turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds. Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedented flood of outside super PAC cash , bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk . The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amid stubbornly high inflation and drooping approval ratings for President Donald Trump. A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised and spent from July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings. If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves. Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals. James Talarico raised $60.2 million in Texas, Jon Ossoff brought in $33.1 million in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed raised $30.7 million in Michigan. Sherrod Brown brought in $23.1 million in Ohio, while Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in Maine, Mary Peltola $14.1 million in Alaska and Roy Cooper $12.2 million in North Carolina. Even in reliably red Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $9.4 million . In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close. Ken Paxton raised about $10.2 million in Texas, Mike Rogers $9.7 million in Michigan, Susan Collins $5.2 million in Maine and Jon Husted $4.8 million in Ohio. Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it. The same fundraising edge stretches into the House. Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, Democrat Jamie Ager raised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for Republican Jennifer Balkcom . The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber. While Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending. The Senate Leadership Fund , the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, the Congressional Leadership Fund raised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing. That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings. Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 million backing Sen. Dan Sullivan , according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The blitz allowed Republicans to hold an aired-ad advantage in seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact. But polls have shown little movement in recent weeks, despite the advantage. No donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.

events.title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
events.summary: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job just five days after starting it, a White House official told CNBC. Zacharia, who succeeded Karoline Leavitt, faced widespread criticism over her performance and came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background. President Donald Trump said Friday afternoon that he told Zacharia, "You don't have to do this if you don't want." New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance , a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday. Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit. "I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House. "'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia. The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role. Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly. By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci. "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday. Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group , had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background. Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms. But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters. In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working "You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House. He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night. Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney." Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied. Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day. White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday. "At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote. CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance." "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'" Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

events.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange before the closing bell in New York City on Oct 16. Wall Street tumbled on Oct 16, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend. The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise. Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data centre operator’s bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%. Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines. Investors on Oct 16 were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries. “There is some fear in the market,” said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at US Bank Wealth Management in ​Seattle. “High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk.” Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points. The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services, down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology. The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June. Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data. While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index’s median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ground in 2026. Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Oct 16 voiced optimism about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been “hanging in there” during a lingering energy shock and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation. Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged in October. Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each in December and January. Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer on Oct 15. Its shares were down 2.9%. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.3-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Canberra businesses battling 'multi-agency maze' to stay open, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businesses affected by Civic construction received 'insufficient' financial relief, committee report finds Ongoing construction in Canberra's city centre has seen a reduction in turnover for businesses in the area. ( ABC News: Lily Nothling ) An ACT Legislative Assembly committee investigating the city's night life has accepted reports that "insufficient" relief has been given to businesses affected by light rail and car park construction. The country's peak hospitality advocacy body has welcomed the committee's 28 recommendations to improve the ACT's night-time economy. The recommendations include establishing an ACT Night-Time Economy Commissioner and offering "stronger temporary relief" for affected businesses. The ACT government should consider stronger relief for businesses affected by construction work and establish a dedicated night-time economy commissioner, a review of Canberra's night life has found. Restaurants and other businesses would be forced to shut their doors without more action to address car park access and construction disruptions, according to findings from the ACT Legislative Assembly committee tasked with investigating the city's night-time economy. Chris Gatfield of the Australian Hotels Association has welcomed the committee's recommendations, but says he doubts they will all be delivered. ( Supplied: Chris Gatfield ) The committee's report, made public on Friday, made 28 recommendations to improve what the Australian Hotels Association (AHA) said was "a little bit of a struggle" for the industry. "The general economic climate is really, really tough for the hospitality industry," AHA ACT branch general manager Chris Gatfield said. "That's not necessarily just related to the various infrastructure projects that are going on in the city. But the committee accepted that there had been "insufficient" relief for businesses affected by light rail and car park constructions. It recommended the ACT government "consider offering stronger temporary relief measures for businesses adversely affected by ongoing disruptions associated with major infrastructure works in the city, such as means-tested rent relief". Charcoal Restaurant owner Anna Gray says financial assistance is the only way to ensure her business survives the construction works. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Anna Gray, the owner of Charcoal Restaurant in the Melbourne building in Civic, said her turnover had reduced by 50 per cent since parts of London Circuit closed in 2024. "Customers don't want to come because there's no parking," she said. Mr Gatfield said businesses need cash flow, but he doubted they would get it. "This will be a decision for government and so far I'm not convinced that they would be in a position to offer that kind of financial support," he said. "You really want the people who are suffering right now to be there to reap the benefits when construction is finished and people return to the city." The committee also found businesses were battling a "multi-agency maze" of red tape to stay open. Josh Dotta, the owner of Fiction nightclub (pictured), told the committee he routinely had to interact with 10 seperate government agencies. ( Facbook: Fiction Club ) Fiction Nightclub operator Josh Dotta gave evidence that he routinely interacted with 10 separate government agencies, while other stakeholders criticised the "silos" and "disconnected sections of government". "Anyone who's ever dealt with a government agency would recognise that sometimes it's very hard to get the person that you actually need to talk to on the phone," Mr Gatfield said. Although the ACT has a dedicated minister for the night-time economy, the committee said a night-time economy commissioner would support that role. The commissioner would consult the industry before major decisions, establish progress metrics, develop a more streamlined red-tape system, support culturally and linguistically diverse workers and take advice from a dedicated advisory group, the recommendations said. "We think it has legs in Canberra and if it works in other places there's absolutely no reason why it wouldn't work here too," Mr Gatfield said. Late-night venues such as Squeaky Clean, pictured during a performance by Citizen Kay, pay significantly more for a liquor licence than similar NSW venues. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Evidence from the AHA also found liquor licence fees in the ACT were significantly higher than other jurisdictions, prompting a recommendation for a review, especially for larger venues that can host more than 350 people.

events.title: Coral overharvesting on Great Barrier Reef investigated by Fisheries Qld
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aquarium industry investigated for overharvesting of coral on Great Barrier Reef Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it has investigated the overharvesting of coral in the Great Barrier Reef. Coral harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually. Fisheries Queensland does not intend to release the findings from the investigation. Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it recently investigated an overharvesting of coral on the World Heritage-listed Great Barrier Reef, but has declined to share the outcome. In the 2025-2026 fishing season the harvest of Pocillopora grandis , known as antler coral, was overfished by 30 per cent according to FishNet data. Coral harvesting is the process of collecting coral from the ocean. Harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually, with much of this destined for the global aquarium trade. Bright colours and interesting shapes are highly prized by 'reefers', who drive demand. But coral catch quotas have been breached several times in recent years, while some operators have been charged with fishing offences. There are quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) The ABC understands an internal investigation has now been completed into this year's exceeded quota. When questioned by the ABC, Fisheries Queensland would not send through the information about the investigations findings. Coral reef ecologist Dr Morgan Pratchett said while this particular species is not under threat, any overharvesting event is of concern. "It sends a bad message given the overwhelming international scrutiny on how this industry is being managed," Dr Pratchett said. Dr Morgan Pratchett is a reef ecologist. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) There are two quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef, known as individual transferrable quotes (ITC) and prescribed commercial catch (PCC) quotas. Individual quotas are where fishers are given a set amount to fish individually. Breaking these quotas can result in prosecution. PCC quotas, or competitive quotas, are where an amount is set and fishers essentially race to harvest until the quota is exhausted. Harvested coral in tanks for shipping overseas. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) According to Fisheries Queensland, this can sometimes result in going over the competitive quota for a coral species, which they say is not "uncommon or unreasonable." A 2024 assessment of the Queensland coral fishery noted that despite efforts to control overharvesting, some species continue to have their catch limits exceeded. It said fisheries would consider "trip limits, increased notifications, and more individual quotas if this issue continues." Do you know more? Email angelaheathcote@protonmail.com or contact her on signal: @angeh.36 At present, several Australian coral species are banned from being imported into the EU due to sustainability concerns. Simon Miller, from the Australian Marine Conservation Society, said he was concerned catch limits are not set at the right levels. "So when you see fishers in a race to fish to go out there where they're competing against each other to catch these corals as quickly as possible, and seeing this overrun of quotas, that's really concerning," Mr Miller said. "They're meant to be some kind of precautionary catch limit yet we keep seeing them overshoot year after year." Simon Miller from the Australian Marine Conservation Society. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) The coral harvesting industry has faced ongoing compliance issues. One recent case of alleged illegal coral harvesting being pursued by the Queensland Director of Public Prosecutions involved coral collector Jardini. The case included Jardini's director Jason Coe, who currently holds five licences in the Queensland coral fishery. Coe has not yet entered a plea. Earlier in 2024, Monsoon Aquatics lead diver and skipper Tim Green was prosecuted by Western Australia Police for offences related to the collection and recording of coral and fish while harvesting on behalf of Monsoon within the Western Australian coral fishery. He was found guilty and fined almost a quarter of a million dollars. Tim Green was found guilty of offences related to the collection of coral in 2024. ( Image: Facebook ) ASIC documents show Tim Green continues to be a shareholder at Monsoon.

SINGAPORE – When I think of Johor Bahru, I think of yummy food, medicine and beauty services – all at one-third of what they would cost in Singapore. The time spent travelling to get these deals is set to decrease with the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link that is slated to begin operations in February 2027 . The cross-border rail service will carry up to 10,000 passengers an hour in each direction, with a journey time of just five minutes.

events.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
events.summary: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” Read full article Comments
