events.title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump denied that the White House had ordered restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet services in Ukraine this week. Ukrainian officials complained on Tuesday and Wednesday that SpaceX had limited internet connectivity via Starshield without advance notice. Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. events.title: Iran-backed militias sending money back to cash-starved IRGC, U.S. says
events.summary: Iran-backed militias in the region have been sending money back to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to relieve the economic pressure it's under after nine months of war , U.S. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said Friday. Why it matters: While the U.S. military has been preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran, the Trump administration continues to put immense pressure on the regime with its naval blockade and severe sanctions. U.S. officials say the economic chokehold is causing serious difficulties for Iran and its security forces, while making the regime frustrated and aggressive. The White House hopes the pressure will induce Iran to make a deal that includes nuclear concessions. But so far, that hasn't happened. Driving the news: Cooper said the naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in lost oil revenue. Additionally, CENTCOM and the Treasury Department have managed in recent weeks to freeze $350 million that Iran had in cryptocurrency. Behind the scenes: In a video message released Friday, Cooper revealed that Iran-backed groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq — which have been funded by the IRGC for years — now have to give the money back. "The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," he said. Cooper said the Iranian government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including the internal security forces and the IRGC. State of play: Cooper attributed the significant increase in Iranian attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz to "desperation" within the IRGC. Despite those attacks, he said that the Strait of Hormuz is still open — with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the last week. Yes, but: In recent weeks, CENTCOM has almost completely stopped conducting strikes against Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers in the area of the strait. The pause in strikes, which was ordered by the White House to avoid escalating the war ahead of the midterm elections, made Iran more confident about launching attacks, a U.S. official said. Consequently, CENTCOM is concerned that the increase in ship attacks will cause shipping companies to think twice about transiting the strait — resulting in less oil coming out and a spike in oil prices. U.S. officials say Iran is also attacking more ships to try to raise oil prices and ratchet up pressure on Trump ahead of the midterms. What to watch: The White House and Qatari mediators are still waiting to hear back from Iran about a U.S. counterproposal to end the war. "It's still in internal deliberations in Tehran," a U.S. official said. Regional mediators told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in recent days that Iran shouldn't wait until after the midterms to give its response, a regional source with direct knowledge said. The regional mediators told Iran there's no guarantee that Trump will be more conciliatory after the midterms — on the contrary, he might be more aggressive.

events.title: Thune enjoys surprisingly clear path back to GOP leader despite Trump's attacks
events.summary: The News John Thune took criticism from President Donald Trump, agitated online conservatives, and occasionally frustrated some of his own members this year. Yet his next leadership election is looking smooth compared with the past couple of bouts to lead the Senate GOP. In fact, Thune may actually run unopposed this year, regardless of how the midterms go. “I’m not aware of anyone who wants the job. I certainly don’t,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Semafor. “I don’t envy the leader’s task.” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who challenged Thune in 2024 and Mitch McConnell in 2022, told Semafor there’s “no wiggle room; I am not running for leader” this cycle. He said Thune is “probably the only person that’s going to run. But I always want to say if other people run and someone comes up with better ideas, you’ve got to listen to them. But I’m not running.” Know More The biggest headache for Thune was the Save America Act, a voter ID bill that lacked a strategy to become law in the Senate. Trump repeatedly leaned on Thune to kill the filibuster in order to pass it, and other senators wanted Thune to try to force Democrats to pull off a talking filibuster to block the bill. Eventually, though, the effort and outrage over its stalled status faded away. With Democrats favored to win the House and potentially even take the Senate, the fight over killing the filibuster is back on ice. That’s all good news for Thune, who says he’ll likely run for another term regardless of whether Republicans lose the Senate. If no one challenges him, it would be the first unanimous GOP leadership election since 2020. Notably, Johnson had backed Scott in previous leadership races. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told reporters on Thursday that Thune “will get elected pretty resoundingly.” “Do I think he’s got broad support? Yes. I don’t think there’s an insurgent movement that’s against him,” Moreno said. “There’s not a single Republican running nationally that’s saying, ‘Hey, if you elect me, I’ll vote against John Thune as leader.’” Several Democratic candidates say they won’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term as leader of their caucus. But no one is indicating they are looking to challenge Schumer, either, which means those could just be protest votes. Former Democratic leader Harry Reid received a handful of “no” votes in his leadership race after losing control of the Senate in 2014. Republicans will have their leadership election on Nov. 10; Senate Democrats are likely to have theirs in early December, although the date isn’t set yet. The midterm results remain an X factor for both Thune and Schumer’s futures. Notable Thune told us in June he’d probably run again. Scott said in September he wasn’t committed to supporting Thune.

events.title: FAA equity talks raise questions about the agency's legal authority
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration’s pursuit of an equity stake in a private company that uses AI to manage air traffic is raising questions about whether it has clear legal authority to strike such a deal. The Trump administration has negotiated stakes in dozens of other companies, but none through the FAA. The agency’s interest in owning part of Air Space Intelligence, first reported by Politico , is too “premature” for there to be specifics, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor. Talks so far have been limited to a handful of internal conversations, the person added. One possible statutory underpinning for a deal: Existing law authorizes Transportation Department financial help for state or local governments to “acquire an interest” in some public transportation companies. That argument, like other agencies’ , would be a stretch. “It’s further proof that the administration doesn’t have a ‘plan’ or ‘strategy,’” said Tad DeHaven, who tracks the stakes for the Cato Institute . — Eleanor Mueller and Shelby Talcott

events.title: Copper thefts leave Perth roads in darkness and cost taxpayers millions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This section of Tonkin Highway en route to Ellenbrook has been without working street lighting for years. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) Major roads and paths across Perth remain dark because widespread copper theft has left street lighting out. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, and police are increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget to replace stolen street lighting cable and upgrade security. More than 100 kilometres of major roads and paths across Perth remain unlit, some for years, because of widespread copper theft. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, which is lucrative on the black market. Police said they arrested and charged a 31-year-old man who allegedly stole more than 190 metres of telecommunication cable from Gidgegannup, before selling the recovered copper to a scrap metal recycler. That theft allegedly occurred over the King's Birthday long weekend in September from a Telstra site, where about 500 kilograms of copper was pulled out of the ground. Roads across Perth's metro area are in darkness at night due to the theft. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "This had a significant impact on the Gidgegannup and surrounding areas," Mundaring sergeant Tony Signal told 102.5 ABC Perth. Sergeant Signal said police were increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. "They're obliged by law to record any second-hand dealing of copper at the moment and we find that that's slipping through the cracks," he said. Col Blanch says organised crime groups would find illegal ways to get away with breaking the rules. ( ABC News: Kenith Png ) Police Commissioner Col Blanch previously told the ABC organised crime sought to circumvent those rules when offloading stolen metal. "We know that some scrap metal dealers are doing the wrong thing and doing a lot of business under the table … that's what [the] police's job is to stamp out," he said. "However, when they can't sell it to a second-hand dealer, scrap dealer here, they will put it in a container and they will send large amounts of scrap metal overseas." It's far from an isolated incident involving telecommunications infrastructure , with detectives charging a man with stealing around 50 metres of copper cabling from an exchange site in Wattleup last month. A Telstra spokesperson said copper theft widely impacted service companies and that the telco's copper theft prevention team works closely with police agencies across Australia. Streetlights don't work when the underground copper wiring is removed. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "We encourage anyone seeing any suspicious activity near our facilities to contact police immediately," the spokesperson said. Street lighting also continues to be targeted, with police arresting a 41-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman this week, after a member of the public reported suspicious activity along Tonkin Highway in Ellenbrook. Police stopped a vehicle in the vicinity a short time later and allege they found a significant amount of stolen insulated copper wiring. Copper thieves taking exceptional risks Demolition sites are being stripped for copper at an escalating rate, according to a Perth demolition contractor, risking electrocution and asbestos exposure to sell the scrap metal on the black market. Main Roads WA said as of October 2, more than 1,400km of cable had been stolen from its network, taking more than 100km of street lighting and nearly 30km of pedestrian/cycle paths lighting offline. "Since cable theft became a widespread issue, Main Roads have replaced 480km of copper roadway and PSP lighting cable as well as re-cabling and re-energising over 500 individual poles," a spokesperson said. "Currently, Kwinana Freeway, Tonkin Highway and Reid Highway are the three priority routes that Main Roads is focusing on for cable replacement and anti-theft treatments. "Works are also planned in key locations along Forrest Highway, Great Northern Highway, Mitchell Freeway, Roe Highway, Albany Highway, Ennis Avenue, Mandurah Road and Armadale Road." The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget for street lighting cable theft replacement and security upgrades but still faces an uphill battle. Main Roads director of metropolitan operations James Pinnington said he expected the program to take several years.

events.title: Tariffs pose a risk to US-India relationship
events.summary: President Donald Trump faces a deadline Sunday to decide whether to impose certain penalties on other countries under a bipartisan sanctions law he signed last month. Any move by him to waive sanctions on Russian individuals or entities will be met with criticism, as would a decision not to impose tariffs on China for buying Russian gas. But Washington is hoping he’ll spare at least one country: India. “Both the United States and India should not buy Russian oil and gas, but I don’t think simply imposing big tariffs on India is the way to get them to” reduce their purchases, said Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Punishing India for its reliance on Russian energy “would deal a body blow to the US-India relationship,” argued Sadanand Dhume, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. The US and India are currently locked in trade negotiations, which more tariffs would surely disrupt. Fontaine said it is “100%” possible that the Trump administration uses the sanctions law to pressure India to give in to its demands in those discussions. Trump had previously hiked tariffs on India over its Russian energy purchases, but later removed them as trade talks progressed. Asked whether Trump had made a decision on which sanctions, if any, to impose at the deadline, a White House official said that he “signed the act and the administration will comply with the act’s requirements.” The bill gives the president broad power to waive penalties if he deems it in the US interest. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: From kitsch decor to extinct chains, new book revisits classic eateries
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New book Old Vintage Melbourne, A Culinary Chronicle captures the dining institutions of yesteryear Stalactites in Lonsdale Street has been a Melbourne institution since 1978. ( Supplied: Nicole Konstandakopoulos/Stalactites. Most of the photos featured in this article appear in Old Vintage Melbourne, A Culinary Chronicle, published by Scribe. ) From a sophisticated 70s restaurant with hot-pink light shades, to a St Kilda cake shop and the all-you-can eat smorgasbords of the suburbs, Chris Macheras's latest coffee table book is brimming with Melbourne's culinary history. But the book's beginnings are also quintessentially Melbourne — or at least Melbourne as we knew it in 2020. Stuck at home during COVID-19, the lawyer and artist kicked off an Instagram account featuring vintage photos of the city and suburbs. The page took off, spawning two books and, now, a third: Old Vintage Melbourne: A Culinary Chronicle. Chris Macheras's lockdown project has now led to a third book. ( Supplied: Meghan Lawson ) "It's still crazy to have an idea that was just something that I was sitting there in lockdown, depressed, and then to think that it's created this community and people have found each other via my Instagram page," the author says. But Mr Macheras is clearly someone who thrives creatively in trying times. He produced his latest book while battling Hodgkin lymphoma — a type of blood cancer. "Whilst I was recovering and doing chemo and everything, my brain needed to do something," the 36-year-old says. "They give you a lot of steroids … whilst your body is tired, your mind is very up." The Club Grill restaurant, at the Southern Cross Hotel, was originally for men only. ( Courtesy: Athol Shmith, Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales/Tourism Australia ) He began piecing the book together from home, contacting a large number of restaurants and trawling the archives of the state library, Museums Victoria and the public record office for old images. "I couldn't physically go to the library because I was recovering," he says. "So everything was what I could get by email, and who could send me photos." The late Nick Tsiligiris pictured inside his beloved Olympic Doughnuts van in Footscray. ( Courtesy: Gina Hasapis ) The result is a collection of photos and stories from about 120 food joints, from Marios and Kingsland Chinese Restaurant , to Coles Cafeteria, Glo Glo's, Smorgy's, fresh produce markets and one very popular Footscray donut van. The Olympic Doughnuts van was a landmark for almost 40 years. ( Courtesy: Gina Hasapis ) A Greek grandfather who loved Melbourne Mr Macheras says his grandfather, who emigrated to Melbourne from Greece in 1955, instilled in him a love of history. "We would talk about sort of the difficult life they had as migrants, and that we should really love Australia and love Melbourne because this is a land that gave us the opportunity to leave war-torn Europe, where they were from," he says. The author says the book celebrates Australia's restaurant capital at a time when many people are craving a sense of nostalgia. Melbourne's dine-in Pizza Huts, which began to disappear in the 1990s, are captured in the book. ( Courtesy: Fremantle Media ) Mr Macheras grew up in Preston and Eltham, and remembers eating at places like Jim's Greek Tavern in Collingwood, which is still going strong. "As a kid, we were always going to things that were familiar for an immigrant family," he says. "And then those family restaurants. Dine-in Pizza Hut is super nostalgic for me, going and getting some of that big trough with chocolate mousse, soft serve and jelly." The dessert bar at Pizza Hut lives on in the memories of many a 1980s and 1990s child. ( Courtesy: Claire Sullivan and Rob Breslin ) The story behind the famous Stalactites ceiling A Greek institution on Lonsdale Street in the city is one of many legendary eating establishments featured in the book. Stalactites — named after the handmade structures that grace its ceiling — opened in 1978, when the area was a hub for Melbourne's Greek community, Stalactites operated for 24 hours a day for years, with many daytime and late-night diners eating under its distinctive ceiling. ( Facebook: Stalactites ) "It was a place where all the Greek migrants could come, and they could eat Greek food and speak Greek and maintain that connection," says Nicole Konstandakopoulos, whose parents and grandparents were the original owners of the famous restaurant. "But over time, the Greeks moved out of the city, and they went to suburbs like Oakleigh." The Lonsdale Street institution seen from the outside.

events.title: Invasive fire ants return to organic farms not treated for 14 months
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Invasive fire ants are believed to have spread from organic farms left without treatment options for more than a year. ( Supplied: Scotty Yang ) Treatment on export-certified organic farms was paused in August 2025 after genetically modified ingredients were discovered in baits. The National Fire Ant Eradication Program (NFAEP) says there is evidence some areas have been reinfested from properties that did not have a treatment option for 14 months. A new treatment option has been found, but it requires direct nest injection, making it more labour-intensive than previous methods. Red imported fire ants have re-infested organic farms in Queensland, leaving them without options to control the pest for 14 months. Treatment was suspended in August last year on some export-certified properties in the south-east Queensland suppression zone after genetically modified ingredients were identified in baits used on nests. The National Fire Ant Eradication Program confirmed parts of a 1,110-hectare zone spanning the Lockyer Valley, Scenic Rim and Somerset agricultural hubs were re-infested, though the extent is yet to be determined. Fire ants can fly up to five kilometres, making their spread difficult to control. "We do have evidence of reinfestation of areas from properties that haven't been treated [since the suspension]," senior director of operations Robbie Wilson said. The genetically modified ingredients found in fire ant bait cannot be used on organic farms. ( Supplied: Johan Augustin ) He acknowledged organic farmers could not use ant-killing bait containing genetically modified (GM) corn and oil without risking their organic status. Fire ant treatment suspended on organic farms Fire ant treatments have been suspended on organic farms, and alternatives sought, after baits containing genetically modified soybean oil and corn grit were found to have been unwittingly distributed. "We've been working with (peak body) Australian Organic Limited … about how we support them in the eradication and limitations of infestation, which has been quite positive." Mr Wilson said the affected areas made up a small part of the 30,000 hectares identified as having gaps in treatment across the wider control area. "But that treatment may already be scheduled," he said. He said approving a treatment suitable for organic farmers was the "first phase" of bringing those properties back into the eradication program, which aims to eliminate fire ants by 2032. On Monday, the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry announced it had granted a permit for a product using concentrated cinnamaldehyde, the organic compound that gives cinnamon its flavour and odour, for use in Queensland. "This treatment product has been assessed as compliant with the National Standard for Organic and Bio-Dynamic Produce," the department said. The tiny fire ants spread quickly and are easy to overlook. ( Supplied: National Fire Ant Eradication Program ) The permit requires application "by direct nest injection and/or as a nest drench" by people authorised by the NFAEP. Mr Wilson said the first shipment of the product from New Zealand was awaiting customs clearance at Brisbane port. "It is an organic product that can be used on certified organic properties," he said. Organic farmer Di Fyson welcomed the new treatment option. ( Supplied: Di Fyson ) But the labour-intensive method could not replace broadscale baiting, which Mr Wilson said authorities continued to work on for larger organic operations. Scenic Rim organic farmer Di Fyson welcomed the new treatment, but questioned why it took so long. Ms Fyson, who grows domestically certified organic leafy greens and pumpkins, received treatments during the suspension. But she said she would be willing to try the new product. "Definitely, particularly if that's going to be the only option," she said. Invasive fire ants detected in Sydney's inner west Specialist fire ant detection dog teams have been deployed to the site in Sydney's Enfield and a nearby area with no other nests having been discovered. Reece Pianta, advocacy director at the Invasive Species Council, which lobbies for better funding for eradication and prevention programs, said he was concerned that substitute treatments were taking too long to deploy "at mass scale." "I'm concerned about the lack of organic farm treatment alternatives creating gaps in fire ant eradication," he said. "We know from past experience when there have been gaps in fire ant treatments, that is when fire ants have spread." "The success of eradication is reliant on keeping those treatment gaps closed.

events.title: Debt is eating up a bigger chunk of your raise, research shows
events.summary: CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board Debt payments consume an estimated 52 cents of every dollar of inflation-adjusted take-home household income gained for a typical worker, new research finds. The share of families spending more than 40% of income on debt payments has reached its highest level since 2013, according to Federal Reserve data. Experts say understanding why you're borrowing, budgeting and comparing prices can help prevent debt from becoming a bigger burden. A version of this article first appeared in ″CNBC's Money 101 Newsletter with Sharon Epperson,″ an eight-week series with monthly updates to help improve your financial well-being. Subscribe now to receive the series in your inbox. It is also available in Spanish . Consumer spending has helped keep the U.S. economy resilient. Yet research shows debt payments are taking a growing bite out of Americans' income gains, leaving less money available to spend or save. A new analysis by the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation and the consumer advocacy group Protect Borrowers found that a typical U.S. household's estimated real take-home monthly pay rose $109 from late 2022 to early 2026. "Real" take-home pay is one's wage after accounting for inflation. Meanwhile, a worker's monthly debt payments rose $57. In other words, researchers estimate that for a one-earner household, 52 cents of every dollar of income gained in recent years goes to higher debt payments. For a two-earner household, they project that the entire real income gain, and then some, goes toward debt. The analysis also found inflation-adjusted debt payments rose nearly 15% over roughly three years — about eight times as fast as household income, which grew less than 2%. The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers analyzed credit records for millions of working-age Americans ages 25 to 64, along with Census Bureau income data. The research includes payments on credit cards, auto loans and leases, student loans and home equity lines of credit. It excludes mortgages and some other borrowing, including many buy now, pay later loans and medical payment plans. Angela Hanks, chief of policy programs at The Century Foundation, said the findings may understate the financial pressure households face. "Even though it shows that workers' wages are getting eaten up by debt payments at a tremendous level," Hanks said, the findings represent "perhaps the rosiest analysis that we could have done using the data." She said adding mortgage payments as well as installment loans not included in a credit file — like buy now, pay later and payday loans — would have made household debt payments higher. Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead. Living abroad doesn't end U.S. tax obligations. What young expats need to know Inheriting a home can leave siblings with financial headaches — how to avoid mistakes Is the K-shaped economy ending? Finance pros weigh in SEC proposes investor exam to expand private-market access — how it could work You can't 'borrow your way out of debt,' expert says, but more people are trying More consumers are relying on credit cards to cover basic expenses when their paychecks fall short, she said. Separate Federal Reserve data underscores the strain. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances found 8.6% of families spent more than 40% of their income on debt payments in 2025, up from 6.5% in 2022 — a level not seen since the 2013 survey. Mortgages and student loans are often considered "good debt" because they may help build wealth or earning power. But even potentially beneficial debt, or debt taken on for necessary expenses, can become a financial burden. "When that debt stretches out for six months or a year or longer, or if you're taking out a seven-year auto loan, or if you're taking out a longer mortgage than maybe you ideally would want to, or a bigger mortgage, that's when things get a little dicey," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More." To avoid taking on more debt than you can afford, he recommends three simple steps: Set a budget. Know how much you can realistically spend before you borrow or shop. Make a list. Shop with specific purchases in mind rather than giving in to impulse buys. Compare prices. Shopping around can reduce costs and how much you may need to borrow. Before taking on debt, consider the total borrowing cost, repayment terms and whether you have enough savings to handle unexpected expenses, Schulz said. — CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting.

events.title: State Department warns travelers to China they risk “wrongful detention”
events.summary: The State Department is updating its travel advisory for mainland China to include an increased risk level for wrongful detention, according to a new plan seen by Semafor. The State Department’s move comes after two US citizens were labeled as wrongfully detained earlier this year, and at a complex moment in the relationships between the two most powerful countries in the world. Despite a personally warm relationship between the presidents, the countries’ deep differences from the Taiwan Strait to trade to artificial intelligence remain. A person familiar with the situation told Semafor the department’s change is connected to the continued detentions of the two Americans, Min Zin and Youlin Chen. Zin is a Myanmar scholar who was detained in June and accused of endangering China’s national security. Chen is a seismologist detained in 2024 and charged with espionage. Both are US citizens. The travel advisory as a whole remains at a Level 2, which urges Americans to “Exercise Increased Caution” when traveling to China, but the department is adding a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention. Previously, the travel advisory for mainland China had an “O” risk indicator, which meant that there were “other potential risks not covered” by the department’s specific risk categories. “The U.S. Department of State has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China,” a State Department spokesman said in a statement to Semafor. “The D risk indicator means the State Department has determined Americans are at risk of wrongful detention by the government of the country.” A group of bipartisan senators introduced a resolution last month pushing the department to add the wrongful detention indicator to its travel advisory, citing the two detained citizens. The spokesman added that wrongful detention is determined by a variety of factors, including having US citizenship or a connection to the US. This is the latest update to the State Department’s China travel advisory — in early September, the department added stronger warnings about wrongful detention, the “arbitrary enforcement of local laws,” and the usage of exit bans. Asked why the travel advisory remains at a Level 2 given the new wrongful detention label, the spokesman said it “identifies a specific risk of wrongful detention” and that “the overall Travel Advisory level reflects a broader assessment of safety and security conditions.”

events.title: Hill leaders brace for miserable 2027
events.summary: Have some sympathy for Capitol Hill's leaders next year, no matter who wins in November. 😩 Why it matters: The next Congress promises a thousand different ways to be miserable. And three of the big four leaders are expected to receive a two-year contract extension, with guaranteed long nights, bad days and short tempers. The fate of the fourth — Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) — rests on the outcome of the election. 🤕 The best (and worst) news for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is that the job as party leader is likely his if he wants it, even if Republicans lose the majority. Like his first two years as leader, Thune's next two will be marked by constant second-guessing , or worse, from a president who commands his party, crushes his opponents and questions Thune's courage . Then there's the GOP base. MAGA influencers are seething over Thune's reluctance to try to nuke the filibuster and jam through a voter-ID bill . Between the lines: Four of Thune's confidants — DHS Secretary (and former senator) Markwayne Mullin and Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.), Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) — have left or are leaving the building. A fresh class of House conservatives will arrive in the Senate. They're likely to want to move fast and break things. The intrigue: Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) has not announced a third attempt to lead his party, but plenty of Republicans on the Hill suspect he will. Scott notably backtracked on his support for Thune in September. But Thune doesn't have to worry about his number two. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) — who would be the top contender if Thune stepped down — has doubled down on his support. ⚠️ Thune's relationship with Speaker Johnson has been rocky throughout the year . If Republicans lose the House majority, Thune could find himself coordinating and strategizing with a new House leader. Most of Johnson's colleagues don't expect him to stay if the House flips. However, in the campaign's final weeks, Johnson has been playing Hamlet , publicly entertaining his next moves. With or without Johnson on stage, Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are widely viewed as top contenders. 😎 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) appears secure in his job as Democratic leader. His longevity in the role — or the Senate — is not. He's up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Many Democrats expect him to retire. One possible result: YOLO Chuck , a 76-year-old majority leader with an angry base and ambitious colleagues, but nothing to lose. 🤬 One urgent task for Schumer is to get on the same page as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whose progressive members have some strong feelings about Schumer and the Senate. Jeffries and Schumer took dramatically different approaches to funding the government in March 2025. These differences would be harder to manage in the majority, especially if Jeffries struggles to maintain discipline within his ranks. However, Jeffries — like Schumer and Thune — doesn't appear to have any formidable challengers for party leader. Jeffries could face many of the same headaches Johnson did — a wing of his party that ran on anti-establishment principles and whose votes cannot be counted on . What we're watching: Trump and Schumer have a complicated relationship . But the president has indicated he sees Jeffries as someone he could work with.

events.title: Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Maybe it was the grey color, the slightly bulbous roofline, or the vaguely SUV-like proportions of the electric Porsche Macan, but as I shuttled kids and groceries around city and suburban streets, I never once noticed a longing stare from other drivers. Unlike with other cars I’ve tested, no enthusiasts stopped to ask me questions. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo simply blended in, leaving in its wake a raft of existential questions. What is a sports car, anyway? Does it need to be overwhelmingly extroverted? Should it match the leaner, lighter look of its gas-powered sibling? Drive one and the questions cease. Maybe that’s because the acceleration makes it hard to breathe? Or maybe it’s because, by the numbers, the Macan is a sports car at heart despite its rather humdrum crossover body style. My passengers would agree. The kids I drove to soccer practice, both my own and others, gave the punchy acceleration high marks. The G-forces it reports on the head-up display ($2,660) can easily mimic the pull of gravity. Stab the accelerator at 70 mph and it lurches as though it were standing still. (Don’t worry, fellow parents. I did not try that with children on board.) On winding roads, the car comes alive, thanks in part to the four-wheel steering ($2,150). Drop it into Sport Plus mode, and the car literally drops on its air suspension. Are we sure this is another anonymous crossover? Maybe anonymity is a useful trait in a car this responsive and powerful. Unlike most two-row crossovers, you get the feeling of sitting in the Macan, not on it. The wheel extends far enough to make a sporty driving position possible, and the classic Porsche chronometer ($1,040) perched atop the dash ticks off the seconds it takes to get the kid to soccer practice. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. The EV, which the automaker provided to me for a week, starts at $112,700. However, the one I drove rang up at $149,610, including destination fees. Yes, the options alone could buy a nicely equipped Chevy Bolt . With Porsche and options, if you have to ask…well, it’s better not to. The Porsche Macan Turbo EV I drove came in Slate Grey Neo (a $2,620 upgrade), which was really well executed and among the best greys I’ve seen. If you crave luxurious anonymity, then this grey is your color. There were a slew of other options, and in my view, not all of them are worth it. I’d skip the passenger display ($1,710); my kids liked that it could play YouTube videos, but they can’t ride up front, and my wife was underwhelmed. “Our washing machine can play YouTube videos,” she said. I’d also forgo the illuminated Porsche wordmark on the front seatbacks ($690), puddle lamps that shine “PORSCHE” onto the pavement ($420), Porsche crests on the headrests ($640), and an illuminated Turbo badge on the door sills ($1,230). That Turbo badge became a point of contention for some of my friends, who were quick to point out that EVs technically can’t have turbos. That is true, though automotive names have long been divorced from reality. Almost every Porsche these days has a turbo, even those not labeled as such. It’s not just Porsche: BMW’s model numbers, for example, stopped reflecting engine displacement decades ago, and the Ford Galaxie never traveled between star systems using its hyperdrive. Sorry, friends, I’m not taking the bait. At least the Macan Turbo’s EV qualities don’t raise too many questions. It charges fast — exactly 20 minutes from 19% to 80% on a 350-kilowatt charger — and gets about 285 miles of highway range. Those big wheels ($4,110) and sticky tires ($660) sapped some range, but it was still more than enough to get from New York to Boston with charge to spare. The advanced driver assistance system ($1,140) works well enough, even if it hunts a bit in the lane. The AI-powered voice assistant did a solid job of interpreting my queries and commands. For a while, I thought it was the only way to turn on the heated steering wheel ($720), which was actually fine because it worked so well. (Surprise! There’s a small button hidden on the inner rim of the steering wheel between two spokes. IYKYK, I guess.) When it’s time to leave the Macan, you can just open the door and walk away. The Burmester sound system ($4,960) will keep bumpin’ until you lock the door, which is a helpful reminder. If you’re a Porsche traditionalist, you can also hit the vestigial power button to the left of the driver’s display. Good to have choices, I guess? At least Porsche doesn’t charge you for that. The navigation system, and specifically how it integrates with the EV, was underwhelming. When the car was at a 22% state of charge, I asked it to find the nearest fast charger. It directed me to two.

events.title: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer
events.summary: Netflix has replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with former Disney executive Peter Rice. Rice brings a wealth of experience in television and film, including scripted and unscripted shows, live sports telecasts, prestige television and theatrical distribution. Netflix's viewership has stagnated in recent quarters. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday. Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes. On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria , who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy . Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget. She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady." Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways." The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees , or 6% of its workforce. The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years. "We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday. In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead. "The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote. Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%. YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. "If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again." Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun." He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup. Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms. Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed. In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade. With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later.

( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) held a three-day hearing into a proposed silver and lead mine near Mudgee this week. A minerals expert told the IPC the nearby Lue Public School should be moved if the project was approved. The IPC is expected to hand down a determination by December 9. The NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has been told a public school should be moved if a proposed silver and lead mine is approved, amid fears it could poison children. The IPC heard three days of evidence this week in Mudgee as it reassessed a proposal to extract 30 million tonnes of silver, lead and zinc over 23 years near Lue. The project has divided the community, with advocates touting the economic benefits and others raising concerns about potential environmental and health impacts. Proponent Silver Mines Limited's managing director Jo Battershill implored the panel to approve the development. "The project would provide investment and economic diversification for the mid-western region," he said. A tractor protest was held in Mudgee on Wednesday in opposition to the proposed silver mine. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Almost 100 people spoke at the hearing, with the majority opposed to the mine. Only a few who spoke in support were not employees. On Wednesday, a group of farmers rode tractors and utes from Lue into Mudgee as part of their protest action. Along with dozens of local residents, experts from around Australia also addressed the hearing. Dozens of local residents spoke in opposition to the Bowdens Silver Mine at the IPC's reassessment. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Among them was University of Queensland professor and principal research fellow at the Sustainable Minerals Institute Barry Noller. He told the hearing he believed the project's potential for lead exposure posed an unacceptable risk to children at Lue Public School, located two kilometres from the mine site. "I recommend that the Lue school, being at the boundary of dust deposition of [the] Bowdens mining project, be moved," Professor Noller said. "The management plan would be underestimating the true quantity of deposited lead that is relevant in terms of assessing the risk to adults and particularly children." Jo Battershill appeared before the IPC on Wednesday as part of its reassessment of the mine. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Mr Battershill told the IPC that while the concern was understandable, the project had undergone extensive independent review. "Predicted health risks from the project, including from lead, are very low and are not expected to result in adverse human health impacts," he said. "It has been carefully assessed, and multiple layers of monitoring and management would apply throughout the life of the project." Mudgee-based general practitioner Peter Bryant told the panel dust from the project would threaten residents across the district. "There are no levels of lead exposure which are known to be without risk of harm," Dr Bryant said. "I don't want to find myself frequently requesting blood tests for children who live in this area to check their lead levels. "I really hope not to be talking with parents about the high levels of lead that have been found in their child's blood and discussing the long-term implications this could have on their blood development and ongoing health." GP Peter Bryant also spoke at the public hearing, citing his concerns. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) As part of the proposal, Silver Mines Limited would use approximately 2,000 megalitres of water a year for processing and dust suppression. Mr Battershill said assessments found average water supply reliability to be approximately 99.4 per cent. "The water balance monitoring found that except during extreme drought conditions, sufficient water would be available to meet operational demands," he said. Dozens of people drove tractors from Lue to Mudgee, where the IPC held its three-day hearing. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Martin Krogh worked for the NSW government as a scientist for more than 30 years, including at the former Sydney Catchment Authority. "In my view, there are significant shortcomings in the Bowdens Environmental Impact Statement surface water assessment," he told the panel. "During drought conditions and very dry years, it appears highly unlikely there will be sufficient water falling in the catchment to support the environment, basic stock and domestic use, and downstream irrigation.

events.title: ICE shooting leads to rare Jeffries-Mamdani collaboration
events.summary: An October shooting by federal immigration officers in New York City has led to a head-turning show of unity from House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Why it matters: This unlikely collaboration between leaders of Democrats' competing establishment and progressive wings shows how opposing Trump-era immigration enforcement has become an area of party consensus. Democrats "are definitely unified across the spectrum re ICE," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the chair of the Queens Democratic Party and a close ally of Jeffries, told Axios. He added that "the Mayor has also reached out ... to me in regards to local issues and I believe Leader Jeffries is also indicating he wants to work with the NY Congressional delegation." Driving the news: Mamdani led a letter dated Oct. 16 with over 100 other Democratic elected officials in New York City, including every Democratic member of the city's congressional delegation, to parking lot and garage owners. "In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend, or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations," the letter reads. The officials argued that the shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in New York's Marble Hill neighborhood in early October was "not an isolated case," pointing to past instances in Queens and Manhattan . "Owners who refuse to take part in these federal civil immigration enforcement operations advance public safety by protecting their own staff and customers, as well as fellow New Yorkers beyond their lots and garages." Between the lines: Jeffries and Mamdani have walked a careful line as two of the most prominent national figures within their respective Democratic Party factions. Jeffries rankled the left, including some members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, by waiting until 11 days before last year's election to endorse Mamdani for mayor. The two came into conflict this summer when Jeffries supported Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat while Mamdani campaigned hard for their primary challengers, though the Democratic leader notably downplayed the clash . Yes, but: The two have also had other notable moments of accord, such as when Mamdani opposed City Councilmember Chi Ossé 's ultimately aborted plan to try to primary Jeffries from the left. They also appeared together at a ribbon-cutting for a housing development in Brooklyn on Thursday. Zoom out: The letter's signers also include Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who accused then-candidate Mamdani last year of making "references to global jihad," for which she later apologized . Goldman and Espaillat, who were ultimately unseated by their Mamdani-backed challengers, signed on as well. So did retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez, who was burned by Mamdani endorsing Claire Valdez over her chosen successor, according to the New York Times . What we're hearing: "It's significant to see Mayor Mamdani lead a letter like this that includes both U.S. Senators and the full NYC Democratic House delegation (including the two he opposed in this spring's primaries)," a prominent Mamdani ally said in a text message to Axios. The person added: "It reflects both how universally hated ICE is by Democrats — and how much work the mayor has done to build bridges." The Mamdani ally spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer candid analysis of the delicate relationship between the mayor and the party establishment. The bottom line: Others argued that Democratic unity around opposing ICE was the overriding factor. One Democratic elected official from New York told Axios: "The fact that everyone signed on has more to do with the power of the issue than the power of the Mayor." A person in Jeffries' orbit similarly argued that immigration is simply "a unifying issue for Dems," but acknowledged that Mamdani "is consistently reaching out to the delegation to build ties and smooth things since the elections, which is smart."

events.title: Private lenders scramble to recover funds after Bathla collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Major Bathla lender La Trobe sells $31.2m loan as private credit firms seek to recover funds Topic: Construction and Real Estate Industry Private credit lenders of Bathla Group are striking deals to recover debts following the property giant's collapse. ( ABC News: Berge Breiland ) La Trobe Financial has sold its senior loan facility, tied to a Bathla Group development, to investors through a fund managed by 360 Capital. The $31.2 million purchase would give 360 Capital greater influence over the Marsden Park project. Morningstar expects private credit fund growth to slow substantially. The fallout from the collapse of property developer Bathla Group continues to reverberate through Australia's private credit market, with lenders taking matters into their own hands to recover money tied up in the failed construction giant. In one of the latest deals, property investment and funds management group 360 Capital has revealed it acquired a senior loan facility for about $31.2 million through its private credit fund, funded by private investors and entities within the 360 Capital group. A senior loan facility is the first mortgage debt in a commercial investment and ranks highest in repayment priority. The ABC understands the debt was acquired from major private lender La Trobe Financial, relating to a Bathla development at 137 South Street, Marsden Park, in Sydney's north-west. An artist's impression of 137 South St, Marsden Park apartments, as listed on the Bathla website. ( Supplied: Bathla ) The Marsden Park project comprises 72 apartments and is nearing completion, according to two sources close to the construction. Half of the apartments have already been pre-sold under contracts worth $25.8 million (excluding GST), 360 Capital said in a statement. In August, La Trobe disclosed it had $38.1 million in loans to Bathla, comprising four residential loans and one development loan. The ABC understands through this deal, La Trobe has sold its development loan, recovering all outstanding principal, interest and late-payment charges and significantly reducing its exposure to the collapsed developer. Deal gives 360 Capital greater control 360 Capital's ASX-listed mortgage investment trust, the 360 Capital Mortgage REIT, already held an $8.9 million loan secured against the development, which ranked behind La Trobe Financial for repayment. The trust has invested a further $5.2 million in the deal. Construction work has stopped at sites and the company is down to skeleton staff. "The step was not taken lightly, but is very important to protect the value of the trust's subordinated position," the company said. The deal means entities associated with 360 Capital now control both the first and second mortgages over the development, giving them greater influence over how the project is completed and the debts recovered. Morningstar equity analyst Winky Tan said lenders holding first mortgages were in a much stronger position to recover their money, while mezzanine lenders further down the repayment queue risked losing most, if not all, of their investment. "When you're able to finish the project, you can sell it as a finished product, which will have a much higher valuation than a half-finished project," she said. New Victorian laws reveal auction reserves, so buyers stop wasting weekends Lifestyle benefits outweigh costs of apartment living for some downsizers Real estate agents urged to 'enhance responsibly' as AI use rises Outcry over council's 'extortionate' fee hike on short-stay homes Following the purchase, advisory firm Wexted was appointed as receiver, with a focus on speeding up the process of obtaining occupancy certificates and settling the 36 pre-sold apartments. 360 Capital executive chairman Tony Pitt said the group expected to recover the full amount owed to it under the loan. Ms Tan cautioned that the ultimate financial outcome for any lender would depend on whether the remaining apartments could be sold and at what price, particularly given the downturn in the property market. 'Perfect storm' unfolding in private credit sector Lenders including Centuria Bass and CVS Lane suspended withdrawals from some funds in August amid concerns about their exposure to Bathla. MA Financial, which says it has no exposure to Bathla, also introduced withdrawal limits on some of its funds amid concerns more investors could seek to pull out their money. Major private credit manager Metrics Credit Partners, which also says it has no exposure to Bathla, suspended withdrawals from some unlisted funds amid scrutiny of asset valuations.

events.summary: The sell-off in AI-related stocks pushed the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months. A cluster of trades suggests it could go even higher. In a series of eyebrow raising trades, investors purchased a number of November VIX calls that payoff if the index stays elevated through November. Specifically, one trader bought 9200 of the November 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million and 12,500 of the November 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million, wagering that the VIX will close above 23 by the third week of November. "The speed at which VIX increased today, combined with elevated VIX options volume suggests traders are actively monetizing October VIX positions and rolling to hedge a larger market downturn. We note several +$1 million call VIX prints for November," said Brent Kochuba, founder of SpotGamma and a CNBC contributor. Cracks in the AI complex and fears around neo-cloud provider CoreWeave caused the Nasdaq to shed 2%, its worst day since June 5th. CoreWeave lost 13%. Of the top ten most popular VIX contracts to buy in Friday's session, nine were calls, and six were at strikes above where the VIX fell to after its initial spike. Nearly $27M in premium was traded across those nine contracts, or just about 36% of the total premium traded in VIX options on the day. The market faces a key test next week when Tesla, SpaceX and Meta report earnings.

events.title: The AI behind Formula One race-day decisions
events.summary: Sunday, May 3, 2026, Miami International Autodrome, Miami Joseph “Joey” McMillan has been watching the numbers, and the skies above. With the start of the Miami Grand Prix just a few moments away, the Lead Race Strategist for the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team sits at his console, perched on the pit wall above the start line, listening to multiple different intercom channels at the same time, checking the weather reports and thinking about the race ahead. The team’s drivers have performed well over the race weekend, both in practice and in qualifying. British driver George Russell is starting fifth on the grid but, ahead of him, Kimi Antonelli is in pole position. The Italian teenager has been the breakout star of the season so far and is aiming to win his third Grand Prix in a row. At 19, Antonelli would be the youngest driver ever to achieve that feat. Antonelli and Russell are just two of Mercedes’ vast F1 team, around 1,300-strong, mainly engineers dedicated to making their cars go faster. But McMillan isn’t an engineer. His job is not about squeezing an extra ounce of speed from the engine, but saving time by executing a plan of action on the track, analyzing the variables his drivers can’t see and can’t control. “The strategist is sort of the black sheep in the sense that we are not really focused on making the car [go] faster,” explains McMillan. “Our job is to try and navigate those two cars through the race weekend. And to do that, we’re often looking at a lot more than just our car. We’re focused on every car on the grid, what every team is doing.” Like all sports, F1 is obsessed with marginal gains and McMillan’s mission is to find an edge on rival teams, making decisions based on multiple streams of data and running multiple simulations. In a sport where a thousandth of a second can be the difference between winning and losing, every factor needs to be considered. “By far the most important thing we do is decide what tire compounds to use in the race and what laps to make pit stops on,” he says. “That combination is known as the strategy.” There are five types of tires to choose from during a race, all color coded for different conditions: three types of slicks for dry conditions (soft, medium and hard), and two treaded tires (intermediates for light showers and wet tires for heavy rain). “If we knew the degradation rate of each of those compounds, essentially how much slower they get each lap in milliseconds, strategy would be so easy.” But things are rarely easy in F1. As well as monitoring the pace of rival cars and trying to judge how the tarmac will affect the tires, the strategy team’s simulations also need to know the answer to the question dominating McMillan’s thoughts as he sits at his trackside console. Is it going to rain? And in Miami, a storm is coming. The race is taking place at the start of May, six weeks before Florida’s Atlantic hurricane season usually begins, but the bad weather is ahead of schedule. The threat of lightning strikes is so severe that the organizers have brought the start of the race forward by three hours. Rain briefly fell in the morning, and McMillan is being fed local weather radar data that suggests rain might fall again during the race. Will it be a passing shower? Or a deluge? A decision has to be made about which tires to start on: the faster slicks, the intermediates or the wet tires. That choice could win or lose the race before it even starts. McMillan and the team make a play based on the data at hand and their instincts. The drivers will not start on wet tires, they will be on slicks and hope the weather holds. As the lights go out and the race begins, the drivers roar toward the first corner on a dry track under skies pregnant with rain. And then all hell breaks loose. “When we run our simulations, we run an entire race. We want to run thousands, if not millions of these races. Now, with Azure Batch, we can” McMillan has been a race strategist for a decade. The softly spoken Englishman was hired by the Mercedes F1 Team after finishing his mathematics PhD at Imperial College London. It was his first job after college and he’s been there ever since, moving up to Senior Race Strategist and, eventually, Lead Race Strategist. “We use about five or six strategists a weekend,” he says. “Out of those, maybe one or two of them will ever end up being the pit wall strategist who’s making the final decision, but you need a whole lot of people running models.” Mathematics is only part of the job. What separates a good strategist from a great one is the ability to function under pressure. “It’s not super difficult in the sense that I don’t need high-level mathematics, nothing like the mathematics I was doing for my PhD,” says McMillan. “What makes a good general strategist? Someone who is a logical thinker, really good at modeling and data analysis. But what really makes you good at the pit job is to be able to make the decision in the moment, to do it very, very quickly, with very good communication skills… when you’ve got drivers, team principals, race engineers, lots of excitement and intensity. Once you realize you can do that, I think it’s pretty clear you’re going to be good at this.” Machine learning, as McMillan calls it, has always been a huge part of his job – but in recent years, AI technology has greatly improved his ability to analyze more and more data at faster speeds. “My day-to-day, the actual Sunday doing the strategy, hasn’t changed a huge amount yet,” he says. So, what has changed? “I write quite a lot of code, but I’m really not a coder. I’m a mathematician, a statistician, a game theorist, but I’m not a coder. I understand what data we’ve got. I understand what I’d like to do with it. And [with] the advent of AI, like coding tools, I can do those things a huge amount quicker. I can now write models, write analysis, do things at a speed I could never dream of before.” At the start of 2026, Microsoft signed a deal with the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team, a partnership that put Microsoft technology at the heart of its operation. After dominating Formula One for much of the 2010s, winning seven consecutive drivers’ championships between 2014 and 2020 and eight consecutive constructors’ championships between 2014 and 2021, the team was looking to build on that legacy. With a radically reengineered car performing strongly in testing, there was growing belief that 2026 could see the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team challenge for championships once again. For the F1 strategy team, one of the biggest benefits of working with Microsoft is access to Azure’s vast cloud computing capacity. Using Azure Batch, they can run huge numbers of race simulations simultaneously, testing multiple scenarios before, and even during, a Grand Prix.

events.title: Celebrating the next generation of Latin American game creators
events.summary: Multiple Adventures Await as Stories: The Path of Destinies Arrives on Xbox One Upcoming Changes to XBOX Cloud Gaming Free Play Days – NBA 2K27, Crusader Kings III, The Alters, Bus Simulator 21, Soccer Story and Ravenswatch Coming to XBOX Game Pass: Battlefield 6, Valor Mortis, Forever Ago, and More Learn how XBOX is helping creators across Latin America bring new ideas to life through the ID@XBOX Developer Acceleration Program, the inaugural XBOX Game Camp Mexico City, and six upcoming titles from the region. Across Latin America, developers are creating some of gaming’s most distinctive new worlds by turning personal memories, local history, cultural traditions, and bold ideas into experiences that resonate far beyond the region. Games such as Despelote , Mexico, 1921: A Deep Slumber , and SOPA – Tale of the Stolen Potato show the remarkable breadth of this creative community, from intimate coming-of-age stories and interactive journeys through history to magical adventures filled with heart. For years, XBOX has worked alongside creators across Latin America, helping studios of all sizes bring their games to players around the world. Through the ID@XBOX Developer Acceleration Program (DAP), we’ve worked with more than 60 studios from Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Honduras, Uruguay, and beyond, helping developers bring over 30 culturally distinctive games to XBOX since 2023, while strengthening the region’s growing game development ecosystem by providing access to technical resources, business support, and mentorship. XBOX Game Camp Heads to Mexico City As XBOX continues to support game creators across Latin America, XBOX Game Camp is expanding its reach with a Mexico City debut on October 17 alongside Xbox FanFest. Taking place during Xbox’s 25th anniversary year, the event will celebrate Mexico’s game development community and the extraordinary talent already shaping games across the region, while creating new opportunities for developers to learn, connect, and grow. XBOX Game Camp Mexico will bring together a select group of Mexican studios, including developers both within and beyond the existing XBOX ecosystem, for a day focused on industry knowledge, community, and connection. The program will feature advanced developer seminars, keynotes and fireside conversations with industry leaders, along with opportunities to connect directly with industry professionals and members of Team XBOX, including Jens Bergensten, Chief Creative Officer at Mojang Studios. His fireside conversation with Peter Zetterberg, Founder of XBOX Game Camp, will explore his career journey and lessons from Sweden’s game development ecosystem, with a focus on collaboration, supporting fellow creators, and the role community can play in building a stronger industry. With a passionate development community and a strong culture of collaboration, Mexico City provides an ideal setting for XBOX Game Camp to celebrate locally developed games, strengthen connections across the ecosystem, and create new pathways for Mexican creators to bring their ideas to audiences around the world. As we support the next generation of creators through initiatives like XBOX Game Camp, we’re also celebrating the developers shaping Latin America’s game development community today. Here’s a look at six upcoming games from Latin American creators to keep on your radar. Six Upcoming Games from Latin America to Watch Mariachi Legends — Halberd Studios, Mexico Studio Contact: Miguel Hasson, Creative Director Studio location: Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico Mariachi Legends is a brutal, combat-oriented Metroidvania wrapped in gorgeous pixel art and set in the heart of Mexico. Players step into the shoes of Pablo Cruz, a Mexican detective who strikes a deal with Death herself. Granted the ability to transform into the supernatural entity “La Sombra,” Pablo must battle an evil syndicate known as the Mariachi Legends. It’s a journey that blends intense hack-and-slash action with RPG mechanics, all unfolding around the Day of the Dead festivities. What truly separates Mariachi Legends is our deep, authentic integration of Mexican culture and folklore directly into the gameplay loop. Beyond standard combat and exploration we’ve also introduced a unique culinary mechanic: players explore the world to collect ingredients and cook traditional Mexican dishes to gain strength. Coupled with a Day/Night cycle driven by Sun and Moon gates, where different map sections are accessible depending on the time of day, the game offers a distinct flavor you won’t find in other Metroidvanias. How has DAP supported development of your title? ID@XBOX has been instrumental in helping us bring our vision to life without compromising on quality or cultural authenticity. The program provided us with the resources and technical support needed to ensure Mariachi Legends runs flawlessly on XBOX Series X|S, utilize features like XBOX Play Anywhere. The marketing amplification and the opportunity to bring the game to a massive audience via XBOX Game Pass has given our studio the runway to focus fully on creating a polished experience. What do you hope players take away from your game? We hope players walk away with a profound appreciation for the richness of Mexican traditions. We want them to experience the thrill of a tight, challenging Metroidvania, but more importantly, we want the world, the food, the music, and the folklore of Mexico to resonate with them long after they put the controller down. Studio Location: Villa Alemana, Valparaíso, Chile In Colorbound , color is more than just a hue. Join Anku on a heartwarming journey, using color to shape the world around you. In this puzzle-platforming adventure, you will solve challenging puzzles, uncover secrets, and help a family of musicians reunite, just like in the old days, for a farewell concert. Colorbound stands out primarily for its aesthetics and core mechanics. The ability to change the colors of the environment creates an experience that draws attention through its very concept. Furthermore, the narrative, music, and art reflect the Andean culture of Latin America, successfully connecting with the region and showcasing a culture unknown to many. Primarily by providing some of the funding for the project’s production and post-production, which allowed for a faster development process and more comprehensive publishing work. On one hand, I hope that during the process you are surprised by the different mechanics associated with the colors and enjoy solving the game’s challenging puzzles. But above all, I hope you take away a fond memory of a simple, touching experience about friendship and grief. Studio Contact: Valnei Costa, Co-founder, Orbit Studio Sky Dust is a single-player cyberpunk action-adventure with RPG elements, set in a dystopian future after the destruction of the Moon.

events.title: Trump: White House didn't impede satellite system in Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump said Friday that his administration did not disrupt an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine to wage war against Russia. Why it matters: The restrictions imposed earlier this week on the system hampered the Ukrainian military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones for 24 hours. It raised concerns that the Trump administration and possibly Musk were retaliating against Ukraine for its attacks on Russian oil refineries and President Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of Trump's diesel deal with Russia. What he is saying: "I just checked this morning — it wasn't us," Trump told reporters. "I don't know if it was anybody, because it wasn't me and I don't think it was Elon." He was responding to a question about a Reuters report that the order to slow the satellite system came from the White House. The other side: Ukrainian officials remain highly skeptical of Trump's claims and believe someone in the U.S. government participated in throttling the systems. "Our guys who speak to SpaceX say the White House was involved in the decision," a Ukrainian official said. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. In a post on X on Wednesday, Musk hinted the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. The big picture: The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president.
