events.title: JP Morgan deepens critical minerals push
events.summary: JP Morgan has appointed an executive to lead the company's critical mineral efforts under its $1.5 trillion drive to invest in industries deemed significant to US national economic security. Andrew Frame will oversee the Security and Resilience Initiative's critical minerals strategy across extraction, refining and processing, a company representative confirmed to The National . Mr Frame's mandate will centre on addressing bottlenecks across the value chain for an industry considered essential to advanced manufacturing, energy and defence, they said. Mr Frame's appointment was first reported by Mining.com. JP Morgan launched its 10-year, $1.5 trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative last year. The drive spans four sectors – supply chain and advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, energy independence and resilience, and frontier and strategic technology. The bank said those are then divided into 27 subsections ranging from fishing to critical defence components. Critical minerals fall under the supply chain and advanced manufacturing category, while battery storage and grid resilience fall under defence and aerospace. Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and quantum computing make up the initiative's frontier strategies sector. The $1.5 trillion builds on the previously announced $1 trillion the company planned to finance over the next decade. The commitment includes a separate $10 billion allocation for direct equity investments. “It has become painfully clear that the United States has allowed itself to become too reliant on unreliable sources of critical minerals, products and manufacturing – all of which are essential for our national security,” JP Morgan chief executive Jamie Dimon said. Mr Dimon told analysts during the company's third-quarter earnings call this week that the company “probably” deployed more than $200 billion in the first year. Mr Frame's appointment makes him an integral part of the US critical minerals push amid a string of private and federal capital injection into the sector to strengthen the country's supply chain . Since 2025, the US government has announced $10.8 billion in investments , including $5.1 billion in total private capital, in 14 critical minerals companies, using a range of tools from equity stakes to grants, loans and offtake agreements, according to the Council of Foreign Relations. In September, Houston-based start-up Hertha Metals said it had closed a $133.65 million Series A round that includes a $65 million equity investment from the Pentagon. The company is planning on producing high-purity iron for rare-earth magnets needed for F-35 fighter jets and missile-guidance systems. The US government also holds equity stakes in companies across the critical minerals supply chain including MP Materials, USA Rare Earth, and Canada-based Lithium Americas. Also in September, Glencore and Mercuria became the first two companies to participate in VaultCo, a public-private partnership designed to implement the administration's Project Vault initiative. Glencore said its $500 million commitment from Export-Import Bank will allow it to create a critical minerals reserve in the US. Mercuria also announced a $500 million commitment, bringing the total pledge from the companies to $1 billion. “Mineral security is national security. VaultCo is working to ensure the US industrial base has access to the critical minerals needed to build the products everyday Americans rely on and lead the world when they need it most,” ValtCo executive chair Brett Lambert said.

events.title: China targets AI technology exports with new controls as US trade truce frays
events.summary: China has proposed new export controls on 40 strategic technology systems, including 23 linked to artificial intelligence, in a move that could test its fragile trade truce with the US and deepen the rivalry between the world's two largest economies . The draft rules, unveiled on Friday, would give Beijing greater oversight of technology transfers spanning AI chips, large language models, solar energy and biotechnology. China said the move was aimed at curbing the misuse of the technology. Most can still be exported without heavy restrictions and licensing would be simplified. Beijing will seek public opinion on the proposal until November 15, after which it will announce a final version of the controls. “The announcement is extremely expansive and it will take time to fully assess its implications,” said Leonhard Xu, a senior consultant at Sinolytics, a Berlin-based consultancy. “AI seems to be the big centrepiece … but the registration requirement starts immediately, even for exports that have already started shipping. Also, always important to note that export control does not equal an export ban in most cases,” he said. China and the US have been locked in a largely bitter trade war, as Washington seeks to control Beijing's global influence. Technology, and AI in particular, has become a major driver of the rivalry. AI has become key for Chinese exports, which jumped more than 36 per cent year-on-year in September, markedly better than a previously anticipated 25.5 per cent, underscored by AI products, according to IndexBox data. Industry observers believe the move will have notable implications on China's economic engine and its trade strategy against the US, with which it is competing for leadership in the AI race. Last month, Washington and Beijing ​agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods and start dialogue on AI, after Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House. Erin Browne, the US Treasury's undersecretary for international ‌affairs, told Reuters that Washington was pushing for its partners in the International Monetary Fund to rename AI “super intelligence”, a term championed by the Trump administration. China's move indicates that the “fragility of our trade truce cannot be overstated”, said Wendy Cutler, a senior vice president at the New York-based non-profit Asia Institute, who also warned that it is “only be a matter of time” until the US responds with its own restrictive measures. “Despite the agreement on constructive strategic stability, China has announced it is working on a new export restriction tool on solar, AI and other products, allowing Beijing to have better control over export levels, destinations, etc,” she said. “This once again shows that despite the two-month extension of our trade truce, Beijing is going full steam ahead in efforts to control exports of strategic goods to the US and others.” Ting Peng, a partner at BZW Law Firm in Shenzhen who specialises in trade compliance, said the registration requirements extend beyond conventional technology transfers, as they cover certain cross-border IP transfers and licensing arrangements, as well as changes in ownership or actual control of domestic technology, to overseas entities. These implications may extend to cross-border investment and corporate transactions, she noted. “Companies involved in cross-border acquisitions, IP restructuring or international licensing arrangements should assess whether their transactions involving the relevant technologies trigger the new registration requirements,” Ms Ting said. “This is particularly relevant to the biopharmaceutical sector, which has seen significant M&A [mergers and acquisitions] activity over the past two years.”

events.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way. Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy. The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.” That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking. “I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.” When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea. “I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.” He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness. “I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Annual Electric Power Industry Report We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country—California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida—are in regions with more abundant solar resources . Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives. The year-over-year change in generation was particularly high in 2022, when total generation grew by 25% compared with the previous year amid record capacity growth . Changes in different programs supporting rooftop solar partly explain this increase in generation. For example, California’s Net Energy Metering (NEM) 2.0 program was available through April 2023. This net metering program offered higher export compensation than the subsequent Net Billing Tariff, or NEM 3.0 . All the capacity built under the NEM 2.0 program was grandfathered in, incentivizing higher capacity installation before the current NEM 3.0 took effect. California accounted for 37% (34,411 GWh) of total U.S. small-scale solar generation in 2025. Between 2024 and 2025, rooftop solar generation in the state grew by 8%, largely due to an increase in capacity. Small-scale solar capacity in California increased from 18 gigawatts in 2024 to 20 gigawatts in 2025. The state with the next largest amount of small-scale solar power generation is Arizona, accounting for over 6% of total U.S. generation, or 5,795 GWh. Year-over-year generation in Arizona grew only 6% in 2025. The largest increase happened between 2022 and 2023 when generation from small-scale solar grew by 22% in the state. Arizona customers can access a 25% state income-tax credit and other incentives for adding rooftop solar to their properties. States such as Florida and Texas have seen rapid growth in small-scale solar generation in the last decade as more capacity has been added. Generation in Texas grew from 391 GWh in 2016 to 5,408 GWh last year. Over the same period, Florida’s generation grew from 205 GWh in 2016 to 5,198 GWh in 2025. These two states provide incentives through property tax exemptions and other programs specific to each state and, in some cases, utility. Programs in states with lower irradiance levels are also supporting growth in rooftop solar generation. New York offers incentives, which have encouraged small-scale solar growth in the state. Other states with similar programs include New Jersey , Massachusetts , and Illinois . Although generation from small-scale solar continues to grow year over year, the rate of growth has declined since 2022. EIA uses its surveys of electric utilities to collect information on the number of customers with small-scale solar systems and the aggregated capacity. Electric utilities do not necessarily know how much electricity is generated by rooftop solar on their distribution systems, so generation must be estimated. To develop estimates of generation, we rely on tools such as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's System Advisor Model and PVWatts . Data on commonly used tilt angles and orientations for small-scale solar systems in California were used as inputs to be representative of tilt angles and orientations in other states. events.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “ superfakes ,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods. Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app. Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link. “Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said. The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass. “The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.” This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified. The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story. The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine. Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops. Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon . events.title: Zuma’s illness raises questions for South Africa opposition
events.summary: The News Concerns over the health of former South African President Jacob Zuma have raised questions about the future of uMkhonto weSizwe (MK), the populist party built around him that has redrawn the country’s political landscape. The 84-year-old was taken to hospital two weeks ago. Since then, MK officials and the Zuma Foundation have circulated conflicting accounts about his condition. The party initially described Zuma as healthy and undergoing routine checks before returning home. That claim was later contradicted by the foundation, which said he remained in hospital and declined to provide regular updates. In a sign of the impact on the party, MK canceled its flagship Siyathatha rally less than three weeks before South Africa’s municipal elections. The uncertainty has become a political issue because of Zuma’s central role in the party he publicly launched nearly three years ago, after switching from the African National Congress (ANC) ahead of a general election. MK emerged from the 2024 poll as one of the biggest forces in South African politics, winning nearly 15% of the vote on promises to scrap the constitution, expropriate land without compensation and nationalize banks, insurers and strategic mines. Its performance accelerated the slide of the ANC, once led by Nelson Mandela, which lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid and was forced to form a coalition government. Still, the MK’s rise has been punctuated by leadership turmoil, internal purges, and recurring disputes over candidate selection. Zuma’s absence from public campaigning has heightened questions about whether the movement can maintain its momentum without him. Natasha Marrian, a political analyst at the Bureau for Economic Research, a South African think tank, said the MK party, launched as a breakaway outfit for Zuma supporters who opposed the ANC leadership of President Cyril Ramaphosa, was a Zuma project from the outset. “He is the party’s central drawcard,” she said. “There’s no clear center holding it together in his absence.” Know More Zuma’s son, Duduzane, serves as the party’s first deputy president and is widely regarded as a potential successor, but analysts question whether he can replicate the appeal of his father, who led South Africa from 2009 to 2018 before being ousted amid corruption allegations and a wider state capture scandal. “Duduzane is a completely unknown political figure,” said André Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africa’s North-West University. “He comes from a business background.” The ANC may benefit from Zuma’s absence, said Musa Xulu, an independent political analyst, adding that if he remains largely absent from the campaign trail, some ANC voters who followed him could drift back. “The ANC is becoming the biggest beneficiary of Zuma’s current disappearance from public politics. The MK party is Jacob Zuma and Jacob Zuma is the MK,” Xulu said. Notable The ANC secured a legal victory ahead of the 4 November 2026 local government elections when the Constitutional Court ruled in its favour, ordering the electoral commission to reinstate 181 disqualified candidates onto the ballot papers.

events.title: African energy's 'Big Bang' moment
events.summary: Alexis’s view The Iran war is shaping up to be the catalyst of a seismic shift in Africa’s energy sector. And, in the case of the continent’s richest man Aliko Dangote, the conflict has proven the old adage that luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity. Dangote’s mega-refinery on the outskirts of Lagos State has revealed the scale of a West African market underserved by locally refined fuel, while upending conventional thinking by showing African refineries can supply markets in Europe and Asia. At the same time, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of nations that are heavily dependent on fuel imports: South Africa and Kenya have hiked prices, which runs the risk of driving inflation. Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubu’s removal of Nigeria’s subsidy three years ago has allowed prices to skyrocket, turning the cost of fuel into a key campaign issue ahead of January’s election. Policymakers have been quick to react to the altered energy dynamics. South Africa announced plans to increase its strategic oil reserves for the first time since the end of apartheid to mitigate supply shocks, Angola wants to implement faster exploration concessions while urging southern African governments to help finance a new refinery , and plans to build refineries in Uganda and Tanzania have gathered pace. Fola Fagbule, who heads the Kenya regional office of multilateral lender Africa Finance Corporation, which helped to finance Dangote’s Lagos refinery, called the impact of the Nigerian billionaire’s project a “Big Bang” moment. He told me various projects are being developed across the continent “as a result of the new realities in the energy market.” The shift has potential pitfalls. Daniel Evans, global head of fuels and refining research at S&P Global Energy, acknowledged the increased appetite for downstream investment across Africa, but warned difficulties remain around projects that require high levels of capital expenditure. But a new generation of refineries has the potential to transform economies, not only protecting countries from future energy shocks but providing the baseload power needed to ramp up manufacturing. As Fagbule put it, the legacy of this paradigm shift could be how it triggered “massive, large-scale industrialization in Africa that nobody expected.” Notable Dangote Refinery is pushing to extend the sale of its shares to Egypt , indicating that Africa’s largest IPO is likely to take a more pan-African shape .

events.summary: AI experts are coming — and the pretenders too. “Anybody who knows anything about AI” is in high demand from investors trying to play the AI trade, said Gemma Postlethwaite, CEO of expert network GLG. And there are plenty of deepfakes and people using AI chatbots willing to play the part. “We have to be able to deliver experts that not only are who they say they are, but know what they say they know,” Postlethwaite tells Semafor. To test for authenticity, GLG is doing additional screening and ID verification — increasingly on camera with questions designed to trip up AI avatars. It’s also parsing transcripts to find “situations where somebody’s expertise is going off-piste,” she said. “Think of it like a digital fingerprint of knowledge.” Verify, then trust. GLG is also connecting frontier AI labs with subject-matter experts to help train models in sensitive subjects, such as child psychiatrists who can craft responses to kids in crisis and nuclear or bioweapon experts to respond to bad actors looking for instruction manuals. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Congo Basin deforestation nears Amazon levels
events.summary: Forest clearing in the Congo Basin nearly matched losses in the Amazon for the first time in a decade of monitoring, even as deforestation slowed worldwide, a new study found. The destruction releases vast stores of carbon, adding to climate change that is already contributing to drought and forest fires across the tropics. Expanding farming, timber, and mining activities are driving the clearances in the basin, which is home to the world’s second-largest tropical rainforest, the Forest Declaration Assessment group said . In DR Congo, where most of the forest is situated, decades of conflict — along with poor oversight — have fueled uncontrolled logging, driving up the rate of tree loss in central Africa this decade. Meanwhile, there has been a steep decline in deforestation in Latin America and the Caribbean, leaving the two regions almost on a par. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: 777 Partners founder’s guilty plea deepens scrutiny of Wall Street’s insurance trade
events.summary: The founder of 777 Partners, the poster child for the underbelly of Wall Street’s insurance push, pleaded guilty to fraud Thursday. A Semafor investigation in 2023 found that 777, which announced itself with a bold bid to buy UK soccer club Everton, had been funneling insurance policyholders’ money into risky bets that it ginned up itself. The collapse of 777, and the spotlight on exactly what it had been doing with policyholders’ life-insurance money, threatened to bring new scrutiny to what has become Wall Street’s favorite trade. It turns out the party pooper, as we wrote a few weeks ago , wasn’t 777 founder Joshua Wander, a hotshot outsider, but rather a consummate insider: Mark Walter, who did as much as anyone to invent the private equity-insurance trade and is now embroiled in a DOJ investigation that has generated scrutiny of the entire industry. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Singapore-listed firm faces Indonesian probe over suspected land clearing by burning amid haze
events.summary: Several Singapore-listed plantation and agribusiness companies have faced scrutiny over fires in Indonesia. Indonesia has opened a preliminary probe into suspected land clearing by burning in a Kencana Agri subsidiary’s North Kalimantan concession, after fires and haze spread across the region. Kencana Agri, Wilmar, GAR, Bumitama Agri and First Resources said fires affected some concession areas, but many started outside their land or in community areas before spreading. Singapore’s National Environment Agency will issue preventive notices to seven Indonesian firms, mostly in timber and pulpwood, as authorities step up action over the haze risk. SINGAPORE – The Indonesian authorities have started a preliminary inquiry into suspected land-clearing fires in a concession area operated by a subsidiary of Singapore-listed palm oil producer Kencana Agri. The company disclosed on Oct 16 that investigators had inspected the affected area in North Kalimantan in September, and that the inquiry was ongoing. Kencana acknowledged that fires had affected approximately 62ha within concession areas operated by its subsidiaries in North and East Kalimantan, although it maintained that the fires had spread from adjacent land rather than originating from its operations. The disclosures came in response to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) over recent forest and peatland fires in Indonesia and the resulting transboundary haze affecting Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Kencana is among several Singapore-listed plantation and agribusiness companies that have faced scrutiny over fires in Indonesia in recent days, with some acknowledging fires within their concessions but disputing that they had started them. The company, which has plantations and mills in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, said the affected area was small compared with its total planted area of around 67,862ha. It said its firefighting teams had worked with the local authorities and communities to contain the fire, using drones and fire observation towers to identify active fire fronts and to direct ground crews. “The incidents are under control, with ongoing monitoring and precautionary response measures being maintained.” Agribusiness giant Wilmar International also acknowledged on Oct 16 that fires had been detected in small areas of some of its Indonesian concessions, but said they had originated outside its concession boundaries or on land farmed by local communities within them. The group said its field verification indicated that the fires had subsequently spread into areas under its management. Wilmar said its firefighting teams, working with the local authorities and communities, had extinguished all such fires quickly. It also said it had not undertaken any new oil palm planting at its company-owned plantations in Indonesia since 2013. Its field activities since then have been limited to replanting existing cultivated areas, which it said was carried out mechanically without the use of fire. Wilmar added that it had maintained a strict no-burning policy since 2006, covering its subsidiaries and third-party suppliers. Suppliers that breached the policy could have their commercial relationships terminated. Meanwhile, Golden Agri-Resources (GAR) said on Oct 16 that the recent forest and land fires had not materially affected its operations. GAR, which operates oil palm plantations across Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua, said it had received inquiries from various stakeholders about the fires and whether its concessions or activities were connected to the incidents. However, it said that, to the best of its knowledge, there had been no allegations, claims or findings that its operations had contributed to the recent fires and haze. The company also said neither it nor its subsidiaries had received any formal notice of investigation, enforcement action or allegation from regulatory or government authorities in connection with the fires. Its Indonesian-listed subsidiary, Sinar Mas Agro Resources and Technology (SMART), had separately responded to queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange on Oct 15. SMART said the fires had not materially affected its operations, 2026 production targets, revenue, profit or asset values. Indofood Agri Resources also disclosed on Oct 16 that its Indonesian-listed subsidiary, Salim Ivomas Pratama (SIMP), had responded to queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange over forest and land fires. SIMP, which operates plantations across Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, said it is monitoring hot spots using satellite data, and any detected hot spots would be addressed promptly to prevent fires. It did not specify whether any hot spots had been detected within its plantation areas. Bumitama Agri, which requested a trading halt on Oct 16, said fires had damaged some areas within or adjoining its Indonesian concessions, particularly community-managed and unplanted land.

events.title: South Africa tightens rules on weight-loss drugs
events.summary: South Africa is planning to tighten the rules around pharmacies making their own compound versions of medicines, including the popular weight-loss and diabetes treatments Ozempic and Mounjaro, Reuters reports . The move is likely to be welcomed by pharmaceutical giants such as Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly as they seek to curb the pharmacy-made products competing with their blockbuster GLP-1 drugs. South African Pharmacy Council CEO Vincent Tlala said his organization was working with the industry regulator to update standards governing the compounding of medicines because they are worried that some pharmacies have become, in effect, “small-scale manufacturers,” producing large quantities of treatments in advance, rather than for specific patients. The discussion on new guidelines, expected to be published around March next year, follows June’s court victory for Novo Nordisk against local compounding pharmacies making unauthorized copies. With the highest adult obesity rate in Africa , at 30%, the drugs are in high demand in South Africa, but the cost of the trademarked version puts them out of reach for most people. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: South Africa’s Black firms face $45B funding gap
events.summary: South African Black-owned businesses face a funding shortfall of $45 billion, a new report shows, citing “explicit investor bias” alongside barriers such as limited collateral and governance concerns. The findings come three decades after the democratic government introduced a raft of measures — known as Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) — aimed at reversing the dispossession suffered by Black people under apartheid and colonialism. Despite the efforts to redress the problem, South Africa remains one of the world’s most unequal societies. The study, published by British International Investment and Sweden’s Swedfund, both state-owned development finance entities, lands as Washington steps up pressure on Pretoria to dismantle BEE. US Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III has put scrapping the policy on a list of demands tied to improving the investment climate. Pretoria has refused, despite disagreements within the coalition government. Instead the policy conversation has moved to creating a $60 billion fund to help scale up small Black-owned businesses. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Nigerian firm launches $200M SME fund
events.summary: Nigerian investment firm Cascador and lender Sterling Bank launched a $200 million fund for small and medium enterprises, in a bid to close a credit access gap that constrains the growth potential of a vital pillar of African commerce. More than 90% of African businesses are categorized as SMEs, accounting for more than half of GDP in most countries and the majority of employment. But a $331 billion SME financing gap means that, despite being the backbone of the continent’s economies, many African entrepreneurs lack capital to invest in production and generate growth revenue. Cascador recently published a paper that found only 22% of sub-Saharan Africa businesses hold a bank loan or line of credit, compared with 36% globally. The firm’s new facility with Sterling Bank will offer loans of up to $1 million per business in an attempt to help the enterprises secure larger and longer-tenor capital. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Dangote extends refinery share sale to Egypt
events.summary: Africa’s largest initial public offering is set to take a more pan-African shape with the Dangote Refinery’s push to extend the sale of its shares to Egypt . The sale will involve the use of depositary receipts, the same instruments that will be used to offer ownership in the continent’s largest refinery to prospective shareholders in Botswana and Kenya . The IPO aims to raise $1.6 billion through the sale that started mid-September in Nigeria. The company has imposed a hard cap of $2.1 billion, but has “received subscriptions amounting to more than three or four times” the target, billionaire owner Aliko Dangote said this week. A two-week extension on the subscription period to Oct. 27 is designed to accommodate efforts to add more African bourses to the process, he said. Dangote set a minimum entry price of 40 cents per share to attract potential retail investors. Policymakers around Africa see in the IPO a sign that capital markets can be deepened by broad-based participation, but the process of creating sale instruments in individual stock exchanges has highlighted a need to simplify regulations to allow more cross-border investment on the continent. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Wee Hur enters Singapore student housing market with 1,398-bed NTU project
events.summary: A hall of residence at Nanyang Technological University. The new development will mainly house postgraduate students. Wee Hur Holdings is entering Singapore’s purpose-built student accommodation market with a 1,398-bed Y-Suites project at NTU. NTU issued a Letter of Award after a competitive process. The award covers design, construction, financing, operation and maintenance. The project may become Singapore’s largest privately developed and operated student housing on an autonomous university campus. Construction is due in Q3 2027, with operations by the start of the 2029-30 academic year. Wee Hur says the project will grow its pipeline and regional Y Suites platform. SINGAPORE – Wee Hur Holdings is entering Singapore’s purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) market with a 1,398-bed Y-Suites development at Nanyang Technological University (NTU). The Singapore-listed property and construction group said on Oct 16 that NTU had issued it a Letter of Award for the project, following a competitive expression-of-interest and request-for-proposal process. The award covers the design, construction, financing, operation and maintenance of the accommodation facility. The parties are working towards finalising an agreement, with the award subject to its terms and conditions. Upon completion, the project is expected to be Singapore’s largest privately developed and operated student accommodation facility within an autonomous university campus, Wee Hur said. The development will mainly house postgraduate students, with a limited number of beds allocated to undergraduates. It will also be Wee Hur’s first Y Suites-branded asset in Singapore. Construction is targeted to begin in the third quarter of 2027, with operations scheduled to start by the beginning of the 2029- 2030 academic year, subject to approvals from NTU and the regulatory authorities. The project will be undertaken through a special-purpose vehicle, with Wee Hur responsible for the development from design and construction through to operations and maintenance. The roughly 6,000 sq m greenfield site is located next to 30 Nanyang Link within NTU’s main campus. The project vehicle will be granted an initial 20-year land lease, with options for two five-year extensions, subject to the definitive agreement. Wee Hur Property chief executive Goh Chengyu said the award will add to the group’s development pipeline and provide greater visibility for its construction activities. He added: “By developing the PBSA from the ground up and operating it over the long term, we can apply our experience across the full real estate life cycle – from design and construction through to operations.” The project also expands Wee Hur’s student accommodation business into a third market, after Australia and Hong Kong, as the group builds out its Y Suites platform across the Asia-Pacific. Goh Wee Ping, Wee Hur Holdings’ chief investment officer and chief executive of Wee Hur Capital, said bringing Y Suites to Singapore was “an important step” in the group’s ambition to build a regional PBSA platform. “Working with NTU allows us to bring our experience to our home market while further scaling a platform that we believe can create long-term value for the group,” he said. events.title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them. He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste. “The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said. He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year. “Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.” Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed. And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent. “You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained. The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on. “We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.” He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.) “There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added. events.title: Saudi's online war response takes a militaristic turn
events.summary: Saudi social media looks different this week. Throughout the first six months of the war, the widespread response to Iranian attacks was posting images of the flag, the crown prince, and a prayer for the country. Now, following Houthi strikes on the kingdom, my social feeds (algo: female, Gen Z, relatively liberal) are full of soldiers saluting the flag, or reading the Quran beside missile racks. Nationalist language has sharpened too: One viral post tells Saudis to defend their homeland and warns against “traitors” who would “cast doubt on their loyalty.” Many are repeating the official mantra that “ there is no fear in the Saudi dictionary .” The framing of the war has also shifted, from a US conflict to the kingdom’s. — Manal Albarakati

events.title: IRH and Zambia's state miner resolve copper financing dispute
events.summary: Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding and Zambia’s state miner ZCCM-IH say they have patched up their financing dispute over Mopani Copper Mines. The statement skirted the charges in ZCCM-IH’s September letter, which accused IRH — part of Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed’s International Holding Company — of failing to provide equity funding and taking on unapproved debt. Instead, the partners pointed to new joint-exploration projects, saying they “remain aligned on the long-term development” of the mine, but left funding questions open. The truce followed a meeting in Abu Dhabi between Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema and IRH’s CEO on the day the letter became public. IRH paid $620 million in 2024 for a 51% stake in Mopani as part of a deal worth more than $1 billion. Neither side can afford a fight: Zambia needs Gulf capital for its bid to more than triple copper output to 3 million tons a year, and IRH aims to lift Mopani’s production from 66,369 tons in 2025 to 300,000 tons by 2029. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Houthi strikes expose Saudi Arabia's vulnerabilities
events.summary: The deadliest week for civilians in the Gulf marks a turning point in the US-Iran war that has engulfed the Middle East from Beirut to Aden, and from Irbil to Salalah . Saudi Arabia stepped up strikes on Yemen’s Houthis after the group hit Riyadh’s airport 20 times this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 . Despite Riyadh’s considerable air defenses and vast military spending, the militants have been able to outsmart the systems using relatively cheap drones and missiles. Iranian attacks on the Gulf have brought the region closer together, and the latest strikes by Tehran’s allies in Yemen have galvanized support for Saudi Arabia. Authorities in the region are reinforcing this message of unity: In today’s Friday prayer sermons in Kuwait, imams were instructed to praise the kingdom’s support during Iraq’s 1990 invasion and condemn the Houthis . Similar expressions of support were also voiced in Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE. While security is by far the most pressing priority, new projections from the IMF have revealed the war’s deepening economic toll. Jihad Azour, the fund’s regional director, told Asharq Bloomberg that the Gulf’s financial reserves, diversified export routes, and government interventions have cushioned the shock . But the IMF now predicts a deeper contraction than previously expected, with GDP trailing pre-war forecasts even after energy production and trade recover. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less
events.summary: Many employees see having the freedom to work from home as a benefit. DigitalVision/Getty Images If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise. Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, 36% of American workers in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. I’m a management scholar who studies how, when and where people work . Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives. The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected. Learning more about colleagues Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be published in an upcoming issue of the management journal Organization Science. Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent researchers of workplace relationships – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong. In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work. For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer. “Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office. Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen. In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked. “Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work. When you’re a remote employee, you may get more quality time with your pets. Moment/Getty Images Growing psychological safety Psychological safety is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively. Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including learning, creativity and speaking up . Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers. People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress. After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives. Supporting work and nonwork activities And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another. When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together. “I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.” The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it. This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.” Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety. My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better. Vanessa M. events.title: The Download: failed social media bans, and extending pets’ lives
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve. —Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.  The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.  Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe . Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered. —Jessica Hamzelou I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension . This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available  exclusively to subscribers . As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours. The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges. See how Form Energy hopes to make renewable power more reliable . —Jonathan W. Rosen Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from electric buses to portable rubber dams . RTX Spark delivers up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory — enabling AI developers, creators and gamers to run frontier AI models locally, render 90GB+ 3D scenes and play AAA games at 1440p at over 100 frames per second, all on a slim, portable device. Day-one support across local AI agents, creative apps and major games helps users put RTX Spark to work immediately — from editing with Adobe Photoshop and Premiere to running Hermes and OpenClaw agents and playing titles including Gears of War: E-Day and NBA 2K27 with NVIDIA DLSS 5. NVIDIA today announced the availability of  NVIDIA RTX Spark ™ laptops, bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI — rolling out from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. Combining decades of NVIDIA innovation into a single superchip, RTX Spark delivers up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance to run large language models and AI agents locally. On a single device, creators, developers and gamers can move seamlessly between their everyday workflows and emerging AI agents on the familiar Windows platform. “RTX Spark brings the power of NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and CUDA together with Microsoft Windows in one PC for creating, gaming and running personal AI agents,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with Microsoft and our PC industry partners, we’re bringing creators, developers and gamers a new generation of Windows PC, built for the work they do today and the personal AI agents they’ll work with next.” “We’re building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed,” said Yusuf Mehdi, executive vice president at Microsoft. “Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark unlock powerful new local compute for creators and developers, expanding what they can create, build and run on Windows.” A New Beginning for Windows PCs RTX Spark brings NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform to a new generation of portable Windows PCs. At its foundation is a single superchip combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That shared memory allows demanding creative projects and local AI models to run simultaneously and efficiently. MediaTek collaborated with NVIDIA on the custom CPU design, contributing to its best-in-class power efficiency, performance and connectivity. All of NVIDIA’s platform innovation comes together in RTX Spark — NVIDIA CUDA ® , DLSS, OptiX™, Reflex, G-SYNC ® , TensorRT™ and hardware-accelerated video — in a device that fits in a messenger bag. Slim, efficient designs and all-day battery life bring these capabilities wherever users create, develop and play. From Tool to Teammate RTX Spark gives users the capabilities to deploy local AI agents that turn the PC from a tool into an everyday teammate that can complete tasks, generate assets and write code. Users can put agents to work immediately. Guided setup and easy installers help users get started with agents, including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy, without requiring a command line. “Personal AI becomes more useful when it can work with your tools and help get things done,” said Dillon Rolnick, CEO at Nous Research, creators of Hermes Agent. “We brought Hermes to RTX Spark so people can put open AI models and agents to work locally on a Windows laptop, with greater control over their data and the freedom to shape AI around their own workflows.” NVIDIA’s models and tools build on that ecosystem. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74-billion-parameter model optimized for tool calling and multistep tasks, brings more capable local AI to supported RTX Spark configurations. The NVIDIA OpenShell ™ secure runtime and Microsoft Execution Containers help users control agent permissions, while NVIDIA agent skills let compatible agents work with tools including NVIDIA Broadcast , RTX Remix and Omniverse ™ libraries. For example, compatible agents can adjust Broadcast effects during a stream or batch-process recorded clips, all on a local PC. That experience extends across devices with NVIDIA PAIR , letting RTX Spark serve AI inference to compatible Windows, Linux and macOS computers on a home network while keeping other PCs free for creating and gaming. Create, Innovate, Play RTX Spark helps creators move from an idea to finished content wherever they work, with the ability to edit 8K 4:2:2 video and render large 3D scenes up to 90GB, even when unplugged. With the arrival of RTX Spark, Adobe is enhancing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, with NVIDIA TensorRT acceleration in AI-editing features. In Premiere, creators can work faster across some of the most intensive parts of post-production, from playback and rendering to effects, color grading and more. Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases available at launch, with Substance coming soon. “Creatives are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible across image, video, audio and 3D, and they need tools that can keep up with their ambitions,” said Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for creative professionals at Adobe. “By combining NVIDIA’s advanced computing technology with Adobe’s industry-leading creative applications, we’re delivering enhanced experiences that empower creatives to bring their ideas to life with greater power and speed.” For enhancing recorded content, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 lets creators remove background noise from existing recordings and shape their voice with Studio Voice Mic Profiles. Beta RTX Video features enable up to 4K super resolution and 4x frame generation. In ComfyUI, new RTX Video nodes can turn 15 frames-per-second (fps) AI-generated video into smoother 60 fps footage and convert it to high dynamic range without requiring per-use cloud inference charges. Code, Test and Deploy With One Machine As AI shifts software development from writing code to directing agents, work often spans a laptop, a cloud AI model and a cloud virtual machine for testing. events.title: Lowball retention bonuses doomed Perella-Piper Sandler merger
events.summary: The Scoop A merger between two Wall Street boutique firm collapsed after senior bankers balked at their retention bonuses. The deal between advisory firm Perella Weinberg Partners and investment bank Piper Sandler envisioned paying Perella’s highest producers $2.5 million in shares of the combined company to stay on for as long as three years, according to people familiar with the matter. The rest of its partners were split into tiers and offered bonuses of between $500,000 and $1.5 million. Perella CEO Andrew Bednar called some partners individually to describe their retention packages and gauge their reaction, the people said. They were almost uniformly negative, with the offers deemed “offensively low,” in the words of one banker, compared to the millions that top dealmakers at the firm make per year. That opposition led to the talks ultimately falling apart, some of the people said. The Financial Times earlier reported that the deal had collapsed . A spokesperson for Perella did not respond to requests for comment. Perella Weinberg went public in 2020 and had seen its shares lose half their value since early last year. Bednar had sought a deal with at least one other bank earlier this year, although talks only progressed with Piper, some of the people said. Rohan’s view Expect to see a wave of departures from Perella in the coming weeks and months. Recruiters at rival banks are already fielding calls and making their own, I’m told. Bankers don’t want to work at troubled businesses, and seeking a deal signaled just that. Perella, the junior partner in these talks, had been seeking some kind of deal for months before alighting on Piper. Bankers, especially rainmakers, have healthy egos. It’s difficult enough to lock them up, but it’s a critical step in talent-driven mergers like this. Failing to do so highlights exactly the risk that companies take when they try to strike deals.

events.title: China plans AI export curbs to exert control over key tech
events.summary: Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds. China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to tighten control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector. The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds. Chinese AI startups have in summer 2026 made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s latest editions offer better pricing and Chinese companies also favour the approach of sharing the weights – used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer – of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them. They are also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI making their wares available on US cloud service providers like Amazon Web Services. The proposal forms part of a broader effort to control 40 technologies across industries where Chinese companies have become increasingly competitive. It would also cover five biomedical technologies and 12 solar technologies, including proprietary cell and gene-therapy platforms and production technology for certain advanced solar modules. “This is more than routine maintenance,” said Ryan Etzcorn, a senior director at Ankura China Advisors. “By targeting AI, solar and biotech – industries where China holds a growing edge – Beijing is signalling that steadier relations with the West do not mean it will stand still.” China regularly updates its catalogue of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first Trump administration threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company. The proposed AI export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of the technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defense industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities. “The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement. The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models trained on “important data” and containing at least 2 trillion parameters – like Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8-Max – or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety. China’s cyberspace regulator broadly defines such data as information that, if leaked, may endanger national security, economic operation, social stability or public safety. The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licencing regime and potential US sanctions. The proposed restrictions against shipping mega-parameter models abroad are likely to hamper development given AI labs are training ever larger platforms: in September , Alibaba declared plans to develop models with between 5 and 10 trillion parameters, far larger than what’s common today, for longer and more complex tasks. Open-source technology and research already in the public domain would not be covered, and the government will provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies. Deploying a covered model overseas would constitute a technology export, according to a statement. Deployments on overseas infrastructure owned by the Chinese provider could qualify for automatic licencing. Companies that allow overseas customers to use restricted AI models through apps, websites or online services would not be subject to the proposed controls, the Commerce Ministry said. Beijing said the measures were not aimed at any particular country, region or entity. The ministry also proposed to restrict the export of design technologies for AI chips built using 14-nanometer or more advanced techniques or employing 2.5D or 3D advanced packaging. The proposed restrictions also cover design technologies for certain advanced memory chips. China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. The measure took effect on Oct 16 and applies to transactions already underway but not completed, including intellectual-property transfers, overseas licencing and changes that place Chinese technology owners under foreign control. Time: 3pm – 4pm | Location: Bank of England, Threadneedle Street, London, EC2R 8AH and MS teams The Chair opened the meeting by welcoming Members and outlined the purpose of the meeting. Namely, to consider the results of the 2026 banknote imagery consultation in light of the Bank’s objectives to support counterfeit resilience, and to consider which four animals to recommend to the Governor to feature as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. The Chair reminded Members of the Bank’s obligations under the Public Sector Equality Duty throughout the imagery selection process. Decision: Members agreed to sign off the updated Terms of Reference adding the Banknote Innovation Programme Director as a new Core Member. Members were reminded of the key milestones in the imagery selection process, including the recent consultation asking for the UK public’s views on a shortlist of animals which could feature as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. Respondents were able to choose up to two animals from each of three different categories: Mammals; Birds; and Amphibians, Insects and Fish. Members discussed the response to the public consultation, which received nearly 500,000 responses via an online survey, post, emails and phone calls. Members were pleased with the level of public engagement and suggested it showed that the theme resonated with the public. Item 4 – Choosing which animals should feature on Series H banknotes Members were asked to consider the Bank’s objectives that the chosen imagery supports counterfeit resilience, reflects public preference and celebrates the breadth of UK nature. Members were encouraged to consider the four proposed animals as a set to ensure they are sufficiently varied in their forms, movements and habitats to maximise differentiation between each denomination, thereby aiding counterfeit resilience. Members considered the results of the June 2026 public consultation and agreed on the importance of reflecting the public’s views on banknote design alongside the Bank’s wider objectives to ensure secure and resilient banknote design. Members discussed the proposal to feature the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee, and European hedgehog as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. The Atlantic puffin would bring a marine environment that would not be possible with the fox or kingfisher, which had received more selections in their respective categories. This set would include the most popular animal from each of the three categories as well as the most popular marine animal in the shortlist. Members considered how each of the proposed animals’ forms and habitats could be differentiated to help the public easily identify each denomination, as well as how the proposed animals’ movements could be incorporated into security features to support authentication. It may also be possible to include some of the other animals from the shortlist as secondary imagery in the final designs. This would be subject to further engagement with the members of the Banknote Imagery Expert Panel about the animals’ habitats and note design decisions later in the process. Members concluded that the proposed set of animals met the Bank’s objectives for counterfeit resilience and took into account the outcome of the public consultation.

events.title: SNEF names Poon Hong Yuen as next CEO
events.summary: SNEF chief executive Hao Shuo (left) will be replaced by Poon Hong Yuen, who takes over as chief executive on Dec 1. PHOTOS: SINGAPORE NATIONAL EMPLOYERS FEDERATION SNEF has named Poon Hong Yuen as its next chief executive. He starts as chief executive-designate on Nov 1 and takes over on Dec 1. Poon is now deputy secretary at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information. He also held senior roles at MOM and Spring Singapore, giving him strong policy and digital economy experience. Outgoing chief executive Hao Shuo will leave for a new public service role. Under him, SNEF grew to over 4,000 corporate members and ran transformation programmes for more than 3,200 employees. SINGAPORE - The Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) has named Poon Hong Yuen as its next chief executive, replacing Hao Shuo after a two-year tenure. Poon will join as chief executive-designate on Nov 1 and take over formally on Dec 1, SNEF said on Oct 16. He is currently deputy secretary at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information. He previously served as deputy secretary (workforce) at the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and chief executive of the former Spring Singapore. SNEF president Kuah Boon Wee said Poon’s experience would position him well to lead the federation through technological and economic change. “His leadership experience and contributions to workforce policy, enterprise development and the digital economy will be invaluable as SNEF champions employers’ interests, strengthens tripartism and helps businesses harness emerging technologies for workforce transformation and sustainable growth,” he said. Hao, who joined SNEF as chief executive in December 2024, will leave to take up a new appointment in the public service. SNEF did not disclose his next role. Before joining SNEF, he was divisional director for manpower planning and policy at MOM, where he oversaw workforce planning, labour market policies, foreign workforce policies and HR sector development. Under him, SNEF strengthened its policy, research and communications capabilities, while membership grew to more than 4,000 corporate members employing about 900,000 workers. More than 700 employers have taken part in workplace and workforce transformation programmes administered by SNEF in the last two years, benefiting over 3,200 employees. Kuah said Hao also worked with MOM and the National Trades Union Congress on policy reviews, including the Employment Act review and tripartite work on senior employment. events.title: Coffee’s coming glut may not be enough to calm volatile prices
events.summary: The 2026-27 season is widely expected to produce the biggest surplus in years, helped by a potential record crop in the world’s top grower. Coffee supplies are rising after years of shortages, but exchange-certified stocks are still at their lowest since 1999, keeping arabica prices near US$3.50 a pound. A 2026-27 surplus, led by Brazil, could boost private inventories, but traders doubt enough beans will reach exchange warehouses to stabilise futures. Low exchange stocks may keep prices volatile and risk a short squeeze, which could raise costs for roasters and consumers, including latte prices. After years of shortages, the world is finally getting more coffee. The question is how much of it will reach the exchange warehouses that underpin prices across the industry. The market for arabica coffee has been unusually volatile in 2026, due in large part to a deeply depleted repository of beans available to settle expiring futures. Exchange-certified stockpiles have fallen to their lowest point since 1999, helping push prices close to their highest levels this year, near US$3.50 (S$4.50) a pound (454g). Those stockpiles need to rebuild for prices to become more stable. Otherwise, coffee roasters – and ultimately consumers – could remain exposed to sharp price swings even as global supplies improve. There should be plenty of beans to go around: The 2026-27 season is widely expected to produce the biggest surplus in years, helped by a potential record crop in top grower Brazil. But traders and analysts are unsure whether current futures prices offer enough incentive to send those beans into exchange-managed warehouses rather than private stocks. Exchange deliveries were a “slam dunk” when the premium for delivering coffee sooner rather than later was higher, said Judy Ganes, president of J. Ganes Consulting and a veteran commodity analyst. “The math changed, and all of a sudden it didn’t make sense to deliver as much of that.” That distinction matters because exchange warehouses act as a backstop for the coffee industry. They absorb beans when other buyers show little interest and provide a readily available reservoir when supplies become scarce. Roasters have drawn heavily on that reservoir and are now actively buying beans in the physical market at higher prices, intercepting supplies that might otherwise reach the exchange. Growing private inventories would still be good news for roasters and consumers after years of shortages and record prices. But without a significant recovery in exchange stocks, futures could remain volatile. Prices may have to rise to encourage more deliveries, potentially forcing traders with short positions to buy back futures and amplifying the rally. “There’s the possibility that someone gets squeezed,” Ganes said. That can ultimately feed through to the price of a latte. Futures serve as a basis for the prices that many roasters pay for beans, with their final cost typically based on the futures price plus a premium or discount for quality. Consumers are still feeling the pinch of a historic run-up in coffee costs two years ago, and Folgers maker JM Smucker has cited elevated futures as a reason for delaying plans to cut prices. Oliver Broster, senior manager of coffee analysis at Expana, said the looming surplus creates the risk of a steep decline in prices, meaning the exchange should already be an attractive destination for some beans. Some beans are starting to arrive. More coffee from Brazil entered certified stocks in September than in each of the prior 18 months. But the sudden influx of tens of thousands of bags sent futures plunging, and arrivals have since slowed. The fact that around 72% of Brazilian coffee bag arrivals passed an exchange quality test that month – an unexpectedly high rate in line with past years – also pressured prices, since heavy rains had raised fears about potentially widespread damage to the crop. “It’s a huge crop. So in comparison with last year, there’s still a large quantity of excellent-quality Brazil,” Broster said. Still, Brazilian growers have little reason to rush. Flush with cash from record coffee prices in previous harvests, producers have been able to hold beans for longer than usual while waiting for higher offers. Brazilian coffee likely to meet the Intercontinental Exchange’s quality standards is also good enough to be “really getting a premium in some markets” beyond what the exchange can pay, said Marcelo Moreira, a Brazil-based analyst with Archer Consulting. A surge in Brazil’s currency in October on election results may further discourage farmers from selling unless the dollars they receive for exports also rise. Beans from sought-after origins like Colombia are likewise commanding higher premiums, making near-term deliveries to the exchange a less profitable option, according to StoneX senior trader Tomas Araujo.
