events.title: Beyond The Specification: What Really Determines PCIe Retimer Reach?
events.summary: As AI servers, storage platforms, networking equipment, and high-performance computing systems continue to scale, PCIe links are being pushed farther than ever before. System architects frequently ask a seemingly simple question: how far can a PCIe retimer extend a connection ? Unfortunately, there is no single answer. The effective reach of a PCIe retimer is influenced by multiple interacting factors that span silicon design, controller intelligence, channel quality, and the transmission medium itself. In trying to answer the question, many engineers may initially focus on the PCIe specification and associated channel loss budgets. While specification compliance is essential, real-world reach is often determined by how well a retimer performs beyond the minimum requirements. The difference between a retimer that merely passes compliance testing and one that consistently delivers reliable operation in production deployments can be substantial. Maximizing PCIe reach requires a system-level approach that considers every aspect of the signal path. At the foundation of retimer reach lies the quality of the SerDes architecture. The SerDes serves as the electrical engine that receives, conditions, and retransmits high-speed signals. PCI-SIG specifications define channel-loss requirements that compliant devices must support. For example, designs are commonly expected to accommodate around 36 dB of insertion loss at Nyquist frequency. However, leading retimer vendors frequently engineer their products to tolerate 40 dB or even higher levels of channel loss. Those additional decibels may sound insignificant, but they often translate directly into greater deployment flexibility. Additional margin allows designers to support longer PCB traces, extra connectors, more backplane transitions, and greater manufacturing variation. In large systems where every connector, cable, and via adds loss and reflection, the difference between supporting 36 and 40 dB can determine whether a design succeeds without modification or requires a costly board redesign. The ability to achieve this additional margin depends on sophisticated signal-processing techniques embedded within the SerDes. Advanced equalization circuitry, highly optimized clock recovery algorithms, robust jitter tolerance, and adaptive receiver technologies all contribute to extending channel reach. As the industry moves through PCIe Gen6 and prepares for future generations, these capabilities become increasingly important because every speed increase reduces the available system margin. While the analog performance of the SerDes establishes the foundation, controller intelligence frequently determines how well that foundation performs in real-world environments. Modern PCIe systems operate under conditions that are far more complicated than laboratory compliance tests. Temperature fluctuations, voltage variations, component aging, process variation, and interoperability challenges all affect link stability. One particularly important capability is the handling of corner cases. Specifications cannot anticipate every possible combination of endpoint, root complex, cable, switch, and retimer implementation. Real-world deployments often uncover scenarios that sit at the edge of compliance boundaries. Retimers with sophisticated controller designs are better equipped to manage these situations without causing system instability. As a result, controller quality frequently becomes a major differentiator among retimer solutions that appear similar when viewed purely from a PHY performance perspective. Closely related to controller intelligence is the concept of designing beyond the specification. Compliance testing validates that a device meets defined requirements, but interoperability in production systems often requires more than simple compliance. Different vendors may interpret implementation details differently, resulting in subtle variations during link training, equalization, recovery, or power-state transitions. The most robust retimers are designed with these realities in mind. They include additional logic and protocol awareness to handle unusual behaviors, accommodate implementation differences, and recover gracefully from unexpected situations. This philosophy of engineering beyond the specification can significantly improve compatibility across diverse ecosystems. For hyperscale operators, server manufacturers, and storage vendors, successful interoperability often matters as much as raw signal-integrity performance. Another factor that significantly influences practical reach is observability. As PCIe speeds increase, diagnosing link issues becomes more challenging. The ability to see what is happening within the channel can determine whether a link operates reliably or remains a persistent source of field failures. Modern retimers increasingly include sophisticated diagnostic and monitoring capabilities. Engineers need visibility into link-training behavior, equalization status, signal quality, error statistics, lane margins, and environmental conditions. This information helps identify weak channels, optimize system performance, and accelerate root-cause analysis during deployment. Although diagnostics do not directly improve insertion-loss tolerance, they often increase achievable system reach by allowing engineers to discover and resolve issues that would otherwise remain hidden. In many deployments, better visibility effectively creates additional operational margin by enabling more informed tuning and troubleshooting. No discussion of retimer reach would be complete without considering the quality of the transmission channel itself. Even the most advanced retimer cannot fully compensate for a poorly designed channel. PCB material selection, impedance control, via construction, connector quality, routing practices, and crosstalk management all influence signal integrity. As signaling rates continue to climb, low-loss PCB materials become increasingly attractive because they reduce attenuation and preserve signal quality across longer distances. Likewise, careful connector and via design can dramatically improve channel performance. A high-quality channel allows the retimer to devote its equalization resources to extending reach rather than simply compensating for avoidable losses and reflections. The transmission medium also plays a critical role. Within a chassis, PCB traces dominate the channel budget. Beyond the board, copper cables provide additional flexibility and enable connectivity to external accelerators, storage systems, and expansion modules. High-quality active copper assemblies can often extend PCIe connectivity to approximately two meters while maintaining acceptable performance. However, this capability depends heavily on cable construction, shielding effectiveness, copper quality, and connector design. Looking forward, optical connectivity is poised to redefine expectations for PCIe reach. Emerging P

events.title: Strengthening Advanced-Node Interconnects Through Automated Via Insertion
events.summary: As the semiconductor industry pushes deeper into the sub-5nm realm, the physical design landscape has shifted from being dominated by gate delays to being defined by interconnect performance. In modern system-on-chip (SoC) designs, the wiring that connects billions of transistors has become the primary bottleneck for power, performance, and area (PPA). Among the various components of the interconnect stack, vias – the vertical connections between metal layers – represent one of the most significant points of vulnerability. At advanced process nodes, via resistance increases exponentially as dimensions shrink. This rising resistance, coupled with higher current densities, exacerbates challenges related to electromigration (EM) and IR drop. Traditionally, design teams addressed these issues during the final signoff phase, often resulting in late-stage engineering change orders (ECOs) that could delay a project by weeks. To maintain aggressive time-to-market schedules while ensuring long-term silicon reliability, a new approach is required: shifting signoff-aware interconnect optimization into the implementation phase. The physics of via failure and interconnect resistance To understand the need for automated via optimization, first consider the physical challenges at play. In a typical advanced-node interconnect, the resistance of a single via can be significantly higher than that of a corresponding length of metal wire. As current flows through these narrow vertical structures, the resulting heat and atomic displacement can lead to electromigration – the gradual movement of metal atoms that eventually creates voids or shorts. Plus, the cumulative effect of via resistance across a massive power delivery network (PDN) leads to IR drop. If the voltage reaching a logic gate falls below a certain threshold, the gate’s switching speed slows down, potentially leading to timing failures. In the worst cases, the gate may fail to switch entirely. Historically, designers mitigated these risks by manually adding redundant vias to critical signal paths and power grids. The redundant vias provide parallel paths for current, lowering the effective resistance and reducing the current density through any single via. However, at 5nm and below, the sheer density of the layout and the complexity of foundry design rules make manual insertion practically impossible. Figure 1 illustrates the problem. Fig. 1: The increasing complexity of advanced-node layouts requires automated solutions to identify valid locations for redundant via insertion without violating foundry rules. The limitations of traditional implementation flows Most place-and-route (P&R) tools include basic capabilities for via redundancy. However, these routers are primarily optimized for connectivity and timing closure, not for the exhaustive reliability enhancement required for high-performance silicon. Router-based via insertion typically comes with several limitations: Lack of signoff awareness: Implementation routers typically use simplified versions of foundry design rules to maintain performance. While this is sufficient for initial routing, it often leads to DRC violations when the design is subjected to the full signoff rule deck. Limited search space: Routers often give up on via insertion in congested areas to avoid creating shorts. This leaves critical parts of the design – often the very areas that need the most help – under-optimized. ECO overhead: When a router-based enhancement triggers a signoff violation, the resulting ECO cycle requires re-running parts of the implementation flow, which consumes valuable time and can disrupt timing closure. To overcome these hurdles, many design teams adopt a “shift-left” methodology that uses signoff-quality engines earlier in the design cycle. By integrating the same logic used for final verification into the enhancement process, designers can achieve “correct-by-construction” results that are guaranteed to pass final signoff. Methodology: Automated signoff-aware enhancement The shift-left approach to via optimization involves a specialized enhancement platform that operates on the design database during the implementation phase. This platform reads standard design formats – such as LEF/DEF or OASIS – and applies a multi-step process to strengthen the interconnect. The first step is a comprehensive analysis of the existing layout to identify every potential location where a redundant via could be placed. This is not a simple proximity check; the tool must account for complex multi-patterning constraints, voltage-aware spacing rules, and enclosure requirements. By leveraging a signoff-grade geometry engine, the tool can navigate these constraints with a level of precision that far exceeds traditional routers. Once the valid insertion points are identified, the tool strategically adds redundant vias to the user-selected nets. This can be applied globally to the entire power grid or targeted toward specific high-priority signal nets, such as clock trees or long-distance bus lines. The result is a layout that is significantly more robust, with lower overall resistance and improved EM margins. Fig. 2: By moving signoff-aware optimization into the implementation phase, design teams can resolve interconnect issues before they become late-stage bottlenecks. Navigating layout imperfections with short-resilience One of the most innovative aspects of modern automated enhancement is the ability to handle “dirty” or incomplete layout data. A typical design database is rarely perfectly clean during the implementation flow. Localized shorts, routing overlaps, or incomplete power grid definitions are common as the design matures. Traditional optimization tools often fail when encountering these imperfections, either crashing or producing illegal layout modifications. A robust enhancement platform must be “short-resilient.” This means the tool can identify regions with existing connectivity conflicts and automatically designate them as keep-out areas (Figure 3). Fig. 3: Short-resilient DE-Via flow; avoiding insertion on identified short-prone regions. By protecting these suspicious regions, the tool can continue to optimize the rest of the design. This lets design teams run via enhancement early and often, even before the layout is fully DRC-clean. This iterative approach is essential for maintaining productivity in a fast-paced design environment, as it prevents minor layout issues from stalling the overall reliability enhancement of the chip. events.title: Building AI Infrastructure For Greater Choice And Flexibility
events.summary: AI infrastructure is changing fast. Training and inference are putting different demands on compute, memory, connectivity, and networking, and there is no single architecture that fits every workload. For system architects, this opens up an important question: How much flexibility can be built into the system from the start? The answer increasingly involves giving designers more choices across memory, compute, connectivity, and packaging, while making sure those technologies work together. Different workloads, different requirements AI training and inference may run on much of the same underlying infrastructure, but they don’t behave the same way. Training places heavy demands on memory and communication between accelerators. Inference has a different mix of requirements, including memory capacity, latency, throughput, and efficiency. Those differences matter when choosing an architecture. A memory technology that’s right for one workload may not be right for another. The same applies to interconnects and networking. This is why AI infrastructure is becoming more heterogeneous. Architects are combining different technologies based on what they need the system to do, rather than trying to force every workload into the same design. Fig. 1: Heterogeneous applications demand distinct solutions for optimized implementations. More choice through open standards Open standards give designers more options for how they put those systems together. UCIe is one example. The standard provides a common approach to die-to-die connectivity and is aimed at supporting an open chiplet ecosystem. It gives the industry a standardized way to connect dies within a package rather than tying the architecture to a single implementation. System architects are also working across a wider range of process technologies, packaging approaches, and functions. A chiplet-based approach provides another way to partition those functions, allowing compute, I/O, memory interfaces, and other functions to be integrated within the same package. UCIe provides a standardized die-to-die connection for that environment. This gives designers a common interface as they evaluate how different functions should be partitioned and integrated. For designers, the value is choice. Different functions can be brought together in a package while using a common interface between them. That freedom becomes particularly useful when architects are balancing performance, power, cost, packaging, and process technology. Interoperability matters Open standards provide a common foundation for bringing technologies from different suppliers and foundries into the same system. Interoperability helps designers understand how those different implementations will work together. Verification plays an important role here, particularly as systems incorporate more functions, interfaces, and technologies. The same thinking applies across the AI factory The need for choice doesn’t stop at the package. An AI system can include several kinds of connectivity, each serving a different role. PCIe, CXL, UCIe, UALink, and Ethernet-based technologies address different parts of the architecture. Memory brings another set of decisions. Fig. 2: Different connectivity, different scope, same goal: economical, rapid data transfer. The requirements also change depending on where data is moving. HBM4E and LPDDR6 address different memory needs, while PCIe supports high-speed host and device connectivity. UALink addresses accelerator-to-accelerator communication, 224G high-speed SerDes provides the underlying high-speed signaling needed for demanding connectivity applications, and UCIe connects dies within packages. Designers need to consider what they are connecting, how much data needs to move, and the requirements of the workload. Looking at those decisions together provides a more complete view of the system than treating each interface independently. That perspective changes the design conversation. Rather than optimizing individual pieces independently, architects can look at how memory, compute, and connectivity fit together across the system. Designing with room to evolve AI infrastructure will continue to change as workloads, memory technologies, accelerators, and interconnects advance. Building flexibility into the architecture gives designers more options as those requirements change. Open interfaces and interoperability are an important part of that flexibility, allowing designers to choose technologies based on the needs of the system rather than a single approach. For a deeper look at the memory, compute, and connectivity technologies shaping these systems, read our Building AI Factories with IP Solutions white paper . events.title: AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity
events.summary: In this blog post, we introduce AMBA C2C, a new specification being developed with the AMBA ecosystem. It provides a unified and scalable approach to connecting AMBA protocols across chiplets, including AMBA AXI and AMBA CHI. The evolving C2C landscape Chiplet technology and AI are evolving rapidly, bringing new benefits and protocol requirements. AMBA CHI C2C has established strong momentum as a foundational protocol for chiplets and chip-to-chip (C2C) connectivity. It is particularly suited to fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute and superchips. However, chiplets span a much wider range of use cases. These include memory expansion, IO and accelerator attach, and advanced heterogeneous systems. Each use case comes with different requirements and trade-offs in functionality, performance, bandwidth efficiency, and implementation complexity. AMBA CHI C2C already supports scalability in implementation complexity through a property negotiation mechanism . Implementations can support only the capabilities they need while preserving interoperability across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. Our continued collaboration with the ecosystem has highlighted an important additional requirement. Many chiplets do not need the full feature set of advanced coherent systems and require an even simpler approach for C2C connectivity. This is particularly important for the vast installed base of AXI-based designs. These designs can benefit from the greater reuse and composability that chiplets enable. This has been an important focus area since we first introduced AMBA CHI C2C in 2023 . At that time, we discussed how C2C connectivity could extend to simpler, often AXI-based use cases. Partner feedback since then has reinforced the need for a unified and converged C2C approach for AMBA protocols. This approach includes both CHI and AXI, rather than separate, protocol-specific point solutions. Introducing AMBA C2C To address these evolving requirements, we are developing AMBA C2C. AMBA C2C builds on the success of AMBA CHI C2C. It provides a converged and scalable C2C foundation across AMBA protocols, including AXI and CHI. At the heart of AMBA C2C is protocol subsetting. Defined subsets enable the protocol feature set and complexity to scale across different use cases. For example, device or accelerator attach subsets can support the simpler requirements aligned with AXI-based IO and non-coherent traffic. More advanced subsets can support the richer functionality required by coherent and heterogeneous systems. AMBA C2C uses defined protocol subsets to scale functionality and implementation complexity across different use cases. These subsets can align with on-chip protocols such as AXI and CHI. AMBA C2C then defines how these protocols are packetized for chip-to-chip transport. The packetization is optimized for each subset while providing a common approach across AXI- and CHI-class traffic. Interoperability remains fundamental to the architecture. AMBA C2C builds on the property negotiation mechanism introduced with AMBA CHI C2C. This mechanism enables implementations with different capabilities to interoperate across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. This includes backwards and forwards compatibility. A layered architecture for an evolving industry An open chiplet ecosystem requires open standards and a clear, layered standardization approach. This includes a clear separation between the protocol and the underlying transport. This is a proven industry model that UCIe and the broader ecosystem have adopted. AMBA CHI C2C, for example, uses UCIe Streaming as discussed in the UCIe 1.1 specification announcement . Similarly, PCIe and CXL protocols can be transported over UCIe. More recently, UALink has adopted a similar layered architecture. It defines a packetization strategy alongside its protocol functionality while separating it from the underlying data-link and physical layers. AMBA C2C follows this same principle. AMBA defines the protocol and packetization mechanism, while transports such as UCIe provide the underlying die-to-die connectivity. This enables AMBA C2C to work with a variety of die-to-die and chip-to-chip transports. More importantly, it provides a clean architectural boundary that enables AMBA protocols and underlying transport technologies to continue evolving at pace. Fig. 1: Transporting AMBA protocols over UCIe with AMBA C2C. For AMBA AXI, this separation is particularly important. AXI is widely adopted across the industry and continues to evolve. However, unlike packet-based protocols, AXI defines interface behavior rather than a native packet format. AXI is also highly configurable, and capabilities vary between implementations. Transporting AXI over a C2C link therefore requires an architectural definition. This definition specifies which AXI semantics are carried and how they are packetized. That definition must evolve alongside AXI itself. Putting it all together AMBA C2C is the next evolution of AMBA’s C2C work. It builds on AMBA CHI C2C and extends the approach to a broader range of AMBA-based chiplet systems. AMBA C2C provides a common foundation that can scale from simple AXI-based designs to advanced, CHI-based fully coherent heterogeneous systems. Interoperability is built into the architecture. AMBA C2C follows the development and licensing model that has supported the AMBA ecosystem for decades. We are developing it in collaboration with industry partners. The specification will be freely available, royalty-free, and architecture-neutral. Over decades, this model has helped establish AMBA as a dependable and trusted industry foundation. It has supported widespread adoption, a thriving ecosystem, and a broad marketplace of compatible solutions. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the industry to enable an open, interoperable chiplet ecosystem, with AMBA C2C evolving alongside complementary industry standards. The post AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Why Open-Weight AI Matters
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Local inference and model routing can help manage cost and protect sensitive data, but chip architects must account for memory capacity, sustained performance, changing models, and deployment security. For EDA, model quality depends on clean, trusted design data and integration into workflows, not just on choosing a larger model or fine-tuning its weights. Open weights can reduce dependence on proprietary AI services, but they do not automatically provide open training data, source code, or unrestricted usage rights. Open-weight AI models are creating new challenges for chip architects as rapidly changing workloads strain memory, interconnects, and compute flexibility. The focus is no longer just peak TOPS. The checklist has grown to include the best way to feed memory-hungry models, sustain performance across long-context and multi-agent inference, support rapidly changing numeric formats and sparse computation, and isolate models, data, and tools as part of the security boundary. Model architectures can change in weeks while silicon takes years, so the winners will build adaptable hardware-software platforms, rather than accelerators optimized for a benchmark that may be obsolete before tape-out. Massive data centers are not a prerequisite for AI-driven scientific advances. Science has different infrastructure needs from consumer AI platforms serving millions of users. Open-weight AI models — whose trained parameters are publicly available — can be deployed locally, potentially widening access, improving compute efficiency, and supporting independent research. Open weights also raise questions about control, cost, and who can build on AI technology. Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder at Expedera , said publishing weights can reduce vendor lock-in as it allows users to host a model themselves or choose a service provider. “If you want to use a service, or host it yourself, there is no vendor lock-in in terms of who is providing the next token for you or who is servicing your next request. But there are geopolitical and investment sides to it. There is also a push for open hardware, like what Meta and others do to enable different competing solution providers. As of September 2026, the larger open-weight models come primarily from outside the U.S., either Europe or Asia, and we are moving toward trillion-parameter models.” Open-weight models make trained parameters downloadable, letting users run and adapt them on their own hardware rather than relying on a provider’s API, according to Guillaume Boillet, vice president of strategic marketing at Arteris . “They are not necessarily open source: training data, code and usage rights may remain restricted.” While open-weight AI model releases publish trained parameters, open-source releases aim to publish the full recipe, and closed models publish neither, said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise . Representative open-weight releases include Meta Llama, Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Google Gemma, Microsoft Phi, and OpenAI’s gpt-oss family. OpenAI reports that gpt-oss-120b runs on a single 80 GB GPU and gpt-oss-20b can run on devices with 16 GB of memory; both use MXFP4 quantization, Darbari noted. “These specifications illustrate the widening range of deployment options, but memory fit alone does not establish useful performance.” Some U.S.-based AI companies use knowledge distillation to develop smaller models from larger teacher models, but approaches vary. Smaller models may also be pretrained independently or developed through a mix of techniques. Large-scale pretraining remains computationally intensive, while distillation and post-training are important parts of the model-development process. Chole said the largest models continue to push toward trillion-parameter scales, while models intended for devices or local AI are often distilled into smaller versions. “It’s not like suddenly we’re going to have 100-billion-parameter models breaking all the benchmark records,” he said. He cited an effort to distill a 400-billion-parameter DeepSeek-C model into an 8-billion-parameter Qwen model, while noting that model distillation itself is not new. The broader point is that users now have many choices across model size, capability, and deployment method, and the largest model is not necessarily the right choice for every task. On Hugging Face, the ‘GitHub for AI models’, there have been approximately 250 open-weight models released in the last two years by major companies, not including quantized variants or models from smaller companies, Chole noted. But abundance is not the same as readiness, and turning this expanding model catalog into useful design intelligence requires EDA teams to supply trusted domain data, workflow context and rigorous ground truth. From general-purpose models to EDA workflows Whether commercial or open-source, general-purpose LLMs aren’t built for chip design tasks, according to Thomas Andersen, vice president for AI and machine learning at Synopsys . “A lot of them are very good at common tasks. They’re very good at creating PowerPoints and summarizing things. They’re good at coding, obviously, because there’s a lot of code out there. Those have been optimized to death. They’re not necessarily well suited to hardware development, not even the RTL coding, because even the RTL that’s out there is just not nearly as much as software. Because of that, every party, including EDA vendors and customers, needs to add their data, and that data is obviously proprietary. This is the difference versus all these models that take public knowledge and put it into the training data. There are both pre- and post-training capabilities, even beyond the weights themselves, where you can add data, and that’s an important key point. Otherwise, it just doesn’t work. It’s like asking a chatbot a question. It doesn’t always give the right answer because it has conflicting data, searches the internet, and people say all kinds of things. What’s the ground truth?” Accurate results rely on both the query and the quality of the source data. “The source data itself needs to be very clear, very crisp,” Andersen said. “On the internet, it doesn’t exist. You go on Reddit, people will say five different things when you ask them a question. That becomes the problem of the LLM. In our case, we obviously need very crisp data. In a corporate environment, it’s different. You have much better documentation of processes, of tools, and so on, so it’s a little bit easier. Without that, it doesn’t work. Still, general training of run-of-the-mill models is absolutely required.” That said, open-weight models will have a place in chip design. “An open-weight model simply means you have an LLM model where you can train the weights of the model,” Andersen explained. “Agentic is a loop that sits around this LLM and then does certain tas

events.title: Agentic AI Alters The CPU-GPU Balance
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert architectures, and reservoir computing are changing how AI workloads use compute resources. Agentic AI is particularly popular, and because it requires more CPU, CPU supply is coming under pressure. Mixture-of-experts models are becoming very popular, enabling specialized queries that require fewer parameters to load. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and large language models (LLMs) have dominated commercial AI for some time. Proprietary recommender models for companies such as Meta have also had significant societal impact even though only one company employs each such model. GPUs perform the heavy lifting for many of those types of models. But agentic AI needs more orchestration, and that’s a job for CPUs. When AI’s only job is to run a model, it turns to GPUs or dedicated neural processing units (NPUs). Agents still use these models, but each is only part of the solution. Those agents must make decisions based on what the models return, and that requires if-then-else logic, and that’s what CPUs are good at. GPUs, not so much. According to some industry estimates, agentic workloads could alter the ratio of CPUs to GPUs from 1:4 to as low as 1:1. Newer model types are also emerging, most of which are still based on LLM fundamentals. Unlike agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert (MoE) models, and reservoir computing still rely on GPUs. But they’re also ripe for use by agents. Pixels and parsing For several years, practical, commercial AI meant CNNs and recurrent neural networks, or RNNs. The former were good at analyzing camera input, while the latter were proficient at analyzing sound and language. The second “L” in LLM means “language,” but LLMs do much more than language today. The notion is that some piece of text is abstracted into a token, and now practically anything can be a token. The benefit of LLMs over RNNs is that they can maintain an arbitrarily long context, making them better at picking the right words when interpreting and generating text. In addition to requiring fewer resources, RNNs can analyze incoming frames of sound immediately without waiting to establish context, improving real-time response. The challenge with early LLMs was that they had one job — to predict a likely next word in a sequence. That word had to make sense syntactically, but not necessarily semantically, and it certainly didn’t check facts to ensure correctness, hence the frequent “hallucinations.” One way to improve that was through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of just figuring out a word that could maybe work, models could access “embeddings” that contained real facts, helping generate text that was both syntactically, semantically, and factually correct. Secret agent man Today’s hot topic is, of course, agentic AI. An agent is a new entity, not one that replaces or modifies an LLM (or any other model). It effectively represents a higher level of abstraction, acting as an orchestrator of models. It’s not a model itself, although it must be trained. “There is some new research out there that says agentic inference is going to dwarf everything else put together before it,” said Ed Doe, CEO and co-founder of Delos Data. The whole point of an agent is that it does more than find an answer to a question. It does something with that answer. What it does will likely depend on the answers it’s received so far. In other words, it can send tokens to a model and, when it receives the result, decide what to do next, embarking on a sequence of decisions and actions. A well-trained agent is meant to handle a set of tasks without tight supervision. “If, as a leader, you have to tell your team every step to accomplish, you’re going to be more consumed with every step of the way,” explained Rob Knoth, product management director, digital and signoff group at Cadence . “But if you say, ‘I need you to go over there and get this work done,’ then you can go focus on another task, occasionally looking over to make sure that things are going well.” This is a new space. “Since last year, agentic AI took off,” noted Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm . “Now you can say, ‘I want to go to Costa Rica for 10 days. I need hotels, car rental, and entry tickets for these parks. Here is my budget. Go and reserve all of that.’ You give it an outline, just like to a travel agent, then the agent calls APIs to take action on your behalf.” A new job for CPUs An agent’s decisions typically involve if-then-else branching, and that’s not what GPUs are good at. CPUs do far better at such decision-heavy code, so they’re becoming a more important part of the computing cluster. For typical LLMs, they mainly serve as hosts, setting things up and managing communication through PCI for things like scale-out. That’s a relatively light CPU load, allowing it to handle host duties for multiple GPUs at the same time. The ratio of CPUs to GPUs will vary by system, but it’s around 1:4 for typical LLMs. With agents, CPUs will be far busier doing actual work (rather than just enabling the GPUs to do work). So while the GPU has been the belle of the ball for a long time, CPUs are getting renewed respect as the CPU: GPU ratio moves closer to 1:1. That will also raise demand for CPUs, which can nudge prices upward. “The challenge used to be how many AI accelerators we can get per CPU,” said Ron Lowman, strategic marketing manager for IP at Synopsys . “With agentic AI, there’s more CPU load demand, and therefore the ratios have changed.” Bhattacharjee agreed. “Demand for CPU has risen a lot because everyone is looking for a lot more compute and in a power-efficient way to run these agents,” he said. “In the last 18 months, everyone is clamoring over agentic AI,” said Yong Meng Sua, CTO at QCI. “This is why CPUs are getting very expensive right now.” “The CPU is back, but is being used in a very different way than it was used in the rest of the data center,” Doe said. Agentic queries are also more compute-intensive because, instead of just one query, sending a request to an agent typically results in many queries as the agent completes its series of tasks. More advanced agents must also understand sequencing, and that can be programmed. “There is a programming part as well,” Arm’s Bhattacharjee said. “You can run JSON scripts to tune it and sequence it. There’s a lot more that can be done with agents.” Show your work The other challenge with early models is that humans can’t understand them. Models are a big cloud of numbers, and no single number can realistically be tied to anything physical or factual. The weights achieved during training aren’t sacrosanct. Training starts with random weights that get refined over many passes. Start with a different random assignment and the training will evolve to a different — and yet still correct — model. events.title: Riots erupt in Albania's capital as students join anti-government movement
events.summary: Riots have broken out during a student demonstration in Albania’s capital Tirana TIRANA, Albania -- Protesters in Albania attacked government buildings, banks, businesses and other sites during riots that lasted more than eight hours across the capital Tirana on Wednesday in a violent escalation of an anti-government movement that has staged rallies for months. Hundreds of youths smashed store fronts, set fires and caused damage to at least four government ministry buildings during running battles with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon to try and hold back the crowds. Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries, while 35 people were detained. President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.” The latest demonstrations, continuing for a second day, were organized by student groups seeking education reforms. But the protesters have joined a broader anti-government campaign opposed to a development project linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The so-called flamingo movement is calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama over allegations of widespread corruption. The movement earned the name after protesters used signs depicting the pink bird. Rallies staged for months against the proposed coastal project have fueled political tensions in Albania , which is aspiring to join the European Union. It has struggled with repeated bouts of instability since the collapse of a harsh communist regime in the early 1990s. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say 2 women found dead in suitcases leads to multistate hunt for killer Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia On Wednesday, officers in riot gear clashed with youths who dismantled police cordons and set up their own street barricades using burning trash bins. Police struggled to cope with the multiple outbreaks of violence. Health Minister Klodiana Spahiu, who visited the injured officers in hospital, called the violence “intolerable.” The EU delegation in Albania called for a proportionate response from authorities following protest organizers' “allegations of excessive violence by the police against protestors and journalists.” “We express concern on the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana,” the delegation said. “Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values.” ___ Cimili reported from Pristina, Kosovo, and Gatopoulos reported from Athens, Greece. events.title: How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Autonomous chip design is advancing, but human engineers remain essential — at least for now. Systems companies are pressuring EDA to shorten chip design cycles so they can keep pace with rapidly changing AI workloads. Advanced packaging, physical AI, and digital twins require broader co-analysis and co-design for multiphysics. Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys , sat down with Semiconductor Engineering to discuss how AI is transforming chip design and engineering. What follows are excerpts from a keynote interview at SEMICON West this week, which was conducted before a live audience. SE: The big change over the past year, and really the big story right now, is AI. We’re processing more AI data. Chips need to run faster. They need to run cooler. Do we really need to rethink how we’re developing these chips? Ghazi : Absolutely. Actually, we started talking about how to re-engineer engineering, because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections, starting at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack? SE: So where does AI actually fit into chip design? We’ve been dealing with computational software since what, the 1980s? Ghazi : Yes. Around the 2016 time frame, we introduced reinforcement learning in a number of our technologies and tools to take advantage of a large space of parameters that you need to optimize, and to use AI to assist the human engineer in optimizing that large space. Today, we’ve moved from an assistant to an actual orchestration of multiple task agents. We have more than 40 task agents. Those task agents are experts of the tools, where you feed them all the knowledge, the capabilities that the tools need in order to optimize for a certain outcome. So those are specific task agents. The magic that has happened over the last year or so is the advancement in intelligence and reasoning of these models. You have long-horizon orchestration, where these models can orchestrate multiple agents, and all you have to do is give it an outcome you’re trying to achieve. That’s where we are today. So it is truly amazing the progress that we’ve made. SE: Where do you see this going? We’ve gone from GenAI over the past four years to Agentic AI. What comes next? Ghazi : You can look at it this way. We started from an assistant copilot, to generative capability, to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome, and you expect that model is able to reason and trigger actions for multiple agents to achieve that task. So it’s autonomous engineering. Now the question typically comes up then, ‘What happens to the human engineer? What is the role that they play, and is that a risk for the industry?’ Actually, I don’t see it that way at all. Today, there’s a massive demand for more companies to define and specialize silicon, to customize silicon. And if you think about the challenges that the industry is having, it’s the shortage of human engineers to be able to architect, take a spec, define the silicon, and drive toward an outcome. So the whole autonomous orchestration is a very positive thing for the industry, where you still need the human judgment to define the architecture, to guide, and to sign off the final check before you go into product manufacturing. SE: At the Converge conference earlier this year, some of the big chipmakers said that they will be able to develop chips with no human in the loop. Is that realistic? And if so, where does the human play? Is it a matter of, ‘Check this, make sure it’s accurate, it actually works as I expect?’ Ghazi : That’s the ambition. Today, we do have a number of engagements and technologies where you can start with a spec. The spec comes from a system company. The system company can be — think of any hyperscaler, any frontier AI lab, any EV automotive, drone. Think of a system company defining a spec. That spec is based on the end product. At some point, you need to translate it into the electronic spec. Today, we have engagements where the customer can provide a spec to Synopsys Autonomous Agent, and it moves it to a verified RTL, which is the starting point for the chip design. That process used to take many months for many human engineers, to go from the spec to writing the RTL, verifying the RTL, and ensuring that it can be physically implemented and manufactured. So today we have that step being done autonomously. We have it. We have a number of customers engaged in it now. With the intelligence and the reasoning, can it expand into the physical implementation, physical verification, into the sign-off of the chip? I have no doubt we’ll get there. Is this here today? No. Is there an ambition to have more autonomy in that workflow? Absolutely. SE: So do agents now become the new IP? Ghazi : Maybe a different way to ask the question is, ‘What will be the core IP for Synopsys? Is it the tool itself? Is it the agent who is the expert on the tool and needs the tool in order to perform a task?’ So today, the model is fantastic at reasoning and exploring. You still need the tool, i.e., the agent, in order to generate and to validate. Because you can generate an outcome, you can explore many design options and possibilities. events.title: Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics
events.summary: By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich The CPO revolution is at our doorstep. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture, power delivery, mechanical design, and thermal management. Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments. Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments. Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro-ring-based CPO, we want to address it head-on. Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale. Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds Let’s start with the new multi-chip package (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate. This architecture enables a full-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs. UCIe-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I/O chiplets over the MCP substrate. UCIe-A, on the other hand, is used for communication between the I/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges. The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm, housing: 2 XPUs (25.69mm x 32.40mm each) 8 HBM4 memory modules 4 I/O chiplets 8 TeraPHY optical engines (12.5mm x 13.0mm each) The +3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors. This complex multi-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging. The design uses a 9-2-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements. The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large-scale package. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements. What is thermal co-simulation and why is it important? Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip. It lets designers predict temperatures, hotspots, and reliability issues in integrated circuits (ICs) and packages under realistic operating conditions. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications. This is critical for successful deployment. In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine. Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows. In our joint analysis, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance. Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor. Rather than avoiding the hard questions, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns. These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels. This testing allows us to do just that. Thermal co‑sim testing We performed three simulations: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component, plus testing of two different cooling solutions. One solution met spec, and one did not. 3D VC heatsink test We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m/s and 6 m/s at 25ºC. Fig. 1: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using heatsink. This did not meet spec, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I/O die. Thermal resistance analysis We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect (CoWoS-L) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec. Fig. 2: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO Thermal Resistance (Rsa) analysis. The system-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA-ASIC is ≤ 0.008 K/W and RSA-OE is ≤ 0.15 K/W. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance. Cold plate test Finally, we tested an impingement-type cold plate thermal solution at 4.5 LPM. Fig. 3: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using cold plate. This solution did meet spec. All components were below the temperature specifications. Cold plate details We selected the impingement-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel-channel designs. The design uses optimized fin dimensions (thickness: 0.15mm, height: 2.4mm for the ASIC and 3.0mm for the optical engine) with thermal interface materials (K=5.2 W/mK) to achieve the required thermal performance. This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits. Key Results Determined the thermal resistance design targets for each chiplet for thermal sign-off constraints: HBM4 < 95ºC SoC < 125ºC Optical Engine < 100ºC Mapped the location of thermal hotspots. Showed that a traditional air heatsink does not work for this solution. Demonstrated that a real-world liquid cooling device meets the specifications needed. These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment. events.title: Everyone has the same question in the midterms — where's the beef? (And how much does it cost?)
events.summary: In the midterm elections, meat has become a surprising political battleground In the midterm elections , meat is on the menu. As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war , they're also having a food fight over who's the most red-blooded carnivore. The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, “you know you have so many proteins to choose from.” The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, “Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead.” The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it's the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they're culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough. In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico boasted that his campaign, then for the Texas statehouse, was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he's not a real Texan. In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed. Rutinel, 31, is now running against Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th district, which includes a vast swath of the northeastern part of the state dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat “as little as possible.” Rutinel, who's made a point of publicly eating steak tacos on the campaign trail, scoffed at such arguments. “I don't think Coloradans care about what's on my plate, I think they care more about what's on theirs,” Rutinel said in an interview after a recent campaign stop. Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel's meal preferences. “I don't care what he eats personally,” Evans said in an interview. “I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way.” Republicans have gone after two other Democratic House candidates on meat — hammering Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd district, an area filled with hog farms, for supporting “meatless May” in a 2020 Facebook post, and Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st district for his longstanding vegetarianism and animal rights activism. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Also in Iowa, Republican Senate candidate and current Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. “He’d rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms,” she said at a campaign appearance. Democrats have hammered on meat as well, but mainly just as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters' pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally. However, those moves have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office. That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former state agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom's video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the “pick another senator” line in the spot — is running a longshot challenge in Mississippi. A spokesman for Hyde-Smith's campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. “It is Scott Colom who supports Biden-era policies that drove up inflation,” said Nathan Calvert. Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

events.title: AI job losses set to rein in office demand in developed Asia-Pacific economies: report
events.summary: CBRE says 3.9 per cent of office jobs in developed parts of region are vulnerable to replacement by artificial intelligence A mild displacement of jobs across the Asia-Pacific region as companies expand their use of AI would trim five percentage points off growth in office space demand in the next few years, according to property consultancy CBRE. In a report released on Thursday it said 3.9 per cent of office jobs were vulnerable to artificial intelligence-driven displacement in developed markets in the region, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Australia and New Zealand. However, only 1.7 per cent were similarly vulnerable in developing markets, including mainland China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. CBRE’s head of Asia-Pacific research, Ada Choi, said in an interview that occupied office space was still projected to grow under a moderate-displacement scenario, “but at a slower pace of 13 per cent” by 2030 – 5 percentage points less than under the consultancy’s base case, which assumed firms in the region would incorporate AI-related productivity gains without job displacement.

events.title: The Nordics and NVIDIA Show What’s Possible When a Region Commits to Advanced Computing
events.summary: The Nordic countries have become the European leader in unicorn startup density, producing the most emerging companies valued at $1 billion or more per capita on the continent. Now, a new chapter for the region is unfolding as countries race to build one of Europe’s most consequential technology ecosystems. The many computing advancements already underway in the Nordics, combined with the opportunity that lies ahead, signal a region moving from ambition to application. NVIDIA’s Investments in the Nordics Over the past year, NVIDIA has invested in the technology ecosystem in the Nordics, including Sweden’s leading startups Lovable and Legora. Lovable , a Stockholm-based startup, provides a software creation platform that enables anyone to build and run software using plain language. In collaboration with NVIDIA, Lovable is optimizing inference for open models and training its models using NVIDIA Dynamo software and Nemotron tools. Legora provides an agentic operating system for legal work, supporting lawyers in research, review and drafting across complex matters. Nordics Emerge as Infrastructure Hub The foundation for establishing the Nordics as a technology powerhouse is already being built and the region holds a structural advantage: abundant renewable energy, rigorous data governance and a research tradition that bridges academia and industry. The Nordics are one of Europe’s fastest growing hubs for infrastructure. AI clouds are expanding with a projected 1 gigawatts of capacity to be deployed across the region by the end of 2027. Among these cloud providers are Bitdeer, CoreWeave , Crusoe , Hyperstack, Nscale , Verda and Volta . In Sweden, a consortium anchored by Ericsson, AstraZeneca, Saab, SEB and Wallenberg Investments, with SKF as strategic partner, launched Sferical One — a shared supercomputer running on two NVIDIA DGX SuperPODs with 16 racks of NVIDIA DGX GB300 systems and 1,152 GPUs. The consortium will build services using NVIDIA Nemotron open models, which allow researchers to customize and deploy their models in a secure environment. Some of the Nordics’ leading technology companies are now building proprietary intelligence on NVIDIA infrastructure. Spotify , which personalizes music, podcasts and audiobooks for hundreds of millions of listeners, uses NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM inference software to run AI-powered podcast recommendations faster and cheaper at scale. The deployment is a case study in inference efficiency: delivering the same recommendations to a global audience at a lower cost per query. ABB Robotics developed RobotStudio HyperReality using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bridge the gap between robot simulations and real-world performance. By combining NVIDIA’s advanced simulation capabilities with ABB Robotics’ virtual controller, running the same firmware as its physical robots, the solution enables engineers to train, test and validate robots virtually, while using real-world data to continuously improve the digital model. According to ABB Robotics, the solution delivers up to 99% simulation accuracy and reduces commissioning time by up to 80%. Finnish telecom company Elisa is launching a beta of Moontalk AIRI, a real-time enterprise agentic assistant that retrieves information, captures insights and documents decisions during meetings and calls. Built on NVIDIA Nemotron open models and distributed infrastructure, it uses company data and low-latency networking to deliver fast, context-aware responses. Sweden’s startup ecosystem raised $2.8 billion in the first half of 2026 and is projected to reach $5 billion for the year. This next generation is building fast — and on open models. Stilta is reinventing how companies protect their inventions with intellectual property. The Stockholm-based startup is post-training NVIDIA Nemotron open models to scale patent analysis from a single patent to entire portfolios — work that was previously out of reach. Nemotron gives Stilta the language model accuracy for continuous portfolio monitoring at scale, across the thousands of patents that large industrial and technology companies hold. ConfidentialMind’s SampoTron , built on NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed, delivers more than 20% improvement in cross-lingual retrieval accuracy across English, Finnish and Swedish. Agaton , a platform that analyzes customer conversations in real time, is using NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to speed up Revenue Mining solution on live sales calls. By routing knowledge retrieval to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Agaton can cut response latency to deliver fast responses that inform customers’ buying decisions. Klang , a Swedish speech lab, fine-tuned the NVIDIA Parakeet v3 model to create Pianissimo — a Swedish transcription model that reduces errors by 75% while being 64x faster than the most accurate alternative. Built on over 50,000 hours of Swedish speech using the open source NVIDIA NeMo framework, the model is freely available on Hugging Face. Embedl , founded in Gothenburg and a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups, and Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled an onboard prototype that monitors protein crystallization, flags anomalies and recommends actions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module, without continuous ground connectivity. Sweden AI Factory — one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories — announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises across industries, including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Autonomous Machines on Nordic Roads and Factory Floors In Sweden, advanced computing is also powering vehicles on the road and machines in factories. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA Hyperion , Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Autonomous freight company Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using the NVIDIA Halos safety system and NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. Meanwhile, Toyota Material Handling Europe — the world’s leading forklift manufacturer — is bringing autonomous machines to factory floors. In a collaboration with NVIDIA and SoftServe, Toyota Material Handling Europe is adopting a simulation-first approach to autonomous material handling, cutting autonomous solution deployment time by up to 50% across its global engineering, manufacturing and innovation teams. Norrsken Foundation and NVIDIA are opening the Stockholm AI Lab, a physical hub for AI-native founders working on global challenges, set to open in 2027. Quantum Meets Accelerated Computing Finally, Swedish companies are advancing quantum research using NVIDIA’s quantum computing platform.

events.title: Roller coaster rider's death puts spotlight on the safety of ever more thrilling rides
events.summary: A man's death on a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia has raised questions about ride safety and regulation The horrific death of a man who was ejected from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia is drawing attention to the safety of amusement park rides that have become increasingly faster and steeper in their quest for the biggest thrill. Fatal roller coaster accidents are extremely rare, and Georgia officials have said little about why Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, was thrown from his seat on Monday while riding the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia, striking other patrons before falling below the ride. Four other passengers, all minors, suffered injuries that were not life-threatening, Cobb County police said. Goliath sends riders plunging from 200 feet (61 meters) at speeds reaching 70 mph (112 kph). Rather than upside-down loops and corkscrews, the two-decade-old coaster focuses on velocity and downhill plunges. Six Flags temporarily closed nine similar coasters across North America as a precaution. The ride's manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard, said it was “actively investigating the incident and will not comment further until we have a better understanding of what happened.” To his family, Kariem was a beloved and intelligent man who died during an outing with people he loved. “He was just a great, smart guy,” said She Robinson, who identified herself as Kariem’s cousin. “He was a gentle giant that everybody loved.” He loved Atlanta and Six Flags Over Georgia, Robinson said, and was visiting the park Monday with his significant other, her daughter and her niece, Robinson said. Another cousin, Kelvin Johnson, described Kariem as kind and considerate. “He’s just a very helpful, positive kind of person," Johnson said. "He’s that person that would step up first to volunteer for anything.” The federal government does not regulate roller coasters at major amusement parks. Instead, oversight falls to states, creating what some call a patchwork of rules that range from strict regulations to minimal oversight. U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly sought to close what he calls a federal safety “loophole” that allows the Consumer Product Safety Commission to regulate traveling carnival rides but not stationary attractions at major parks. Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections, is “conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review” of Monday's death, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson. Amusement parks worldwide generally adhere to what are known as ASTM standards set by industry experts, which cover everything from ride design and construction to how much acceleration and force each rider is allowed to experience. The industry has multiple layers of inspection, said Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group. Park operators are under pressure from insurance carriers that could face a hefty payout if something goes wrong. “With the checks and balances that are put in place, theme parks are really one of the safest places to be on the planet,” he said Tuesday. Industry figures show 1.27 serious and reportable injuries per million roller coaster rides in 2024. Across all amusement park rides, the trade group said “guest behavior” contributed to 66% of the injuries that year, with 15% due to technical factors and 9% to operational factors. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded The trade group's current president, Jakob Wahl, offered condolences to Kariem's family Wednesday. Martin Lewison, a roller coaster expert and a professor at Farmingdale State College, said it was difficult to imagine there being a mechanical malfunction on a roller coaster such as Goliath because of its design. The ride features a pull-down lap restraint called a “clamshell” that works with a ratchet mechanism that makes clicking sounds as you press it down over your hips. They have multiple disks to ensure redundancy if one fails, Lewison said. “They’re dependable. They’re not so technically advanced that theme parks have difficulty with operations,” Lewison said. The operator then has a safety system that displays a green “go” light for every seat on the train before it can be dispatched. The train should theoretically not be allowed to proceed unless all restraints are locked, Lewison said. In 2022, a 14-year-old Missouri boy fell to his death from an Orlando amusement park ride when the harness didn't lock properly due to his size. In 2013, a 52-year-old Dallas woman was killed when she slipped from her seat on the Texas Giant ride at Six Flags Over Texas.

events.title: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons consider leaving UK as tax concerns mount
events.summary: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found. The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth. Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth. The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The mass departure of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE , Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US. The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs. CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says. Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai -based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”. “UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National . Tax overhauls intensify debate Under the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains. Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules. The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon. UAE leads inquiry list Enquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds. Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent. Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. A further 21.9 per cent concerned residency, relocation or visas, while 13.9 per cent related to wealth structures such as trusts, foundations and holding companies, data shows. “ Tax efficiency may start the conversation, but it is rarely enough to complete the move,” Mr Gordon says, before adding that the UAE’s connectivity, business infrastructure and access to markets across the Middle East, Asia and Africa appeal to families seeking a commercial base. Switzerland and Singapore offer established wealth management sectors, while Portugal and Malta continue to attract those seeking European residency and lifestyle benefits. Across all UK-origin enquiries to the group, 42 per cent referenced business or company set-up, while 28.9 per cent involved wealth or succession planning. The UK-origin enquiries have averaged about 19 per cent of the group’s total leads over the past four years, according to Mr Gordon. Meanwhile, the broader migration outlook remains significant. Henley & Partners and New World Wealth forecast a record 165,000 millionaire relocations worldwide in 2026, with the UAE expected to remain the leading destination for inflows. For Britain, the challenge is to balance tax reform with its ability to retain mobile investors and entrepreneurs. For the UAE, the opportunity is to convert initial interest into durable investment and economic activity. “The UAE’s long-term challenge is not simply to attract wealthy residents, but to convert initial tax and residency interest into enduring business activity, investment and family connections,” Mr Gordon says.
